A full return to concerts in front of audiences was undetermined, however, until March.

"This year, I'm getting the best gift of my life. I'm getting the chance to see you, to perform for you once again, in Paris," Dion wrote on her social media, announcing the residency on her 58th birthday.

The initial series of 16 concerts in September and October will be followed by 10 additional shows starting in May of 2027, all at Europe's biggest indoor concert venue, Plenitude Arena.

Dion fan to see their 100th show

As Estevam Peric landed in Paris, he says he felt a rush of emotions.

There was fatigue from the overnight flight from Montreal certainly, but mainly, he says he felt overwhelmingly excited.

The self-proclaimed Dion superfan made the trek across the Atlantic to see his favourite celebrated diva — for the 100th time.

Estevam Peric, a self-proclaimed Céline Dion superfan, says he travelled to Paris to see the singer for the 100th time. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

"I'm very, very, nervous, very excited, very emotional," Peric said, holding back tears.

"It's the soundtrack of my life. I've been following her since my teenage era, and each song, each album, there's always something special that connects to my life each time."

He says he's met Dion at least 10 times, describing her as humble and kind. Every concert is different, he says.

"The voice, it's like oxygen and the rest is just magic."

Peric has managed to snag tickets for seven of her concerts in Paris, which is no easy feat as all the performances quickly sold out. The arena has a capacity of up to 45,000 seats.

Dion waves to fans as she exits the Royal Monceau hotel in Paris on Sept. 3, ahead of a series of concerts in the French capital. (Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images)

Lead-up to first concert filled with excitement

Dion's love affair with France spans decades. French songwriter Eddy Marnay was among one of the very first to work alongside a teenage Dion. She also has a penchant for fashion, often partnering with French haute couture labels, like Dior and Chanel.

"I understand she's a huge star in Quebec, but here she's also a very big star because she's the only star at her level to have lots of great songs, both in English and in French," says Lutaud from Le Figaro.

It's that star power that has so many fans invested in Dion's comeback, with the hope of more concerts to come.

World.title: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The upcoming U.S. midterm elections will determine whether Republican President Donald Trump will be free to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office or whether he'll face constraints from a Congress where the Democrats hold new power.

Here's what you need to know about the midterms.

Why do U.S. midterms matter?

The midterms are a contest for control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which together make up the U.S. Congress.

The party that controls the Senate holds sway over presidential appointments to cabinet, the courts and senior posts in federal agencies. The party that controls the House can launch impeachment proceedings and has the power to initiate budget bills .

If one party controls both, it has broad influence over legislation as well as the potential to thwart some presidential actions.

How is the race shaping up?

The Democrats are generally excited about their prospects in the midterms and the Republicans a little worried.

History gives the Republicans plenty of reason to fret. The incumbent president's party has suffered a net loss of seats in Congress in all but two midterms since the 1930s. The only exceptions were Bill Clinton (1998) and George W. Bush (2002), when each had sky-high approval ratings.

Trump's approval rating is anything but sky-high .

What's at stake?

With slim majorities in each chamber, the Republicans have little wiggle room to lose seats and still maintain their hold on Congress.

The Democrats need to flip just four districts to take control of the House (if they hold on to all their current seats). The Democrats also need to take just four Republican-held states to win control of the Senate. But that's a tougher task than flipping the House because there are far fewer Senate seats up for election and winning each requires a statewide victory.

A person votes in a primary election in Oak Park, Mich., on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for grabs, as members of the House are elected to two-year terms.

Only 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election this fall. U.S. senators are elected to six-year terms.

When does voting happen?

Midterms, like the word implies, come at the two-year mark of a president's four-year term. This year, midterm election day is Nov. 3.

Many U.S. voters will choose to vote before then, either in advance polls or by mail-in ballots, a method the Trump administration is trying to restrict.

You may also have heard that people across the U.S. have been voting at various times since the spring in primaries, which are the contests to select each party's candidates. In most states, only people who are registered Republicans or Democrats can vote in the party's primaries.

How does Trump factor in?

Trump is not on the ballot in the midterms, but his influence on the campaign will be unavoidable.

Only one president si nce 1950 has headed into a midterm with an approval rating below 40 per cent: George W. Bush in 2006 (at 37 per cent), when his Republicans lost 30 seats in the House and six in the Senate.

Despite his low polling numbers, Trump is vowing to give "a lot of speeches" in states and districts where the races are tight to help Republican candidates. Some of those candidates are quietly asking the White House to keep him away, according to reporting by Politico.

What are the key issues in the midterms?

While U.S. polls differ slightly on the precise numbers, there's a strong thread of consistency suggesting the top issue of concern among voters right now is the cost of living.

Whether it's gas prices pushed up as a result of the war against Iran or the prices of consumer goods rising because of Trump's tariffs, pocketbook issues predominate the midterm polling.

Only one U.S. president since 1950 has held a polling approval rating below 40 per cent on the day of a midterm election. Trump is on track to be the second. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Trump, as the dominant figure in U.S. politics for the past decade, will undoubtedly be an issue, particularly for moderate Republican or swing voters who backed him in the 2024 presidential election but have soured on him since then, according to polling.

Turnout in midterms is always lower than during presidential election years, so each party will be striving for ways to motivate their base. For the Democrats, weakening Trump's power could be that driving force. For the Republicans, stoking fear about what a Democratic-controlled Congress would do to the economy is a key advertising message.

Where are the key Senate races?

Of the 35 Senate seats up for election this time, fewer than 10 are considered by campaign analysts to be at risk of changing hands.

The Republicans are considered most vulnerable in North Carolina and Maine, but polling suggests they also are in tough to hang on to their Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and even Texas, where no Democrat has won a statewide election since 1988.

The Democrats' biggest challenges to hold appear to be in the Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Where are the key House races?

More than 80 per cent of House seats are considered safe for either the Republicans or the Democrats, according to the University of Virginia Center for Politics newsletter Crystal Ball, which has forecast and analyzed every election for U.S. president, House, Senate and state governors since 2002.

That political inertia leaves only a few dozen districts across the country truly "in play," as campaign strategists describe races where the outcome is in doubt.

Crystal Ball has labelled 17 Republican-held districts as toss-ups, including three in Pennsylvania and two in Michigan. All will be races to watch because they're prime targets for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the House.

World.title: Bears, caribou and other animals are messing with this researcher's equipment, and he's got photos to prove it
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher's work: Quirks and Quarks 9:38 How lynx, moose and bears keep destroying this wildfire researcher’s work

Lucas Brehaut was hoping there’d be a lot of interest in his research, though it might be a case of “be careful what you wish for.”

Seemingly every animal in Newfoundland's wilderness wants to know what he's up to — and they're not always gentle with his equipment.

Brehaut, a wildfire research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service, is studying how forests in Atlantic Canada regrow after forest fires. Though the region is cooler and wetter than much of the rest of the country, forest fires are getting more common.

After a forest fire hit south of Grand Falls-Windsor, N.L., in 2022, he set out to understand how forests might regrow on a planet when temperatures are rising due to climate change.

To do that, he and his team needed to lug 19 open-top chambers (OTCs) through the forest and set them up around seedlings they’d planted. OTCs are like mini greenhouses, and look like clear hexagons with an opening at the top. They can increase the temperature anywhere from one to three degrees, mimicking the effects of a warming planet. Brehaut's study is currently in year three of five.

Brehaut says he expected some difficulties — the treks of up to a kilometre in difficult terrain, and the infamously dour Newfoundland weather, for example.

But in September 2023, on one of his regular check-ins, he ran into a problem he didn’t expect.

“That’s when we started to notice that some of these greenhouses had some visitors, and might not have been as strong as I had hoped,” Brehaut said.

Those “visitors” included caribou, moose, black bears, wolves, rabbits and owls. Brehaut found out who the culprits were because of cameras set up around the sites that were originally meant to look at snow depth over the winter.

A black bear dismantles a plexiglass greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Out of 19 sites, 11 have sustained damage at some time or another. And the animals wouldn’t just trample the greenhouses — some made off with the temperature sensors.

“The greenhouses had been completely obliterated. And by obliterated, I’m talking broken, smashed to smithereens,” Brehaut said.

“There were certain times where we would spend more time at a site finding the temperature sensors than we would actually measuring the seedlings themselves.”

In Brehaut’s case, four — not 13 — is the unlucky number.

“I have a site that I specifically call the problem child. Because every time I went to that site, it was damaged in one way or another,” he said.

“It’s site number four, but I call it 'The Problem Child.' Every time I walk to it, I know that it’s going to be challenging.”

But the animals aren't always smashing — they’re grazing. Brehaut has seen moose and rabbits go into the greenhouses for a bite to eat. They even occasionally manage to get through the top of the greenhouses without damaging anything.

A baby moose walks over a mangled mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Brehaut isn’t mad, just disappointed. He hopes that the animals are enjoying themselves, even if it’s at the expense of his research.

“You see the amount of joy that, potentially, a black bear is experiencing by actually sitting in a greenhouse and playing with that plastic, and taking that temperature sensor and moving it,” he said.

“Yes, the research gets damaged to some capacity, but we’re in nature. This is their habitat. We are only visitors to this spot.”

A caribou rests near a mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

What are you doing in my backyard?

That's exactly why some animals are so keen to mess with equipment, says Kaitlyn Gaynor, an assistant professor at the University of British Columbia.

"If someone puts something weird in your backyard, wouldn’t you want to go investigate it?" she said.

Gaynor, who studies the impacts of human disturbance on animal behaviour, said intelligent animals are especially curious about anything novel in their environment. After all, it could be a new source of food, or it could pose a threat. This boldness and willingness to explore could have been an advantage as species evolved.

Bears are a great example, Gaynor says.

"It’s in their nature to be curious about whether new objects are resources to be exploited," she said.

"They’re these generalist omnivores that will eat a whole bunch of different things, and so when they see something new, the first question is like, is this food?"

A black bear walks by a plexiglass mini greenhouse in Newfoundland. Kaitlyn Gaynor, a professor at the University of British Columbia, said bears are especially curious about new objects in their ecosystem. (Submitted by Lucas Brehaut)

Also, there's the smell factor — we stink.

"Often these objects we leave behind have our scent on them, and so our scent might attract animals to these places and to these objects," Gaynor said.

She added that researchers can lessen the effect of research on animals by getting in and out of the field as quickly as possible, by leaving as little scent as possible, and by obscuring or camouflaging research equipment.

Down in Africa

Animals interfering with research is a worldwide phenomenon.

Gaynor has seen a lot of it during field work in Mozambique.

"Baboons are always coming up to the cameras. We get a lot of great baboon selfies," she said.

"Hyenas just want to chew on everything, so they’ll chew on our research equipment."

A baboon takes a selfie in Mozambique on one of Kaitlyn Gaynor's research cameras. (Submitted by Kaitlyn Gaynor)

But the worst offenders are the elephants. They like to knock down trees and feast on leaves, which is bad news for research equipment.

"Elephants are also just highly intelligent, and curious, and very large and destructive," she said.

Gaynor said animals are her biggest cause of equipment loss or failure.

"It’s not that the electronics go out, and it’s not that things get stolen by people, it’s that animals tend to be a little bit destructive."

Hartebeests stare at one of Kaitlyn Gaynor's research cameras in Mozambique. Gaynor says animal interference is the biggest factor for equipment loss. (Submitted by Kaitlyn Gaynor)

But, to be fair, Brehaut has also had issues with that most destructive animal — the homo sapien.

"We've had some visitors accidentally run over these sites in the winter," he said.

"We have an extremely snowy winter in Newfoundland, and snowmobiles basically went over one of my plots."

World.title: A million-dollar math problem may just be the beginning for OpenAI
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two mathematicians, 10,000 AI agents and a million-dollar prize are all part of yet more AI drama this week, with heated back-and-forth over allegations of stolen work and academic malpractice.

But despite the controversy, some experts say it's indicative of the unmistakable force of artificial intelligence in helping break through sticky problems. To others, it misses the point of academic research and careful human collaboration.

So what happened in the world of pure mathematics this week and why is it controversial?

The claim

On Tuesday, OpenAI said it had solved a legendary problem in mathematics involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

Easier said than explained, the equations describe how fluids — including gases and liquids — move and change over time. As equations do, they give us a way to try to predict what will happen if you plug in the variables. The issue — and why this is one of the famed Millennium Prize Problems that come with a million-dollar award if a solution is verified — is not knowing exactly whether the math can blow up and produce physically impossible results.

The Navier-Stokes equations deal with predicting the behaviour of fluids. (Ben Margot/The Associated Press)

"It's a very deep mystery," said Ravi Vakil, mathematics professor at Stanford University. "It seems this huge thing that's out of reach, like this mountain you see in the distance, and the question is: can we get there?"

Vakil says it's a way to understand the universe and whether it works the way we think it does. The problem with Navier-Stokes is kind of like saying you can know everything about your foot, your shoe and a ball — but there's no ruling out you can kick that ball into space.

So "resolving" the problem is about figuring out whether this breakdown can happen. OpenAI says yes: in a certain circumstance, you can get a bonkers, physics-violating result — at least, on paper.

Moreover, the task "involved on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents" — AI that can perform tasks independently and doesn't need to be prompted constantly — that "had access to tools such as the ability to read from a cached version of the internet and the ability to run code."

OpenAI says this 3D model of a vortex visually describes how the equations can lead to a 'breakdown.' (OpenAI)

Within 88 hours, the company said, its agents had found the solution to this problem, which has roots going back more than 200 years. It's worth mentioning that while this problem is a curiosity, the equations are used for practical applications including the design of airplanes, artificial heart valves and climate modelling.

Vakil isn't surprised the company was able to achieve it, but is still impressed, though he and other experts point out that the claim now needs to be rigorously verified.

"No one is yet ready to fully vouch for all the details because that requires human time," Vakil, who is originally from Toronto, told CBC News from Stanford, California.

"It passes machine checks, but we know better than to believe those."

WATCH | AI factors into lower scores for students: Experts blame AI, screens for slipping Canadian student test scores | Duration 2:05 While Canadian students still perform well globally in math, science and reading, scores have dipped significantly in recent years. Some educational experts blame the rising overuse of AI and too much screen time.

The counterclaim

The controversy began before OpenAI announced its findings and involved two other mathematicians, Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works for OpenAI competitor Anthropic.

Among other things, Buckmaster — who used AI tools such as Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex — suggested OpenAI learned the pair were close to a solution and pursued it themselves. He alleged OpenAI tried to offer him credit so long as Alpöge's name wasn't on it because he works for a competing AI company.

At the time, he said he didn't get a response when he asked if OpenAI's agents had been able to see his own use of its Codex tool before coming up with their solution.

OpenAI acknowledges pursuing the solution after hearing rumours of a potential solution. But it denies its internal system of agents learned from their work , saying after an investigation, it "confirmed that Buckmaster's Codex prompts … could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training."

To Davide Gaiotto, who specializes in theoretical and mathematical physics at the Perimeter Institute in Waterloo, Ont., it's the modern version of an age-old problem. He uses an example of a professional seminar where you hear about upcoming research.

"Normally, this would require you to be so fast and capable that you can see what they told you at the seminar and use it to do the final step," Gaiotto said. But now, it may soon be possible to use AI tools to leap faster and farther off those giants' shoulders, so to speak.

WATCH | The next wave of AI doesn't need you to prompt it: AI agents could change how you use the internet | Duration 6:39 OpenAI and other big tech companies are starting to roll out the next wave of artificial intelligence, designed to operate with more autonomy. CBC’s Nora Young breaks down how agentic AI works and why some think it will change how you use the internet.

"Because if you have enough money, you can compress months of work into a few hours," Gaiotto told CBC News.

It's worth noting that this Navier-Stokes work does not exist in a vacuum, and that Buckmaster credits Spanish researchers Diego Córdoba from the Institute for Mathematical Sciences and CUNEF University's Luis Martínez-Zoroa for work on this approach.

The drama, Vakil says, is unfortunate and overshadows the real human accomplishment.

"These are things that people have been chasing for a hundred years that we didn't think would be within reach," Vakil said, "And it's this sequence of people assisted by technology that made something new happen."

Quick math

Buckmaster, in his Sept. 7 statement, said his original intent was to show "the significance that a mathematician and an LLM model can now do all this work in a month."

Vakil agrees that these tools are changing the game.

"I do believe that it's clear we're going through a massive transition in how we do science. And we are among the first mathematicians."

Not everyone is happy with that transition. At least 25 winners of the Fields Medal, one of mathematics' most prestigious awards, signed an open letter saying that AI is "misaligned" with the goals of the mathematical community and a "general threat to intellectual work."

Terence Tao, seen here in November 2014, is among the notable academics calling for better solutions around AI and mathematics. (Steve Jennings/Getty Images)

But the furor over the tools to help answer deep questions perhaps misses a point made by Fields Medal-winning UCLA mathematician Terence Tao: Pure math is driven by curiosity.

In recent social posts, Tao talked about the greater value of not just solving the problem, but seeking what could be learned by studying it. He likens it to kids trying to one-up each other by playing 'who can name the largest number?' The process of exploration is more valuable than the answer.

"In this modern era of heavy AI use, it is important to remember what it is like to be a child," Tao wrote.

World.title: Iraq scrambles to address fallout from alleged militia attack on Saudi oil pipeline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Iraq's government was racing Saturday to contain the fallout after local Iran-backed militias were accused of attacking and shuttering a key Saudi pipeline.

Though an umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied their involvement, Iraq's government confirmed the attacks had originated from its territory. The government pledged to investigate and dismissed a military commander.

The country is under mounting pressure to prevent local militias from aiding other Iran proxy groups across the region. The Iraqi government has set a Sept. 30 deadline for non-state groups to disarm, but several of the most powerful militias have said they will not comply.

Pressure to disarm the militias is especially acute as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels make an advance across Yemen’s west coast in a major setback to the Saudi-backed coalition that risks escalating the war in the region. The Houthis on Friday seized an island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key shipping lane through which about 12 per cent of global trade passes.

Their virtual control of the strait could send global oil prices — already inflated by the six-month Iran-U.S. war — spiralling. The strait has become a vital commercial lane for Saudi oil ever since the Iran war disrupted shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Asked about the region on Saturday while speaking to reporters in Dublin, U.S. President Donald Trump said Iran was "probably" responsible for the pipeline attack but tried to calm concerns.

He said his administration has "had discussions" with the Houthis, though he did not specify to which talks he was referring.

"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us," Trump said. "They would much prefer not having us involved, and they're letting most ships go through."

Iraq to investigate attack on Saudi pipeline

A group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied in a statement on Saturday that they were responsible for the attacks on the East-West crude oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia, while praising the Houthis for their "ongoing battlefield victories against Saudi forces."

The group said it would co-operate with the Iraqi government's investigation.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said earlier Saturday that he'd ordered an investigation into the operations command of Maysan province, along the border with Iran, and dismissed the province's commander.

Saudi Arabia shut down the major, cross-country oil pipeline on Friday, calling it a "precautionary measure" after the pipeline came under drone attack. It blamed the attacks on several drones that came from Iraq but said the kingdom would not retaliate, to give the Iraqi government "an opportunity to take the necessary measures."

Several Arab countries, including Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Oman and Egypt, condemned the attack on Saturday, according to the Saudi state news agency.

Built in the 1980s, the East-West pipeline has played an important role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil following the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. By early June, Saudi Arabia had more than doubled oil exports from the Red Sea port at the pipeline's end to more than five million barrels per day, according to the International Energy Agency.

Tehran-backed Iraqi militias have carried out strikes on U.S.-linked targets both inside and outside of Iraq since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, and have co-ordinated with Yemen's Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia.

Iraq closes border crossings with Iran

In a move possibly linked to the investigation, Iraq closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq's state-run news agency reported Saturday.

The report said that Iraqi officials were at the border, investigating previous "violations and infractions" at the crossings.

Valiollah Hayati, the deputy governor of Iran's southwestern Khuzestan province, named the closed crossings as Shalamcheh and Chazabeh. They are among the main official border crossings between Iran and Iraq.

Iranian state media said the measure would halt all passenger and commercial traffic through the two crossings until further notice.

Saudi Arabia and the United States bombed Iranian-backed militias in Iraq in July after blaming them for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that had been claimed by the Houthis. Regional officials told The Associated Press that the Houthis helped the Iraqi militias plan and execute the attacks.

Fighting threatens to reignite Yemen’s civil war

The escalating fighting threatens to end a fragile truce that had largely halted Yemen's civil war since 2022. At stake are 40 million people in the Arab world's poorest country. The conflict killed 150,000 and brought many others to the brink of famine.

The surge in fighting in the past week has sent more than 46,000 people fleeing, the United Nations migration agency said Friday.

The Houthis have been at war with Yemen's government since 2014, when the rebels seized much of northern and central Yemen and the capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabia entered the war the following year on the side of the government.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
