For expats in Montevideo, the next ten days offer the city’s most family-friendly festival — contemporary circus from Uruguay and abroad, much of it free.

Ten Days of Circus

Uruguay’s International Circus Festival opens its seventh edition on September 17, turning Montevideo into the Southern Cone’s circus capital for ten days — performances, workshops and street programming through September 27.

The festival is the country’s principal showcase for contemporary circus, an art form Uruguay has cultivated seriously for two decades, with companies now touring internationally from a Montevideo base.

A City-Wide Map

The venue list spreads the festival across the city’s geography: the Centro Cultural Terminal Goes in the former bus terminal, Sala Lazaroff, the Teatro Politeama in the center, and the open spaces of Parque Capurro on the western waterfront.

The prestige slot belongs to the Teatro Solís — Uruguay’s great opera house hosting circus, a combination that tells you how seriously the art form is taken here — while the El Picadero big top keeps the classic under-canvas tradition alive.

Contemporary Circus, Explained

Forget the animal-ring cliché: contemporary circus is theater built from acrobatics, aerial silks and trapeze, juggling, clown and physical storytelling — closer to dance-theater than to the circus of childhood memory.

Uruguay’s scene is particularly strong on the ensemble and the poetic — expect shows that are funny, moving and technically astonishing in the same hour.

Free, Hat-Pass and Popular Prices

The festival’s access model is part of its identity: a deliberate mix of free shows, ‘a la gorra’ performances where the hat passes at the end, and popular-priced tickets that keep every production within reach.

For expat families, the practical effect is simple: you can sample the festival all week without planning or budget — check the day’s program, show up, decide at the door.

Why Uruguay Does Circus Well

The country’s circus ecosystem — schools, companies, a supportive ministry and an audience that turns out — has made Montevideo a reference point for the art form in South America.

The festival doubles as the scene’s annual meeting: international programmers attend, Uruguayan companies premiere new work, and the city’s theaters give circus the stages usually reserved for drama and dance.

What Expats Should Know

Language is no barrier — contemporary circus is physical theater, and the festival is the rare Montevideo cultural event where Spanish is genuinely optional.

Programs run through the Ministry of Education and Culture’s channels and the venues’ own listings; for the Teatro Solís and big-top nights, arrive early — the free and gorra shows fill on reputation.

The Terminal Goes Factor

The Centro Cultural Terminal Goes — a working cultural center built inside Montevideo’s former long-distance bus terminal — is the festival’s engine room: multiple spaces, workshops, and the everyday bustle of a building the city actually uses.

For newcomers, it is a destination in itself: the conversion is one of South America’s better examples of infrastructure turned into culture.

A Family Plan That Works

The weekend matinees at Parque Capurro and the big top are designed for children without being childish — the contemporary circus trick of playing to every age in the room at once.

Pair a morning show with the Capurro waterfront and the Mercado del Puerto for lunch: a full Montevideo day with the festival as its spine.

For expats in Montevideo, this is the spring’s first big night out — the region’s indie royalty at the city’s beloved open-air theater by the water.

Indie Royalty on the Rambla

Cruce Fest returns to the Teatro de Verano on Saturday, September 26, pairing the Río de la Plata’s most beloved indie band with its fastest-rising one — El Mató a un Policía Motorizado and Niña Lobo sharing one open-air bill.

The undercard keeps the regional logic: Eté & Los Problems bring the new Uruguayan wave, and DJ Chismosa closes the gaps between sets on the rambla-side stage.

El Mató: The Cult That Filled Stadiums

El Mató a un Policía Motorizado spent two decades as the Southern Cone’s best-kept secret — the La Plata band whose bittersweet indie rock became a shared language across Argentina and Uruguay.

Their songs — ‘Chica de oro’, ‘El tesoro’, ‘Mas o menos bien’ — are sung at Uruguayan parties with the same ferocity as at home, which is why their Montevideo shows read as homecomings.

Niña Lobo’s Moment

Niña Lobo arrives as the scene’s new center of gravity — the Montevideo project that turned bedroom-pop intimacy into festival-scale sing-alongs in a couple of years.

Sharing top billing at the Teatro de Verano marks the local passage of the torch: the city’s own next generation headlining its most storied outdoor room.

The Teatro de Verano

The Teatro de Verano — officially the Ramón Collazo — is Montevideo’s summer stage par excellence: an open-air amphitheater on the rambla in Parque Rodó, with the Río de la Plata behind the audience and the city’s skyline beyond the stage.

Late September is early spring on the river — mild afternoons, cool nights off the water; bring the layer that the sunset will make necessary.

Tickets via Tickantel

Tickantel sells the festival in sectors from UYU 980 to UYU 1,790 — the floor and the favored lateral positions moving first, as always at this venue.

Buy through Tickantel’s site or its physical network; Montevideo’s informal resale scene is small but exists around the Teatro de Verano on sold nights.

What Expats Should Know

This is the gentlest possible entry into the region’s indie culture: one night, two generations of bands, and a crowd that treats concerts as community rather than spectacle.

The venue sits a short ride from Pocitos and Centro — buses run the rambla constantly, and post-show ride-hailing works best a block inland from the main exit flow.

The Río de la Plata Scene

The Buenos Aires–Montevideo axis is one of Latin America’s great indie ecosystems: bands cross the river constantly, audiences know both catalogs, and a festival bill like Cruce Fest is that relationship onstage.

El Mató’s presence guarantees the Argentine contingent in the crowd — the ferry from Buenos Aires makes the night a weekend trip that porteños have made for years.

Spring on the Rambla

The Teatro de Verano season opening is a Montevideo ritual: the city comes out of winter, the rambla fills again, and the first big open-air night of spring doubles as a civic celebration.

Arrive before sunset if you can — the light on the Río de la Plata from the venue’s approaches is the opening act no band can match.

The Festival’s Place in the Year

Cruce Fest has become the hinge of Montevideo’s concert calendar — the night the outdoor season opens and the summer’s Teatro de Verano program effectively begins.

Its booking logic is the city’s own: regional before global, bands before brands, and a price point — from UYU 980 — that keeps the night within a student’s reach.

For expats in Bogotá, the city’s busy September concert month adds the Australian pop-rockers — a Thursday night arena show with one of the genre’s most durable catalogs.

A Thursday Night at the Movistar

5 Seconds of Summer plays Bogotá’s Movistar Arena on Thursday, September 24 — a 9:00 p.m. arena show with doors from 6:00 p.m., landing in the middle of the Colombian capital’s busiest concert season in years.

Tickets run through Tuboleta, the arena’s official platform — the only safe purchase route for a date that has been circled on Colombian fan calendars since its announcement.

The Sydney Quartet, a Decade On

5 Seconds of Summer grew from YouTube cover band to one of Australia’s biggest musical exports — four members, a string of chart-topping albums, and a catalog that moved from pop-punk energy to polished arena pop without losing the hooks.

Songs like ‘Youngblood’, ‘She Looks So Perfect’, ‘Teeth’ and ‘Amnesia’ are generational sing-along material — the kind of setlist where the crowd handles the choruses by reflex.

A Band Built for the Live Room

The group’s reputation rests on the stage show: real instruments, real volume, and a front-of-house energy that converts casual plus-ones by the second song.

Recent tours have leaned into the band’s musicianship — extended arrangements, drum-forward production and the easy chemistry of four players who have shared stages since their teens.

The Movistar Arena Routine

Bogotá’s Movistar Arena, on the Salitre side of the city, is Colombia’s principal indoor concert room — a modern arena with the full rig of international productions and a capacity that keeps big nights feeling big.

Logistics are classic Bogotá: arrive early because Avenida El Dorado traffic stacks up at showtime, use ride-hailing with the official pickup zones, and expect a cool evening — the city sits at 2,600 meters.

Tickets via Tuboleta

Tuboleta handles the sale online and through its physical points; for high-demand international dates, the platform’s queue system opens ahead of the announced time, so log in early with an account already created.

Colombian resale caution applies: buy only through Tuboleta or the venue, since screenshots and PDF tickets from informal sellers are the standard fraud vector at Bogotá’s big shows.

What Expats Should Know

A 5SOS crowd in Bogotá skews young, loud and fully bilingual in its singing — a fun first Colombian arena show even if your Spanish is still in progress.

Altitude is real: if you arrived in Bogotá recently, hydrate through the afternoon, take the stairs slowly, and let the band do the cardio.

Bogotá’s Concert Season

The 5SOS date sits inside the capital’s densest concert stretch of the year — the Movistar Arena’s calendar through December reads like a global touring summary, from rock veterans to reggaetón headliners.

For the local industry, nights like September 24 confirm Bogotá’s status as South America’s second great concert market after São Paulo — a routing stop no major pop tour now skips.

The Fan Culture

Colombia’s 5SOS fandom is organized and devoted — fan projects, coordinated light moments and queue communities that start outside the arena hours before doors.

If you go, join the queue culture rather than fighting it: the early line is where the night starts, and Bogotá’s fans are famously welcoming to foreigners who know the songs.

Why the Timing Works

A Thursday show in late September catches Bogotá at its best: the dry-ish window between the year’s two rainy peaks, cool clear evenings, and the city fully back from the mid-year break.

For visitors pairing the concert with Colombia travel, the date slots neatly before the weekend — fly on to Medellín or the coffee region on Friday, or stay for the city’s own weekend circuit.

For expats in Medellín, this is the vallenato night of the season — one of the genre’s defining voices in the city’s classic bullring-turned-concert-ring.

Vallenato’s Voice Comes to Medellín

Jorge Celedón plays Medellín’s La Macarena on Saturday, September 26 — the ‘La Historia Mía’ tour stopping in Colombia’s second city with the catalog that made him vallenato’s most elegant ambassador.

The 8:00 p.m. show at the Centro de Eventos La Macarena — the city’s historic bullring, now one of its principal concert venues — carries an 18+ rating and tickets through TaquillaLive.

The Man Behind ‘La Historia Mía’

Celedón’s story is the genre’s modern history: the Villanueva kid who sang with Binomio de Oro, then built a solo career that carried vallenato from the Caribbean coast to Latin Grammy stages.

Songs like ‘Ay Hombe’, ‘Que Bonita Es Esta Vida’ and ‘Me Vio Llorar’ are standards — the kind of material a Medellín audience sings from the first accordion phrase.

A Tour Built on Memory

‘La Historia Mía’ is exactly the retrospective the title promises: the hits sequenced as autobiography, with the accordion-driven arrangements that define the genre front and center.

For the uninitiated, the format is the ideal entry point — no deep-catalog homework required, just the songs three decades of Colombian parties were built on.

La Macarena: The Ring as Venue

The Plaza de Toros La Macarena, in the Buenos Aires neighborhood near downtown, has doubled for years as Medellín’s arena for tropical and popular music — circular, steeply banked, and loud in the best way.

The ring format means no bad sightlines and a floor that becomes a dance space by the second song — wear shoes meant for moving, not posing.

Tickets via TaquillaLive

Sales run through TaquillaLive, the event’s official platform — buy there rather than from resale, since vallenato nights of this profile attract the usual informal markup around the venue.

Note the 18+ rating on the event listing, and bring the ID that matches your ticket name; Medellín venues check at the ring’s entrances.

What Expats Should Know

Vallenato is Colombia’s folk-pop heartbeat — accordion, caja drum and guacharaca under romantic lyrics — and a Celedón concert is the genre at its most polished and welcoming.

La Macarena sits close to the city center; ride-hailing in and out is standard, and the September evenings in Medellín are mild — the ‘eternal spring’ cliché earns itself at night.

Vallenato 101 for Newcomers

The genre’s engine is the accordion, backed by the caja vallenata drum and the guacharaca scraper — a sound Colombia’s Caribbean coast gave the world and the whole country adopted as its own.

Celedón represents its romantic school: smoother than the traditional players, built for arenas, and responsible for much of vallenato’s international reach over the past two decades.

Medellín’s Tropical Circuit

The city has quietly become one of Colombia’s strongest markets for tropical genres — vallenato, salsa and popular music fill La Macarena’s calendar in a way that surprises visitors who know Medellín mainly for reggaetón.

September 26 slots into a busy concert month for the city; if you are building a weekend, the show pairs naturally with the Laureles dining strip and a Sunday in the Botanical Garden.

Why the Coast’s Music Wins in Medellín

Medellín’s love affair with vallenato runs through migration and radio: generations of costeños moved to the Aburrá Valley for work, and the accordion came with them until it belonged to the city as much as to the coast.

That history is audible at a Celedón show in Medellín — the crowd sings the Villanueva songbook with the ownership of locals, because by now, they are.

For expats in Mexico City looking for tonight’s plan: one of the great live bands of the American Latino scene plays a beautiful old theater in the Centro — and you can still go.

Tonight in the Centro

La Santa Cecilia plays the Teatro Metropólitan tonight — a Saturday night slot in one of Mexico City’s most characterful rooms, on Avenida Independencia in the Centro’s theater district.

Doors open ahead of the 8:00 p.m. start; the neighborhood rewards an early arrival, with the old cantinas and taquerías around Independencia filling up before showtime.

The Band From Los Angeles

La Santa Cecilia formed on LA’s Olvera Street and built its sound from the whole map of Latin American music — cumbia, bolero, bossa nova, rock and ska, sung in Spanish and English with La Marisoul’s voice at the center.

The band’s Grammy for ‘Treinta Días’ confirmed what the live circuit already knew: this is one of the finest touring acts in Latino music, with a show that moves from dance floor to torch song without breaking stride.

Why Mexico City Loves Them

No city outside Los Angeles claims La Santa Cecilia more warmly than CDMX: the band’s binational story — Mexican roots, American formation — mirrors the capital’s own cultural conversation.

Their Mexico City shows have a homecoming charge to them: full-voice sing-alongs on ‘La Negra’ and ‘Monedita’, and an audience that spans twenty-year-olds to their parents.

The Teatro Metropólitan

The Metropólitan is one of the Centro’s surviving grand theaters — a mid-century movie palace turned concert room with balconies, velvet and the kind of acoustics that flatter a horn section.

Its scale suits tonight’s band exactly: big enough for a party, small enough that La Marisoul’s between-song stories land in the back row.

Getting There Tonight

The theater sits a short walk from Metro Juárez (Line 3) and the Balderas hub; Saturday night in the Centro means ride-hailing is the stress-free option both ways, with pickup easiest on Independencia itself.

September nights in the capital are cool and can turn wet late — a light jacket covers both the walk out and the post-show taco stop.

What Expats Should Know

If you are building a picture of Latin American music beyond the reggaetón charts, tonight is a perfect seminar: the band covers the continent’s songbook in one set, with joy as the organizing principle.

Tickets are sold through Ticketmaster México — same-day purchases are common for this venue, and the official platform beats the informal sellers who work the theater’s block on show nights.

The Setlist to Expect

Recent sets have balanced the band’s own catalog — ‘La Negra’, ‘Monedita’, ‘Tainted Love’ in its cumbia reinvention — with the boleros and rancheras they treat as shared heritage.

The through-line is La Marisoul’s voice, an instrument that moves from party to heartbreak in a phrase; the Metropólitan’s room is exactly the right scale to hear it work.

The Centro After Dark

The theater district around Independencia has ridden the Centro’s revival: pre-show dinners at the classic cantinas, post-show mezcal in the bars toward Alameda, all inside a few walkable, well-lit blocks.

Standard big-city rules apply — keep to the active streets, use ride-hailing after the encore, and you will have one of the better Saturday nights the Centro currently offers.

World.title: Mexico City Residence Cards Now Take 4 to 6 Weeks: What Expats Should Know About INM Delays
World.content:
Visas: Mexico City

Key Facts The delay. Residence card processing at INM Mexico City currently takes 4–6 weeks, up from the usual 1–2.

Residence card processing at INM Mexico City currently takes 4–6 weeks, up from the usual 1–2. Appointments. INM appointments in the capital are booked out more than a month ahead.

INM appointments in the capital are booked out more than a month ahead. The risk. Processing can overrun the 30-day window you have after entering on a resident visa.

Processing can overrun the 30-day window you have after entering on a resident visa. Who is affected. New arrivals doing the Canje registration and expats renewing existing residence cards.

New arrivals doing the Canje registration and expats renewing existing residence cards. The advice. Book the earliest available appointment immediately on arrival — do not wait for housing to settle first.

Mexico City residence card delays have stretched processing to 4–6 weeks: the INM’s post-arrival registration (Canje) and card issuance in the capital now run far beyond the old 1–2 week norm, with appointments booked out for over a month.

INM’s Mexico City office is running 4–6 weeks on residence cards — plan the post-arrival registration early (Photo: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas in Mexico › RT Ask Rio Times Straight answers about living in Mexico, from our reporting. × Cost of living Is it safe? Visas Neighborhoods Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

For newly arrived expats in Mexico City, the bureaucratic math has changed: what used to be a two-week formality is now a six-week project — plan accordingly.

From Two Weeks to Six

The Canje — the in-country step that converts your consulate-issued resident visa into an actual residence card — has slowed sharply at the Instituto Nacional de Migración’s Mexico City office.

Relocation trackers and immigration practitioners report processing times of four to six weeks where one to two was the working assumption, with the appointment calendar itself booked out more than a month ahead.

What the Canje Is

Every temporary and permanent resident who enters Mexico on a resident visa must complete the Canje within 30 days of arrival: register with INM, give fingerprints and photos, and receive the residence card that proves your status.

The card is the document daily life runs on — banks, phone contracts, apartment leases and re-entry after travel all ask for it — which is why a slow Canje freezes more than your paperwork.

The 30-Day Squeeze

The crunch is arithmetic: if appointments sit a month out and processing runs six weeks, the total timeline can exceed the 30-day post-entry window the rules give you to complete the process.

Practitioners’ standard advice is to treat the appointment booking as day-one business — secure whatever slot exists, then prepare documents while you wait, keeping proof of your timely filing.

Renewals Are Caught Too

The slowdown is not limited to new arrivals: expats renewing temporary residence or stepping up to permanent status face the same appointment scarcity and processing lag at the capital’s offices.

If your card expires within the quarter, start the renewal now — the old habit of booking two weeks out no longer survives contact with the current calendar.

Why INM Is Behind

Mexico’s migration institute has been carrying rising application volumes on constrained staffing for years, and the capital’s offices absorb the country’s largest expat concentration on top of asylum and regularization caseloads.

Periodic surges — often after policy or fee changes — push the appointment system into backlog; the current stretch is one of the longest the CDMX expat community has tracked.

What Expats Should Do Now

Book first, optimize later: take the earliest INM slot you can get, even if the date is imperfect — in-person rebooking at the office is sometimes faster than waiting for online availability.

Keep every receipt and filing confirmation, carry your passport with the entry stamp while the process runs, and if travel looms during processing, ask INM about the exit-and-reentry letter (carta salida y regreso) before you book flights.

Documents That Speed the Canje

Arrive at the appointment over-prepared: passport, the visa page from the consulate, your FMM entry record, proof of address in CDMX, and the completed format INM publishes for the tramite — practitioners report incomplete files as the top cause of repeat visits.

Photocopies matter more than people expect: the offices want paper sets, and the copy shops near the INM buildings know exactly what package you need if you arrive one sheet short.

The Broader Backdrop

Mexico remains one of Latin America’s most accessible residence systems for remote workers and retirees — the delays are administrative, not a policy shift against applicants.

The contrast worth noting: while Brazil just moved its temporary visas fully online, Mexico’s process still runs on in-person counters — which is precisely why the backlog lands on expats’ calendars.

World.title: Costa Rica Independence Day 2026 Brings a Tuesday Holiday and Rain
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Independence Day is Tuesday, September 15 so some holidays here get moved to the nearest Monday to make a long weekend, but this one does not. The Labor Ministry has confirmed it stays on the 15th. That means Monday the 14th is a regular workday, and the celebrations run across both evenings.

This year marks 205 years of independence so expect a torch relay over the weekend, lantern parades Monday night, school parades Tuesday and rain on and off the whole time. The Independence Torch crosses from Nicaragua at Peñas Blancas around 11 a.m. Sunday, according to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport. About 22,000 students will carry it roughly 378 kilometers (235 miles) to Cartago, the Ministry of Public Education says.

The relay passes through Liberia, Cañas, Esparza, Palmares, Naranjo, Alajuela and Heredia before reaching San José on Monday evening. The national anthem will be sung at 6 p.m. at Plaza de la Democracia. The flame is due at the ruins in Cartago around 8 p.m. You can track it live at antorcha.mep.go.cr.

If you drive in San José or Cartago on Monday evening, plan around the relay. From about 5 p.m., traffic police will stop cars on Paseo Colón and Avenida Segunda so the runners can cross. Police will do the same at the Fuente de la Hispanidad, the Montes de Oca church, Curridabat and La Galera, and they will control traffic around Cartago’s central park.

The runners are on foot, so each stop lasts only as long as it takes them to pass. At rush hour, though, even short stops back up quickly. Leave early or stay off those roads between 5 p.m. and 8 p.m. On Tuesday morning, expect closures near Parque Nacional and the Legislative Assembly. President Laura Fernández will attend the main civic ceremony there. Traffic police will also be working civic events across the country.

Monday night is the desfile de faroles or the lantern parade. Children carry handmade lanterns through town centers, and Cartago holds its traditional parade that evening. Most towns hold school parades with marching bands on Tuesday. Check with your municipality for start times.

Bring an umbrella to all of it sinceThe National Meteorological Institute (IMN) says tropical wave No. 42 reaches Costa Rica this afternoon, and wave No. 43 follows on Saturday. Both are moving through a humid, unstable atmosphere, and IMN expects that pattern to last through at least Wednesday, September 16.

On the Pacific side, most of the rain falls in the afternoon, with scattered downpours and thunderstorms in the South and Central Pacific. The Caribbean and the Northern Zone are more likely to get rain overnight and in the morning. In the Central Valley, IMN expects occasional showers that become more frequent early next week. That is right when the lantern parades and school parades take place.

Wind is part of the picture too and IMN recorded gusts of 30 to 50 km/h (19 to 31 mph) in mountain areas on Friday, and up to 75 km/h (47 mph) in the North Pacific. IMN also warned earlier this week about saturated soils. Ground soaked by weeks of rain gives way more easily, so landslides and falling branches become more likely after a heavy afternoon storm.

If you are driving to Guanacaste or Puntarenas, Route 1 at Cambronero, near San Ramón, is still closed. A truck damaged the temporary bridge there earlier this week, and MOPT says repairs could take up to two months. Take Route 27 instead. Cars and other smaller vehicles can also use Monte del Aguacate or the local road between Río Jesús and Piedra Blanca.

If someone works for you, the 15th is a paid day off. That includes a housekeeper, a nanny or a gardener. The Ministry of Labor and Social Security (MTSS) says no worker can be required to work that day, and no one can be penalized for refusing. What you owe depends on how you pay. If you pay monthly or every two weeks, the holiday is already built into the wage. You pay the usual amount even if the person takes the day off. If you pay weekly for work outside a commercial business, add one day’s wage for the holiday on top of the days worked.

If the worker agrees to work on the 15th, the day is paid double. In practice, that means one extra day’s wage on top of what you would normally pay. Any overtime that day is paid at triple the regular hourly rate. The rule has a simple purpose. The law treats Independence Day as a day everyone is entitled to take off without losing income and is why working it costs double.

Hotels, restaurants, bakeries, theaters and gas stations are among the businesses the law allows to open on the holiday. Many other shops and most government offices will be closed, so call ahead before you plan errands for Tuesday. The celebrations run from the torch’s arrival on Sunday through Tuesday’s parades. Leave extra time on the road, carry rain gear, and check the latest IMN and MOPT updates before you set out.

World.title: Costa Rica Dollar Exchange Rate Falls to Another Record Low
World.content:
The U.S. dollar has fallen to its lowest level on record against Costa Rica’s colón, extending a decline that is increasing the purchasing power of the local currency while putting more pressure on expats, retirees and businesses that earn their income in dollars. The weighted average exchange rate in Costa Rica’s Monex foreign exchange market closed yesterday at ₡447.93 per dollar, the lowest level since the Central Bank of Costa Rica began the current historical series on December 6, 2007. The previous record had been set just one day earlier, when the dollar closed at ₡448.17.

The decline has continued to show up in the rates consumers see at banks and other financial institutions. For Friday, September 11, the Central Bank’s official reference rate is ₡444.22 for buying dollars and ₡450.06 for selling them. Actual rates offered by individual banks and exchange houses vary. The latest figures mark a substantial change from the start of the year. On January 2, the first Monex session of 2026, the dollar averaged ₡497.07. Thursday’s level represents a decline of nearly 10% since then.

For foreigners living in Costa Rica and receiving pensions, salaries or other income in U.S. dollars, the effect is straightforward: each dollar now buys significantly fewer colones. Someone exchanging $2,000 at a rate near ₡448 would receive about ₡896,000. At the roughly ₡497 Monex rate seen at the beginning of the year, the same $2,000 represented about ₡994,000, a difference approaching ₡100,000 before considering the spreads charged by banks or exchange services.

The strong colón also continues to concern Costa Rica’s tourism industry. Hotels, tour operators and other tourism businesses frequently receive revenue in dollars while paying wages, utilities, taxes and many other expenses in colones. Tourism industry leaders have warned that rising visitor numbers do not necessarily translate into greater profitability when dollars convert into fewer colones. Costa Rica received just over 2 million visitors through July, up 6.4% from the same period in 2025, but tourism groups have said the exchange rate continues to squeeze operating margins.

The exchange rate has become an increasingly important competitiveness issue for Costa Rica as well. A stronger colón makes many locally priced goods and services more expensive when converted into dollars, an issue that matters as travelers compare Costa Rica with less expensive destinations elsewhere in Central America and the Caribbean. Not everyone loses from the stronger currency.

Importers benefit because they need fewer colones to purchase goods priced in dollars overseas. Costa Ricans earning colones who have mortgages, car loans or other debts denominated in dollars also need fewer colones to make the same dollar payment. The Central Bank remains active in the foreign exchange market.

During yesterday’s Monex session, $26.6 million was traded. The Central Bank purchased $17 million to meet the foreign currency requirements of the nonbank public sector and another $2.8 million through stabilization operations intended to reduce excessive pressure on the exchange rate.

The downward trend has been developing throughout 2026. Costa Rica began the year with the dollar below ₡500 for the first time at the start of a calendar year since 2008, and repeated record lows have followed. For those who depend on dollars, that makes the exchange rate increasingly difficult to ignore. A household receiving the same dollar income it earned at the beginning of the year now has considerably fewer colones available to pay rent, groceries, utilities and other locally priced expenses.

Whether the dollar continues falling will depend on conditions in Costa Rica’s foreign exchange market and the balance between the supply and demand for dollars. For now, however, the colón is stronger against the U.S. currency than at any point in the Central Bank’s nearly two-decade Monex series.

World.title: Western Union Cuts Could Hit More Than 1,000 Jobs in Costa Rica
World.content:
Western Union will gradually shrink its operations center in Costa Rica over the next 12 months and shift positions to Guatemala, Lithuania and the Philippines, the company confirmed on Wednesday. Local reports citing sources familiar with the plan say more than 1,000 jobs could be affected.

The Denver-based money transfer company said the changes follow a comprehensive review of its business. Western Union said the restructuring is intended to drive greater efficiency across its global financial network and to place support services where they best meet the needs of customers and agents.

The company stressed that it will maintain an active presence in Costa Rica. Money sending and receiving services for customers and agents in Costa Rica will continue without interruption, Western Union said, as the reduction applies to its corporate operations center rather than the network of agent locations where customers send and collect funds.

Western Union has not disclosed how many positions will be eliminated or relocated. Its Costa Rica careers page describes the site as employing more than 1,200 people representing 32 nationalities and 17 languages. Local business press figures put the workforce at 1,244, with a commitment by the company to maintain 1,100 positions.

The Costa Rica operation serves as Western Union’s regional operations center for Latin America and is based in Santa Ana, west of San José. It operates under the free trade zone regime, which exempts qualifying companies from income tax, and is registered locally as Unión del Oeste de Costa Rica S.R.L.

In an internal communication sent to employees on Wednesday and signed by Ben Hawksworth, Western Union said it plans to move its regional support hub for the Americas to an operations center in Guatemala City. The message said the shift is meant to align the work done at each center with the region in which it is located.

The company told staff that not all work will leave Costa Rica and that it is still evaluating which roles will remain. The transition will take place gradually, team by team, and Western Union expects much of it to be complete by mid-2027.

During that period, employees in Costa Rica will work alongside colleagues in Guatemala City and other offices to hand over knowledge, procedures and best practices, according to the communication. Workers whose roles are affected will receive severance in line with legal requirements and company policy, along with human resources support and benefits guidance.

Western Union acknowledged in the message that the prolonged lack of detail had created uncertainty among staff. The company attributed part of the delay to the drawn-out closing of its planned acquisition of Intermex, a U.S.-based remittance firm, which it said had slowed integration planning and decisions on where to locate operations. The message also recognized 28 years of contributions by the company’s Costa Rica teams.

The decision comes as Western Union accelerates cost cuts worldwide. Reporting second-quarter results on July 30, President and CEO Devin McGranahan said weaker-than-expected performance in the Americas retail business and the delayed Intermex deal had squeezed margins, requiring the company to “accelerate cost reductions more forcefully in the second half of the year.”

Quarterly revenue came in at $1 billion, down 1% from a year earlier, while adjusted earnings per share fell to $0.31 from $0.42. On the company’s earnings call, McGranahan outlined a restructuring program called Beyond Efficiency, which targets $50 million in annualized savings by the end of 2026 and $200 million by the end of 2027.

He cited the transfer of agent onboarding for the Asia-Pacific region from Lithuania and Costa Rica to the company’s Manila operations center as one example of the approach. The $500 million Intermex acquisition, announced in August 2025 and initially expected to close in mid-2026, remains pending. In August, California’s financial regulator suspended an approval extension for the deal to conduct further review, according to a joint statement from the two companies.

The announcement follows other job reductions at multinational employers in Costa Rica this year, including Boston Scientific’s confirmed layoffs and a new round of layoffs at Amazon. Western Union said it will share further details on which positions will move and which will stay as planning progresses.

World.title: Detainee allegedly refuses to stop smoking in police cell, says he has weed, threatens to kill and lunges at officer
World.content:
Detainee allegedly refuses to stop smoking in police cell, says he has weed, threatens to kill and lunges at officer

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City detainee allegedly threatened to kill a police officer and then lunged at him through the bars of a cell block after officers told prisoners that smoking would not be allowed inside.

Chervin Calvin Tench, 25, appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, where he pleaded not guilty to one count of threat of death and one count of aggravated assault upon a police officer.

The allegations stem from an incident at the Precinct 2 Police Station at around 7:45 a.m. on September 10, while officers were carrying out routine checks of prisoners inside the cell block.

According to the police complaint, officers entered a cell containing seven prisoners and informed them that smoking of any kind would not be permitted.

Police allege that Tench objected and told the officer that he would smoke as much as he wanted. He allegedly also indicated that he had marijuana in his possession.

The officer then reportedly left to get additional personnel to conduct a more thorough search of the cell.

Police say that when officers returned, the prisoners became boisterous and Tench allegedly threatened the officer, telling him in part, “I will kill you. It’s a promise.”

The officer informed Tench that he would be charged for the alleged threat.

Police further allege that while the search was being conducted, Tench continued behaving boisterously and, after being told to calm down, thrust his hand through an opening between the metal bars and attempted to strike the officer in the face.

The officer later made a formal complaint and requested court action.

Tench pleaded not guilty to both charges. The prosecution did not object to bail but requested conditions.

He was granted bail of $1,500 plus one surety in the same amount, with conditions that he have no contact with the complainant and not be arrested and charged with another offence while on bail.

During his arraignment, Tench told the court that he had changed his lifestyle since being released from prison and had attempted to move away from his former neighbourhood. The Magistrate cautioned him against discussing the facts of the case further after entering his not-guilty pleas.

Tench is due back in court on November 4, 2026.

He was previously convicted in October 2023 of keeping an unlicensed firearm after police said they saw him attempting to dispose of an unloaded 9mm Glock during an encounter in May 2022. He later served a prison sentence of two years and two months after receiving credit for time already spent on remand.

World.title: Benyahti Brandon committed to stand trial for La Democracia murder of Paul Smith Jr.
World.content:
Benyahti Brandon committed to stand trial for La Democracia murder of Paul Smith Jr.

By Breaking Belize News Staff: La Democracia resident Benyahti Jareai Brandon, 27, has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the murder of Paul Nigel Smith Jr. and the attempted murder of Tyrece Lewis Allen.

Brandon appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday, where his Preliminary Inquiry began and concluded with his committal to the October session of the High Court, scheduled to commence on October 7, 2026.

During the proceeding, the police prosecutor tendered more than 15 witness statements and 13 documentary exhibits forming part of the prosecution’s case. Those include a Scenes of Crime report, post-mortem documents relating to Smith, Brandon’s caution statement and notes of interview, chain-of-custody documents, an arrest warrant and a medico-legal form relating to Allen.

Brandon was also given an alibi warning and provided the court with the names of two men he intends to call as witnesses at his trial.

The charges stem from a February 3 shooting on First Street in La Democracia Village. Police say Smith was walking with his girlfriend and Allen at around 9:00 a.m. when a gunman emerged from behind a house and fired several shots in their direction.

Smith attempted to flee but collapsed and was later pronounced dead at the Western Regional Hospital. Allen suffered a gunshot wound to the knee, was treated and later released. Police subsequently reported that surveillance footage from the area assisted investigators in identifying Brandon as a suspect.

Brandon was arrested and first arraigned on February 5 on charges of murder and attempted murder and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison. In August, he was provided with 83 pages of disclosure, five DVDs and three photographs ahead of Friday’s Preliminary Inquiry.

Brandon has not been convicted of either offence. The charges will now proceed to trial before the High Court.

World.title: Ellis ‘Juice’ Meighan committed to stand trial for 2024 Placencia murder of Roy Lee Burgess
World.content:
Ellis ‘Juice’ Meighan committed to stand trial for 2024 Placencia murder of Roy Lee Burgess

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Ellis Gilbert Meighan, also known as “Juice,” has been committed to stand trial in the High Court for the 2024 murder of Roy Lee Burgess and the attempted murder of American national Maia James in Placencia.

Meighan, who turned 34 on September 5 while on remand, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Friday for his Preliminary Inquiry. At the conclusion of the proceedings, the Chief Magistrate ruled that there was sufficient evidence for the case to proceed to trial.

He was committed to the October session of the High Court, which begins October 7, 2026.

During the Preliminary Inquiry, the prosecution tendered more than 35 witness statements along with numerous documentary and physical exhibits forming part of the case against Meighan.

Among those statements were three given to police by James following the April 14, 2024 shooting. The prosecution’s evidence also includes medical records, a post-mortem report on Burgess, photographs of the crime scene and autopsy, ballistic evidence, recovered projectiles and a firearms report.

Meighan did not provide the court with the names of any alibi witnesses he intends to call at trial. He was informed that he has seven days to submit those names in writing.

The charges stem from a shooting on April 14, 2024, along the Placencia Road, which left 32-year-old Burgess dead and James seriously injured. Contemporary reports said Burgess, James and Burgess’ 13-year-old son were inside a vehicle when gunfire erupted. James, then 26, suffered a gunshot injury to her face or head and was later taken abroad for medical treatment, while the child escaped unharmed.

Meighan subsequently left Belize and was apprehended by U.S. authorities in San Diego in May 2024. After spending more than a year in U.S. custody, he was deported to Belize on September 9, 2025 and arraigned three days later on charges including murder, attempted murder, use of deadly means of harm and dangerous harm. He was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Earlier this year, Meighan was provided with 181 pages of disclosure and 22 original photographs forming part of the prosecution’s case.

Meighan has not been convicted of the offences. The prosecution will now be required to prove the charges against him when the matter proceeds to trial in the High Court.

World.title: Man fined $460 for piece of crack the size of a rice grain and pipe
World.content:
Man fined $460 for piece of crack the size of a rice grain and pipe

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man must pay $460 in fines after pleading guilty to possession of a crack pipe and possession of a small quantity of crack cocaine reportedly found inside the pipe.

Dario Fabian Flowers, 44, a labourer of Magazine Road, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court this week, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a pipe used in connection with smoking a controlled drug and possession of 0.5 grams of crack cocaine.

Flowers told the court that the quantity of crack cocaine was only about the size of a grain of rice.

The Magistrate fined Flowers $155 for possession of the pipe and $305 for possession of the crack cocaine, for a total of $460. He has until November 30, 2026, to pay the fines.

In default, Flowers faces one month in prison on the pipe charge and two months on the drug possession charge. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently, meaning he would serve a maximum of two months if the fines are not paid.

Police say Flowers was stopped at around 1:45 a.m. on September 8 while officers were conducting a mobile patrol on King Street near the terminal area.

During a search, police reportedly found a metal pipe with rubber attached concealed near the front zipper area of Flowers’ three-quarter pants. Officers said a white substance resembling crack cocaine was observed inside the pipe.

Flowers was escorted to the police station and subsequently charged with the two drug-related offences.

World.title: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl
World.content:
Convicted police officer Dexter Diego apologizes to 14-year-old victim for unlawful sex with her; faces separate trial for allegedly raping 10-year-old girl

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Convicted police officer Dexter Diego expressed remorse in the High Court this week as Justice Nigel Pilgrim heard mitigation ahead of his sentencing for four counts of unlawful sexual intercourse involving a minor.

Diego, 29, pleaded guilty on July 27 to the four counts involving a girl who was 13 years old when the sexual relationship began. His trial had been scheduled to begin that day, but he entered guilty pleas before Justice Pilgrim. Public reports say the court subsequently ordered a prison report, social inquiry report and victim impact statement ahead of sentencing.

Addressing the court during Wednesday’s mitigation hearing, an emotional Diego apologized to the victim, her family, the court, the Belize Police Department and his own family.

“I am fully aware of my decisions that I have made. I know that they were wrong,” Diego told the court, adding that he regretted the pain his actions had caused.

His sister also testified as a character witness, describing her brother as a helpful and respectable person who provided for his stepmother. She told the court that the case has taken a heavy toll on their family and asked Justice Pilgrim to show leniency when imposing sentence.

The court also heard an emotional victim impact statement from the girl, who said Diego had gained her trust by acting as a confidant before pressuring her into a sexual relationship. She told the court that the experience left her ashamed and embarrassed, forced her to relocate and affected her life.

Diego is also before the courts in a separate case involving another minor. On May 4, 2026, the interdicted police officer was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on four counts of rape of a child. Prosecutors allege that three of the offences occurred in December 2024, when the girl was 10 years old, while a fourth allegedly occurred in 2025, when she was 11. Diego was remanded to the Belize Central Prison because the Magistrate’s Court could not grant bail on the charges.

The new charges were brought while Diego was already before the courts in connection with the case for which he has now pleaded guilty. The four rape charges remain pending allegations, and Diego has not been convicted in that separate matter.

World.title: Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange
World.content:
Belize and Guyana strengthen cooperation through public sector knowledge exchange

By Zoila Palma: A delegation from the Government of Belize conducted a three-day Knowledge Exchange visit to the Cooperative Republic of Guyana from September 8 to 10, 2026, aimed at strengthening capacity in public-sector management, digital transformation, procurement and project cycle management.

The exchange, coordinated by the High Commission of Belize in Guyana, provided Belizean officials with an opportunity to engage their Guyanese counterparts, examine institutional practices and learn about digital tools and systems being used to improve government service delivery, project implementation and oversight.

The Belize delegation included officials from the Ministry of Finance, Investment, Economic Transformation, Civil Aviation and E-Governance. Discussions focused on project monitoring and oversight, public-sector investment programme planning, procurement reforms, e-Procurement, digital identification and digital government services.

Officials also examined Guyana’s National Digital Management Authority and its experience with E-ID and digital transformation. Presentations highlighted digital systems and innovations supporting service delivery in areas including health, public safety and law enforcement, and agriculture.

Chief Executive Officer for Economic Transformation Carlos Pol said the exchange provides Belize with an opportunity to identify practical approaches that could support the country’s development priorities. “Knowledge sharing among countries in the region allows us to learn from practical experiences, including both successes and challenges. This exchange will help Belize identify approaches that can strengthen project management, procurement, digital transformation, and overall public-sector effectiveness.”

CEO for E-Governance Jose Urbina highlighted the importance of digital innovation in modernizing government services. “Digital transformation is no longer simply about introducing technology; it is about rethinking how Government operates and how citizens access public services,” he said.

The visit is expected to lead to continued technical cooperation, including support for Belize’s digitalization efforts, healthcare workforce capacity-building, PSIP management and oversight, and e-Procurement. The Government of Belize thanked the Government of Guyana, the High Commission of Belize in Guyana and the Inter-American Development Bank for facilitating the exchange.

World.title: International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue
World.content:
International News: Guatemalan Riot police responds to road blockages as fuel price protests continue

By Zoila Palma: Today, road blockades continued across Guatemala as protesters demonstrated against rising fuel prices, disrupting traffic on major highways and sections of Guatemala City.

The demonstrations have affected thousands of commuters and disrupted the movement of essential goods, including food, medicine and fuel., Prensa Libre reports.

Blockades have been reported along several of the country’s main highways, as well as on the Periférico Ring Road near the entrance to the Bethania neighborhood and the Atlantic Highway at key entrances and exits to the capital.

Some blockades, including those in Cuyotenango, Suchitepéquez, and Río Hondo, Zacapa, have lasted more than 24 hours.

Minister of the Interior Marco Antonio Villeda has ordered protesters to clear the roads within 30 minutes, warning that those who refuse could be arrested and brought before the courts.

In addition, Guatemalan officials announced a joint operation involving the National Civil Police and the Army to clear blocked routes, following a Constitutional Court ruling ordering the removal of the blockades.

The business sector has called for immediate action, citing significant economic losses caused by the disruptions.

World.title: International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies
World.content:
International News: Latin America faces growing drone threat as criminal groups take to the skies

By Zoila Palma: Drones are rapidly becoming a powerful tool for organized crime across Latin America, with criminal groups increasingly using the technology for surveillance, smuggling, coordination and attacks, while governments struggle to keep pace.

A report by the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) recorded around 670 armed-drone events since 2018, with more than 72% occurring between January 2025 and August 21, 2026.

The threat has become particularly visible in Mexico, Colombia and Brazil, CNN reports.

In Brazil, a 2025 police operation in Rio de Janeiro saw a bomb dropped from a drone during a massive raid against the Comando Vermelho criminal organization.

Mexican cartels have also used drones to monitor security forces, territorial rivals and border areas, while attaching explosives to some devices.

In Colombia, armed groups have increasingly incorporated drones into attacks and surveillance, with ACLED identifying the country as the epicenter of armed-drone activity in the region.

Experts say criminal groups are moving beyond experimental drone use toward organized and repeatable operations.

Governments across the region are responding with counter-drone technology, intelligence operations and increased surveillance, but experts warn that criminal innovation is advancing faster than many governments can adapt.

World.title: Build better, faster
World.content:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness (right) engages in a lively discussion with Donald Mullings (left), chairman, M&M Jamaica Limited; Martin Miller (second left), managing director, National Housing Trust (NHT); and NHT Chairman Linval Freeman during Friday’s ground breaking for the construction of 700 houses at Greater Bernard Lodge in St Catherine. The houses are being built will under a partnership agreement with the NHT, the Housing Agency of Jamaica, and M&M Jamaica Ltd. Photo: Garfield Robinson

BREAKING ground Friday for the construction of 700 new homes at Greater Bernard Lodge in St Catherine, Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness challenged local contractors to embrace technology and invest in equipment that can accelerate the pace of delivery.

“The building technologies that we are using today are outdated and expensive. We need more of our private contractors and our private developers to start using modern technology. It’s not just to build the houses more cost-effectively, but we have to move away from building the matches boxes, the heat boxes, to building things that look modern, aesthetically pleasing and sustainable. That is my challenge today to our developers,” Holness said, adding that he expects that within the next 18 months he will be back at the location to present keys to the owners of the new units.

“The role of Government is to use legislation, and fiscal incentives, and moral suasion to guide and sometimes direct the private developers into the underserved areas of the market. But we are seeing an influx of overseas private contractors who have solved the problem of being able to build quickly and deliver quickly at a reasonable price because they have integrated significant technology and equipment into their operations,” Holness said.

“Almost every day we are getting proposals. The only thing they want from us would be land. But I am thinking that I want my local contractors to do this. I want my local contractors to develop the capability to deliver these houses quickly. I can’t just give away everything to overseas and foreign investors. I want my local contractors to benefit, but at the same time I want the people to get houses,” the prime minister said.

The units — 280 one-bedroom and 420 two-bedroom houses — will be built under a partnership agreement with the National Housing Trust (NHT), the Housing Agency of Jamaica (HAJ), and M&M Jamaica Limited, across two parcels of land.

They will form the D2 and D3 phases of the Greater Bernard Lodge housing development programme and will include paved roads, storm water drains, perimeter walls, street signs, and other essential amenities.

The $11.62-billion project will expand the supply of housing available to NHT contributors.

Arguing that the practise of squatting will persist if enough isn’t done to provide shelter for the many Jamaicans who have no home for themselves, Holness reiterated that his Administration remains committed to its election promise of building 70,000 houses.

“So, the 70,000 is very ambitious. I’m hanging my hat where I will have to stretch to reach it,” he said.

“We have been stretching. The NHT was tasked to build 42,000 of that, and my last check showed that they have seen their way in terms of what they have already constructed — what is in contracts, what is in procurement, and what is in planning. They are over 40,000, so they have seen the slate of what they should construct. The chairman told you that since the start of the year we have broken ground for 2,000. We are now at over 8,000 houses under construction or out of construction,” the prime minister said.

Lynvale Freeman, the NHT chairman, said that Friday’s ground-breaking represented not just the turning of soil but the expansion of homeownership in Jamaica. He said it was important to do it in St Catherine because of its close proximity to Kingston, among other important factors.

“The common goal is to build as many houses at the lowest price point,” Freeman said.

World.title: ‘EDUCATION EMERGENCY’
World.content:
La Sonja Harrison, president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association, speaking at a meeting of the Rotary Club of Kingston at Jamaica Pegasus hotel on Thursday. Garfield Robinson

DECLARING that Jamaica is facing an “education emergency”, president of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) La Sonja Harrison is urging the Government to implement a five-year national learning recovery and acceleration plan to tackle the existing gaps in the sector.

But Harrison is adamant that the five-year initiative must put educators at the forefront of the conversation.

“If it is as educators, we are the first responders, we are the people on the ground, I am saying that there can be no conversation about how we go nationally without the teachers in a meaningful way. And I’m not talking about us, leaders of the Jamaica Teachers’ Association, I’m talking about the people who are on the ground, the foot soldiers, and the people on whom you will depend [on] anyway to carry out whatever vision you have for education.

“Those persons need to be invited at the table from the beginning of the conversation, not at the tail end,” Harrison told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday following a meeting of the Rotary club of Kingston at the Jamaica Pegasus hotel.

“We have TREND [Transforming Education for National Development], and we have ETOC [Education Transformation Oversight Committee], because they continue to update the nation quarterly concerning same. So ETOC will have some educators represented there, but is it reflective of the system, the people who work in the trenches of the system, and are they at the table for the conversation and posit the solutions that they would see ideal and realistic, in transforming the education system?”Harrison questioned.

In her presentation Harrison highlighted several disruptions faced by the education sector and argued that the urgency displayed by the Government in rebuilding structures and restoring operations has not been given to recovering learning.

“COVID-19 interrupted the education system of an entire generation. Then came Hurricane Beryl [July 2024], Hurricane Melissa [October 2025]. In between, there have been floods…fires, infrastructural failures, and teacher shortages, and that is just since 2019, we have not even gone back decades,”

“We have spent considerable time recovering buildings, and those recovery of buildings have certainly not been to the standard that we are desirous of, and the pace, the alacrity. Because for us to be able to report as a nation that 40 of some 600 plus schools have been rebuilt, that’s 6.67 per cent of our schools that have been retrofitted to provide an atmosphere for safe, comfortable learning of our children,” Harrison frowned.

Pointing to the Government’s emergencies in education plan, including the modification of objectives from the National Standards Curriculum, (NSC) post-Hurricane Melissa, Harrison charged that establishing such a plan after a disaster is ineffective.

“We need to identify those who have fallen behind. We need targeted initiatives. We need additional instructional support where necessary. We need stronger literacy and numeracy initiative benchmarks to support. We need trained teachers and interventionists at varying levels of the system. And we need to measure whether children are actually catching up. Attendance is not recovery. Promotion is not recovery. Completing a grade is not recovery. Learning is recovery. Teachers cannot be expected to recover six years of educational disruption with the same resources, same staffing, and in some cases under staffing, and after these weather challenges and with worsening infrastructure,” said Harrison.

“The Government is going to tell you that we have the emergency in education stuff, but it has to be proactive in nature. It can’t be that it is when the event happens, then we come up with something that will help to take us through another event. So we have to sit down and look and say how are we going to, one, ensure learning, how are we going to engage teachers, how are we going to engage parents.

“Jamaica needs a national foundational learning emergency plan. I deliberately use that language. Not another programme project to treat with the illiteracy problem. Not another intervention to treat with learning gap, as this is just not another education challenge. It is an emergency. Because when children are progressing through our schools without mastering reading, comprehension, writing, and numeracy, we’re not simply dealing with an academic problem. We’re compromising Jamaica’s future,” Harrison charged.

World.title: Garbage truck obstacle
World.content:
Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager addressing Thursday’s regular monthly meeting of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation.

FALMOUTH, Trelawny — A derelict garbage truck is standing in the way of plans by the Trelawny Municipal Corporation (TMC) to establish temporary headquarters, prompting Falmouth Mayor C Junior Gager to give the vehicle’s owner an ultimatum to remove it or face having it towed.

Gager, who is also chairman of the TMC, told Thursday’s regular monthly meeting of the corporation that the truck is occupying the spot earmarked for two newly acquired containers, which are to be converted into offices and a meeting room.

He said repeated attempts to locate the owner have failed, despite the corporation obtaining contact information for a person believed to be associated with the vehicle.

“We have a garbage truck that is parked on the premises of the Trelawny Municipal Corporation for some time now. We have tried all that we can. It seems to be maybe a private contractor. We have tried to reach him. We cannot reach him,” Gager said.

With the project considered urgent, Gager said the TMC would not allow the abandoned vehicle to delay the work.

“If the truck isn’t removed within maybe another day or two, we’ll be taking it out and we’ll be placing it in an open land,” he warned.

The ultimatum comes as the TMC continues to operate from makeshift facilities following severe damage inflicted by Hurricane Melissa to its previous location at the historic Falmouth Courthouse last October.

The local authority is currently operating from containerised units on the grounds of its Roads and Works premises, while other functions have been squeezed into the Roads and Works building. Its monthly meetings are being held at the Port Authority of Jamaica’s conference room at the Falmouth Port.

Gager said the two recently purchased containers are to be retrofitted to provide badly needed office and meeting space, with the work expected to be completed within about a month.

“I would be happy if next month we can move in and have our council meeting there, because you see this room is getting so small, and we want a little more space,” Gager said.

He disclosed that a portion of the funding needed is already available and that technical officers, including the acting chief engineering officer, are being mobilised to expedite the work.

“We have some funding, and we are working with it. But we are going to make sure that next month, when you come back here it is nearly finished, or it is finished, or maybe in another two weeks,” Gager told his fellow councillors.

He described the facility as a temporary but potentially long-term investment, saying it could be used for other purposes even after the corporation establishes permanent headquarters.

The mayor also disclosed plans for an official opening of the facility once the work is completed, with Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie expected to be among those invited.

World.title: Melissa puts PE on pause in some western Jamaica schools
World.content:
Carisbrook Primary and Infant School Principal Patrick Malcolm leads the Jamaica Observer on a tour of the compound on Monday. Naphtali Junior

As temporary classrooms take over playing areas of some schools in St Elizabeth, principal of Carisbrook Primary and Infant School Patrick Malcolm is warning that physical education (PE) is becoming an unfortunate casualty of the push to get damaged schools functioning again.

According to Malcolm, this reflects a wider tendency to treat PE and sport as less important than academic subjects, despite their role in developing healthy, well-rounded children.

The concern is particularly acute at Maggotty High School, where temporary classrooms have left the school without enough space to conduct practical PE sessions, and properly facilitate its netball and football programmes.

Maggotty High’s Principal Sean Graham said the school has been forced to make a significant adjustment, with practical PE sessions put on hold for the current term while administrators work around the loss of playing space.

“The PE teacher expressed concern in terms of how she will facilitate training… because the school does not have a big enough play field. We also facilitate some level of football training here as well, especially for the junior team. So, those are going to be compromised, and we are going to have to find other ways to work it out,” Graham told the

Jamaica Observer on Monday.

He said the school understands the urgency of getting students back into suitable classrooms, but stressed that the temporary arrangement cannot be allowed to become prolonged.

“But we have to figure it out. Because the most important thing is to have the students here. All PE sessions for this term have to be theory-based. So, that is why I really still have to insist that by December, temporary classrooms have to be gone, because we don’t have the space to facilitate physical education, practical, plus the netball training and so on,” added Graham.

The situation is not confined to the high-school level.

At Middle Quarters Primary and Infant School, temporary classrooms are also being constructed on the school’s netball court, forcing administrators to look elsewhere for space for physical activity.

Principal Pauvine Watson-Barrett, who also spoke with the Observer on Monday, said the school intends to use its grassy areas rather than abandon PE altogether, although the loss of the hard surface presents its own challenges.

But Malcolm is adamant that the issue goes beyond finding alternative spaces.

He believes the temporary loss of playing areas exposes a long-standing failure to give physical education the same consideration afforded to subjects such as mathematics and English.

Malcolm, who is also president of the St Elizabeth Football Association, pointed to Carisbrook’s own experience as evidence of the determination required to keep sport alive despite inadequate facilities.

The school has 137 students, including 30 infants, and has built a strong sporting programme despite limited resources.

Malcolm said the school has trophies, medals and plaques reflecting its achievements, while its football field — which he said is the only one in the area capable of accommodating a 200-metre track — is also shared with the wider community.

He charged that the school’s sporting success has often come despite, rather than because of, the resources available to it.

“This is the myopicness of the people around. We all want to be bright, maths and English people, but we don’t want to be fit and strong. So we’re going to be doctors, but sick doctors. We’re going to be teachers, but sick teachers. Sports is such that the impact of it can be felt everywhere in this country,” he said.

Malcolm questioned the decision to place temporary classrooms on playing areas when alternative spaces may be available, particularly at Middle Quarters.

“When you put a temporary classroom on the court, what are you suggesting to those who are interested in PE? That they’ll sit down and do nothing for the next two months, three months?…and it’s just sad because there is more space that they could use,” he said.

He argued that the recovery effort should not treat sport as an optional extra, particularly at a time when children are already coping with disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa and the rebuilding of their schools.

“Somebody has to get up and start to show a little bit more appreciation for sports and physical education in this country. We cannot do without it. It is the stress buster. It is where we go for a break, and if the students are not encouraged to do this, then we are in trouble,” Malcolm added.

He also linked the decline in physical activity to broader concerns about the health of Jamaican society, arguing that schools have a critical role to play in encouraging children to remain active.

“Later on, we’re going to have a sick society… Look at the size of some of the teachers we have around. Look at the size of the society. I mean, probably two-thirds of the society is overweight. We better fix that, and the only way we can fix that is with physical education,” argued Malcolm.

World.title: ‘Happy, relieved, respected’
World.content:
Councillor Garfield James (JLP, Sheffield Division) vows to support Councillor Julian Chang (JLP, Savanna-la-Mar Division), saying he will not allow anyone from inside the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation to bully her. Rosalee Wood Condell

SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Councillor Julian Chang (Jamaica Labour Party, Savanna-la-Mar Division) officially crossed the floor during Thursday’s sitting of the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation (WMC) after a tumultuous time with the People’s National Party (PNP).

She is the third defection from the PNP benches, with Ian Myles of the Little London Division and Garfield James of the Sheffield Division making the switch in 2024.

The formal announcement confirming Chang’s change of allegiance came with WMC Chief Executive Officer Marlette Wellington reading a letter submitted to Mayor Danree Delancy. The initial letter had been emailed, stalling the process as protocol dictates that it has to be submitted in hard copy.

“At this point, in consultation with my constituents, we have come to the decision that I can no longer sit with arrogance, disrespect, and of fundamental importance, poor representation. Hence, my crossing the floor to join the JLP, that practises progressive peopleism. I, therefore, choose Jamaica” said a section of the letter.

Its reading prompted an outburst of applause from PNP councillors within the chamber, raising questions from Myles and James as to whether the reaction was intended as commendation or political sarcasm.

Following the notice, a motion was immediately tendered to strip Chang of her assignments on three municipal committees: Poor relief, human resources, and the finance sub-committee.

Reading from municipal correspondence, CEO Wellington detailed the swift replacements: Councillor Arthur Colly (PNP, Negril Division) now goes to poor relief; Councillor Lidden Lewis (PNP, Frome Division) is now on the human resources committee; and Councillor Jerome Bacchas (PNP, Darliston Division) is now named to the finance sub-committee.

Addressing her abrupt removal from the committees, Chang remained unfazed.

“I don’t feel no way,” she told the Jamaica Observer following the meeting. “I feel happy and relieved. I am now respected.”

Her transition was warmly received by her new JLP colleagues, with James stepping forward to pledge full backing for the Savanna-la-Mar representative.

“I will give you the support that you need,” James asserted. “And we will not allow anyone inside this corporation to bully you.”

Chang emphasised that her decision to align with the governing JLP stems from a desire to deliver tangible infrastructural development to her constituents in Savanna-la-Mar, support she claims was consistently denied to her while under the PNP banner.

“I know and believe that more can be done for the people of Savanna-la-Mar, for the parish of Westmoreland, and for the city that we now live in,” Chang explained.

She pointed to the severe degradation of local infrastructure.

“A classic example is we have a road which is called Segre Street, which is supposed to be maintained by the Municipal Corporation, and right now, there is neither road, pass, nor anywhere for people to walk,” Chang charged.

“Segre Street has deteriorated under the over 40 years of PNP having this council, and it is still not fixed and there are many other roads that are going bad,” she added.

Chang stated that through her new alignment with the governing party, the road has now been slated for rehabilitation under the Shared Prosperity through Accelerated Improvement to Our Road Network (SPARK) programme.

“It will be fixed by the Jamaica Labour Party, by this Government, for the people of Jamaica, for the people here,” she declared. “And it’s time. It’s time. We need Savanna-la-Mar to be fixed. We need structural infrastructure to come into the areas.”

She added that she looks forward to collaborating with agencies such as the National Infrastructure Renewal and Rehabilitation Agency (NaRRA) to address historical deficiencies across the parish.

When asked whether she intends to seek re-election on a JLP ticket in the next local government elections, Chang sidestepped the question, saying, “I will continue to represent the people of Savanna-la-Mar.”

Her formal crossing of the floor marks the culmination of months of escalating internal friction within the PNP.

Elected councillor for the Savanna-la-Mar Division in the local government elections of February 2024, Chang served under the party for two years and four months before tendering her resignation from the PNP on June 29, 2026.

The roots of the rift trace back to February 2025, when she reported experiencing unwanted advances and receiving explicit messages from Member of Parliament for Westmoreland Central Dwayne Vaz. The fallout deepened following the September 2025 General Election, during which allegations surfaced accusing Chang of working against PNP interests within the constituency.

The conflict spilled into the public domain on January 26, 2026, when Chang aired her grievances against Vaz during an interview on

Nationwide News Network. On January 30, the PNP announced the creation of a special investigative committee, separate from its Internal Affairs Commission, to probe the harassment allegations and political fallout.

By late June 2026, citing a two-year backlog of unresolved grievances and institutional disrespect, Chang cut ties with the PNP, paving the way for her formal integration into the JLP this week.

Outside the Westmoreland Municipal Corporation building on Thursday, two loyal constituents waited to greet Chang as she exited, offering enthusiastic approval of her political switch.

Icilda Johnson, a local resident and former PNP supporter who encouraged Chang to make the jump, recalled advising her early on to realign. Another constituent, Carol Waisome, expressed similar joy, recalling how she embraced Chang despite their past political differences.

“My girl this. She a hard-working lady. A di right party she deh pon now. Right side. She deh pon the good ship and the right side,” said Waisome.

World.title: Beyond saving lives, restoring them
World.content:
Level 2 physiotherapist and Lamaze childbirth educator at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) Monique Richmond (centre) shows a model of a human pelvis to (from left) UHWI’s Senior Director Clinical Services Dr Carl Bruce; the hospital’s Acting Chief Executive Officer Sydney Powell; dean of the Faculty of Medical Sciences Professor Joseph Plummer; head of the hospital’s Physiotherapy Department Dionne Bennett; and Opposition spokesperson on health Dr Alfred Dawes, at the department’s open day on Thursday.Naphtali Junior

FOR patients of the University Hospital of the West Indies’ (UHWI) Physiotherapy Department, rehabilitation has meant more than recovering from injury or surgery; it marks the return of independence to their daily lives.

When Dr William Aiken took the stage during the department’s open day on Thursday in a leg cast supported by crutches, he showed up in the capacity of a patient, though he also bore the titles of consultant urologist and head of surgery at UHWI.

“On the 26th of July, I had a little tussle with a croaking lizard, and had severed my left Achilles tendon and had surgery on the 3rd of August to repair it. And as you would know, physiotherapy is a critical part of the rehabilitation process after undergoing an injury like that,” said Aiken, as he chuckled at his misfortune.

He was among other patients who shared their rehabilitation testimonies during the open day which formed part of activities to mark the 2026 World Physiotherapy Week.

For a specialist whose days are dedicated to treating diseases of the urinary tract and male reproductive system, the sudden accident altered Aiken’s routine. However, given the nature of his job, the head surgeon could not stay away from his duties for long. He began occupational rehabilitation, a process designed to return a patient to a functional state within their professional role.

“I reached out to Dr Bennett [director of the physiotherapy department], and she accepted me as a patient with alacrity, and she and her staff have been very kind to me. I have benefited from her expertise.
