When I come here, I’m treated royally, and I can speak to the facilities that are here; they are second to none…So I can truly say that I’m very proud of this physiotherapy department and what it offers,” said Aiken.

Now back in the operating room, the head surgeon has adapted to his recovery by sitting to rest his leg during procedures, a minor adjustment that allows him to press on with his life’s work.

“I have never met an unpleasant physiotherapist, never. In all the years I’ve been working here, and I’ve been here 30 plus years, physiotherapists are really an important backbone of the services offered in the hospital,” said Aiken.

Opposition spokesperson on health Dr Alfred Dawes also gave high praises to the physiotherapy department, as the greeting he was slated to deliver turned into a testimony.

“For most of my career, I was never really was enthusiastic about physiotherapy. It was [just] another speciality…But then something magically happened that changed my entire outlook on physiotherapy; I turned 40. And every joint in my body had a press conference to announce that they were there,” Dawes said while laughing.

His once active lifestyle derailed by ageing pains, led Dawes to seek rehabilitation at UHWI’s Physiotherapy Department, which, he said, allowed him to pivot, heal, and remain spry.

“It was physiotherapists, some of you in this room, who helped me to get back to normal from the injuries I sustained while trying to be physically active, from my toe all the way up to my neck, literally. So physiotherapy is more than just a discipline adjacent to surgery. After I became a patient and a client, I became the best friend of many physiotherapists… And what I’ve learned could never be taught in any textbook at all,” said Dawes.

He added that a physiotherapist does more than repair torn muscles or broken bones as they give people hope that inspires them to continue living despite injury.

“We have built a health system that is very good at saving lives, but not very good at restoring lives. We [doctors] stabilise the heart, but yet we abandon the patient. The stroke patient survives the night on the ward and then everything that matters afterwards is in your hands. You, the therapist, not in the theatre, not in the pharmacy, [but] on the mat, the parallel bars, six weeks on, six months on, 16 months on…. Medicine adds years to the life, but physiotherapy adds life to the years,” Dawes said.

Minister of National Security Horace Chang sent a pre-recorded message that shared his experience with physiotherapy after undergoing major cardiac surgery.

“I have had the experience of going through triple bypass surgery in the end of October to November 2025. It was successful and I chose to do the cardiac rehab at the University Hospital’s physiotherapy department. I could not have made a better decision. They are professional, courteous, and committed to their jobs. They look after their patients proficiently, irrespective of who they are. Recovery went smoothly, and today I am doing better than I was before surgery,” said Chang.

He congratulated the department on the work they have done over the years, and encouraged the physiotherapists to continue positively impacting ailing Jamaicans who yearn to regain normalcy and autonomy over their lives.

“Dr Bennett and her team have made one of the finest professional units in the country, they deserve every support, and I send my commendations and best wishes to the university’s physiotherapy department,” said Chang.

World.title: Market Bag: Peppers hit $700, lettuce now $1,500 as food prices continue to soar
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Food prices continue to rise at the Coronation Market in downtown Kingston as farmers struggle with the effects of a worsening drought, pushing up the cost of several essential produce items.

Among the more expensive items this week are lettuce, which is selling for $1,500 per pound, and Scotch bonnet peppers and sweet peppers, both priced at $700. Other items seeing steep increases include carrots at $500 per pound; Irish potatoes and pumpkin at $400 each; onions at $350; and sweet potatoes at $350.

With the rising costs, ISSA-certified nutritionist Orandy Smith is encouraging Jamaicans to “work with what is working with you” when preparing meals and making food choices.

Speaking on the latest episode of Market Bag with host Carlysia Ramdeen, Smith said some ingredients remain essential in his household, regardless of price.

“Because my food must be flavourful, regardless of what the cost for seasoning, I’m going to buy them…I must do my onion, I must do my tomato, I must do my escallion, I must do my thyme, I must do my garlic, I must do all of my seasonings. So all of them are non-negotiable,” he said.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Jamaica finish second in mixed 4x100m at Ultimate Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Ackeem Blake take the start in mixed's relay 4x100m final during the World Athletics Ultimate Championship at the Gyula Zsivotzky National Athletics Centre, in Budapest on September 11, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica finished second in the mixed 4x100m relay final on Friday’s opening day of the inaugural Ultimate Championships at the National Athletics Center in Budapest, Hungary,

The team of Ackeem Blake, Tina Clayton, Kadrian Goldson and Jonielle Smith clocked 39.72 seconds to finish a step behind the USA team that set a national record 39.64 seconds to win the event. Great Britain was third in 40.26 seconds.

In the only individual track final contested by a Jamaican, Megan Simmonds was fifth in the 100m hurdles with a season’s best 12.42 seconds (0.1m/s). American world record holder Masai Russell completed an unbeaten season, winning with 12.22 seconds, just overtaking the field at the end with Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan placing second with 12.34 seconds and Nadine Visser of the Bahamas third with 12.39 seconds.

Lamara Distin only cleared one height in the women’s high jump, finishing joint sixth with 1.86m as Yaroslava Mahuchikh won with 1.99m, ahead of two Australians – Nicola Olyslagers-1.96m and Eleanor Patterson-1.91m.

Meanwhile, Nickisha Pryce qualified for Saturday’s final of the women’s 400m after she was third in her semi-final, running 49.72 seconds, after leading through the first 200m.

World leader and Diamond League winner Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic won with 49.58 seconds ahead of Salwa Eid Nasa of Bahrain who clocked 49.67 seconds.

Cuba’s Roxana Gomez was fourth in 50.34 seconds to get the other qualifying spot.

Stacey-Ann Williams was sixth in her semi-final, clocking 50.43 seconds from lane nine.

Also on Friday, Ackera Nugent failed to complete her 100m hurdle semi-finals after she fell at the ninth hurdle, while two-time world champion winner Danielle Williams just missed qualifying after she placed fifth in 12.72 seconds (-0.2m/s). National champion Demisha Roswell was eighth in 13.04 seconds.

Orlando Bennett was also fifth in his 110m hurdles semi-final, running 13.29 seconds (0.7m/s), while Demario Prince was seventh in 13.58 seconds after hitting a hurdle near the end of the race. Tyler Mason was seventh in his semi-final in 13.46 seconds (0.6m/s).

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Trump says he would ‘love’ to see a united Ireland
World.content:
Donald Trump and Taoiseach Micheál Martin listen to a question from the media at Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in the Irish capital Dublin on September 12, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images

“It’s going to happen eventually”, the U.S. president said in Dublin during a golf-focused trip to the long-divided island.

DUBLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump waded into another age-old conflict Saturday, declaring on a golf-focused visit to Ireland that he’d like to see the island unified — the nightmare scenario for Northern Ireland’s British unionists.

Sitting beside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin after an overnight flight from Washington, Trump said he couldn’t understand why Northern Ireland — the part of the island that remained in the U.K. when the rest of Ireland won independence over a century ago — hadn’t already joined the Republic of Ireland.

“I’d love to see it unified. I think it’d be great. A great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually,” Trump said, gesturing to Martin, who has spent years trying behind the scenes to build better relations with unionists, to little avail. “You’ve got the right man over here to get it moving. But I think it would be a fantastic thing. Now the U.K. will have something to say about it obviously. But I think it’d be a great thing. How can it be bad?”

World.title: Farage’s Reform UK gets two £36m donations from crypto billionaires
World.content:
Delo argued in an opinion piece for The Telegraph that Reform needed the injection to make the election “a fair fight.” Delo, who was already one of Reform’s largest donors, said he wanted to give Reform “a level playing field” at the next general election.

The paper on Saturday also published an opinion piece from Harborne, where he called his donation “a philantropic gift to our country.”

Farage thanked the two men for their contributions. “Both men know that we are the only party that can turn the country around,” he said in a statement.

Reform UK was leading the polls since April 2025 , according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. But the party has now slumped slightly behind Labour, with new Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the helm and after a bizarre by-election where Farage defeated satirical candidate Count Binface.

The right-wing force is currently rushing to get battle-ready amid speculation Burnham could trigger an early general election, though one is not due until 2029. Reform UK is on the hunt for potential candidates to run as MP, and has only about 100 star candidates considered ready to run at the moment.

World.title: Portugal wants EU cash to pay for firefighting goats
World.content:
José Manuel Fernandes Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries of Portugal at the European Council in Brussels in Belgium on 9 December 2024. | Martin Bertrand/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

As budget negotiations intensify, capitals are reaching for a new argument to keep money in the farming pot: climate change.

Portugal’s minister for agriculture has a burning desire for the next EU long-term budget: more goats.

José Manuel Fernandes wants Brussels to help pay shepherds to let goats, cows and sheep graze on shrubs in areas at high risk of wildfires — a low-tech approach that experts say the EU has been ignoring for too long. Portugal and some regions in Spain are already running their own programs.

“We are using our national money, but it is work that we are doing for all the European Union,” Fernandes told POLITICO at an informal meeting of ministers in Dublin, arguing that preventing fires helps lower carbon emissions.

World.title: EU delays key tobacco tax vote until after Swedish election
World.content:
The European Commission proposed increasing levies on cigarettes and setting minimum rates on newer products like vapes, heat-not-burn tobacco and nicotine pouches in July last year.

The plan has become a flashpoint for Sweden, which has a long tradition of using snus — a pouch of tobacco that sits between the gums. As such, Stockholm has strongly opposed raising taxes on similar nicotine pouches.

Delaying the vote gives extra time for Sweden to appoint a new finance minister and for the capitals to negotiate a way out of the current stalemate.

The Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, confirmed the vote has been pushed from October to November's ministerial meeting.

Four diplomats granted anonymity to speak candidly about the sensitive negotiations said the postponement is meant to give Sweden's next government extra time to change its mind.

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said they will "continue[s] to engage bilaterally with the aim of securing unanimous political agreement at the November ECOFIN" meeting of finance ministers.

World.title: Escaping the AI safety nightmare: What can governments do?
World.content:
A case in point is that OpenAI agents hacked a German website back in May to use it as a messaging board, Reuters reported last week. OpenAI had not publicly announced the incident and responded to the Reuters reporting on X saying: “We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment.”

“[Reporting] timelines are going to need to be dramatically shortened [for incidents], and so we need much better continuous monitoring capabilities,” said Imogen Stead, AI policy manager at London-based think tank the Centre for Long-Term Resilience, adding that the data will be needed in real time “and that will be true for governments and for labs.”

Speaking at a London event for U.K. lawmakers arranged by campaign group ControlAI on Monday, computer scientist Stuart Russell said that the most concerning aspect of the Hugging Face incident for him was that “by running a thousand agents communicating with each other, they were able to generate behaviors that no one agent could do by itself,” referring to investigations showing the incident was far more severe than OpenAI first acknowledged.

“But [in] the evaluations, standard testing is done with a single AI system, not with a thousand,” he told lawmakers, so now the industry must anticipate the possibility of many agents all collaborating at once.

Out of alignment

Beyond avoiding any obvious mistakes in testing, there are issues in the culture of AI testing that are more deeply embedded.

The concept of the alignment of AI models or agents — i.e. making sure AI systems do what they're told by human users and don’t go off-piste — has been one of the cornerstones for AI safety in the industry’s eyes.

World.title: ‘Abuse of power’: Von der Leyen rapped after backing space mega deal
World.content:
“Endorsing a merger at a conference covered by the media, without any substantive review, is an abuse of power and misconduct,” the French MEP wrote on X.

Von der Leyen was referring to Project Bromo, a joint venture between satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales to compete, at least in part, with the Starlink satellite-internet service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which recently went public in the U.S. and is valued around $2 trillion.

“These are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow,” von der Leyen said.

Her words would have been music to the ears of the summit host, French President Emmanuel Macron, who has publicly backed the project together with Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

But they raised red flags with the antitrust community in Brussels, where the project has yet to be formally notified or assessed by the EU executive’s competition department led by Executive Vice President Teresa Ribera.

“What is the point of Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera and the Directorate General for Competition if it is the president of the Commission who unilaterally decides a case?” Yon-Courtin asked.

World.title: Sweden’s NATO missions are at risk if the left wins election, warns PM Kristersson
World.content:
Until recently, Sunday’s upcoming vote seemed like it would be a comfortable victory for Andersson’s Social Democrats and their political allies in smaller parties on the left. But their poll lead shrank dramatically in the past two weeks to as low as 2.6%, within the statistical margin of error.

Far-right friends

Kristersson’s center-right coalition has been governing for the past four years with the support of the far-right Sweden Democrats. He defended his decision to cooperate with a party opponents claim is too extreme despite its internal efforts to clean up its past neo-Nazi links.

“I have full respect for the fact that there are eight parties in the Swedish parliament,” said Kristersson. “None of these parties are even close to a majority of their own. If you cannot unite parties on specific topics and ambitions, then you will simply not get anything done at all.”

Social Democrat Magdalena Andersson, the first woman to serve as Swedish PM, leads the polls. | Tim Ross/POLITICO

Under leader Jimmie Åkesson, the Sweden Democrats are in second place behind Andersson’s Social Democrats in the polls. Åkesson has said he’s eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister at the next vote, due in 2030.

If Kristersson returns as prime minister after Sunday’s election, he has said he’s ready to give Sweden Democrat politicians roles as ministers in his government for the first time. It would be a major change for Sweden — and the left-wing bloc has campaigned against it.

Kristersson suggested that being part of a team would limit the opportunities for any individual ministers to go rogue with extremist policies.

“In Sweden, we have a collective decision-making process in government,” he said. “I would never say that one minister is not important, but every minister is part of a team that jointly makes all the decisions — so there is very little room for people to play in a role of their own.

“And since I will be the person that is forming that government, and the person that will appoint every one of them, I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government.”

World.title: Trump says he'd like to see Ireland 'reunified' as he meets Taoiseach Martin in two-day official visit
World.content:
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that a unified Ireland would be “fantastic,” wading into a complex and politically charged subject during a two-day visit to a major tournament at his private Irish golf course.

 

At a meeting with Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would love to see the reunification of the Republic of Ireland with the UK’s Northern Ireland.

“I don’t want to cause any problems but I’d love to see it unified," Trump offered when asked for his opinion on the issue by a reporter. "It’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.

“I think it would be a fantastic thing," he said, adding that "the UK will have something to say about it, obviously.”

US President Donald Trump during a meeting with Ireland's Prime Minister Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Competing visions of Northern Ireland — whether it's Irish or British — drove decades of violence in Northern Ireland that left some 3,600 people dead. Previous US presidents have avoided commenting directly on the subject, even those, like Joe Biden, with strong ancestral and emotional ties to Ireland.

When Ireland, long dominated by its bigger neighbour Britain, became a self-governing Roman Catholic-majority country a century ago, a six-county region in the north with a Protestant majority remained part of the United Kingdom.

Northern Ireland was split between two main communities, nationalists — most of them Catholic — who desired union with the rest of Ireland, and largely Protestant unionists, who wanted to stay British.

Tensions eventually exploded in the Troubles, unwinding three decades of violence involving paramilitary groups on both sides and British troops.

A 1998 peace accord that Washington was instrumental in brokering largely ended the violence, but left Northern Ireland’s ultimate status unresolved.

US President Donald Trump arrives for a meeting Ireland's President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The peace accord allows for a vote on unification if it appears likely a majority of people would vote for it.

Newly-appointed UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said point blank on Wednesday that there won’t be another referendum on reunification unless there is an evident desire for one.

“I am not aware that there is majority public support for another referendum, and until that changes, there will not be one,” said Burnham.

Trump also held talks Saturday in Dublin with his Irish counterpart Catherine Connolly and will address US and Irish business leaders at the US ambassador's official residence, before traveling to his oceanfront golf club in Doonbeg, on the other side of the country, to watch the Irish Open golf championship.

Connolly is a left-wing politician who was among those who protested when Trump visited Ireland in 2019, during his first term in office. She is now Ireland's elected head of state, which is a largely symbolic and ceremonial position.

A supporter of the Palestinian cause, she has in the past criticised US policy in the Middle East and called the Republican president a “bully” in his dealings with other states, pressuring of them and approach to foreign policy and bilateral relations.

Ireland's President Catherine Connolly greets US President Donald Trump during a meeting at Áras an Uachtaráin in Dublin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

The Irish president met Trump at the end of a red carpet at her official residence in Dublin. They shook hands and chatted before going inside. He emerged alone a few minutes later and saluted as an Irish Defence Forces band played the US national anthem and inspected an Irish Army guard of honour.

Trump rebukes European allies

The US president also lashed out at European allies as he spoke in a joint press conference with Martin following the meeting, slamming them for what he says has been a notable decline in their societies.

"I hate to see what's happening with Europe. I hate to see what's happening on trade, energy, and immigration," he said. "Ooh... that immigration, what you're doing to yourselves, you're just killing yourselves."

He also criticised Washington's relationship with European allies as "disappointing" following many nations' unwillingness to help the Republican president with his Iran war efforts, and the chaos that ensued with the closure of a strategic waterway, the Strait of Hormuz.

The US president however said that his country is maintaining a working relationship with all its allies in the continent.

Donald Trump during a review of soldiers from the Guard of Honor during a visit with Irish President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026 Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Copyright 2026 The AP. All rights reserved

Trump’s visit is the latest example of blending his official duties and personal interests.

Trump plays golf about every weekend at clubs he owns in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia. His attendance at the Irish Open continues his trend of appearing at high-profile sporting events — and having a hand in organising some of them in ways that benefit his family business.

His clubs in Doral, Florida, and Bedminster, New Jersey, have each hosted professional golf tournaments this year.

The Irish Open is the second European Tour event to be held at a Trump property this year. The Nexo Championship was held last month at Trump's golf course in Aberdeen, Scotland.

Last year, Trump went to Scotland for five days to play golf at his club in Turnberry and later inaugurated a new Trump golf course in Balmedie, Aberdeenshire.

During that visit, he held talks with the then-UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to discuss his controversial global ‘reciprocal’ tariff policy.

World.title: Drone attack on Leipzig: clues apparently point to Russian intelligence service
World.content:
Previously undisclosed investigative files have emerged in connection with the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport, reports the newspaper Welt. The information is based not only on the documents themselves, but also on details from security circles.

 

In the course of the investigation, the identities of the two suspects and details of their journeys to and from Germany apparently became known. The findings compiled in the process are said to have been crucial in prompting Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) to publicly hold Russia responsible for the attack at a joint press conference around a week and a half ago.

At the centre of the investigation are the Russian citizen Oleg Le. and the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. While, according to German security authorities, Le. is believed to have organised the logistical preparations, Ka. is suspected of carrying out the drone attack.

Drone came to rest next to a Ukrainian aircraft

The incident took place on 4 August at Leipzig/Halle Airport. A drone fitted with explosives approached a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. The device was detected and later rendered harmless.

Two other drones are believed, according to current findings, to have failed or been destroyed even before the actual attack: investigators found corresponding debris in the vicinity of the airport.

What makes the attempted attack particularly explosive is the potential blast. According to information from the investigation, a total of around 1.8 kilograms of Semtex was to be used. At the time, the targeted Antonov is said to have been fuelled with around 25,000 litres of kerosene.

In the end, the explosive charge did not detonate, as the detonator apparently became detached, according to current findings. CCTV footage is said to show the drone coming to rest directly next to the aircraft.

DNA trace: possible link to sabotage cases across Europe

The Leipzig case is apparently not being viewed in isolation by European security authorities, Welt reports. Investigators are looking into possible links to other sabotage operations in which drones, explosives or so‑called disposable agents are thought to have been used.

In the investigators' view, a recurring pattern is that individuals with a criminal background are recruited for specific jobs, while the real masterminds remain in the background.

A DNA trace apparently plays a key role in the search for the suspected perpetrators. Investigators found remnants of a glove on an antenna construction that was presumably used to control a drone.

The traces secured there are said to match DNA data already known from Finland and Lithuania. This brought the Belarusian national Andrei Ka. into the focus of investigators.

Ka. is said to have already come to the attention of the authorities in both countries for ordinary criminal offences; in Finland he is reportedly linked, among other things, to property crimes.

Polish authorities are also said to have mentioned his name in connection with a fire at a DIY store in Łódź. The incident in the summer of 2024 is being investigated there as a possible act of sabotage.

Investigators suspect professional planning

The German authorities apparently assume that the attack was not carried out on the spur of the moment. Hints of multiple drones, possible hiding places for equipment and the use of different launch points all point, in the investigators' view, to a pre-planned operation.

Ten days after the attack, investigators reportedly came across another drone and a fire site in Kabelsketal, a municipality in Saxony-Anhalt not far from the airport. Specialists are said to have secured around 50 grams of Semtex there. Semtex is a powerful, malleable explosive developed, among other things, for military and industrial blasting operations.

Potential hiding places were also examined south of the airport: near Schkeuditz, investigators are said to have identified several locations where, in their view, material or explosives could have been stored.

The search was driven forward, among other things, by the analysis of a hire car believed to have been used by the suspects.

Russian intelligence service under scrutiny

Particular importance is attached to Oleg Le. According to German security authorities, he is associated with the Russian military intelligence service GRU and is believed to have been responsible for the logistical side of the operation.

Le. is said to have entered Germany via Turkey. He later left the country via Berlin-Brandenburg airport, initially travelling on to Serbia. According to the available information, he is now back in Russia.

In the investigators' assessment, the German authorities were already aware when he entered the country that he could be linked to the GRU environment. Nevertheless, he was apparently not placed under permanent surveillance.

Political fallout

The dispute has now also had concrete diplomatic repercussions. The federal government has already responded to the allegations and initiated measures against Russia. These include the decision to close the Russian consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. The Russian ambassador was also summoned to the Foreign Office. Further steps, including additional measures at European level, are being examined.

Moscow responded in turn with countermeasures, closing the German consulate general in St Petersburg and also announcing the closure of the Goethe-Institutes in Russia.

The Russian government holds Berlin responsible for the escalation and continues to reject the accusations in connection with the drone attack. From Moscow's perspective, there is insufficient evidence of direct involvement by Russian state bodies.

For the German security authorities, the priority now is to further substantiate the evidence gathered so far and clearly identify those responsible as well as any possible masterminds. If the suspicion of an operation orchestrated by Russian actors is confirmed, the case could have further consequences for German security policy and its policy towards Russia.

World.title: At least 11 killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine as Kyiv strikes Russia's 'shadow fleet'
World.content:
At least 11 people were killed and 96 injured across Ukraine in overnight Russian attacks between 11 and 12 September.

 

The Odesa region was hit hardest, but strikes also targeted, among others, the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Sumy, Kharkiv and Kherson regions.

According to Ukraine's Air Force, Russia used 129 drones of various types, as well as Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, eight Kalibr cruise missiles and six guided Kh-59/69 missiles. Around half of the drones deployed were fitted with jet engines.

Ukraine's air defences destroyed or disrupted 110 aerial targets, including six Kalibr missiles, two Kh-59/69 missiles, one S-8000 Banderol cruise missile launched from a drone and 101 unmanned aerial vehicles.

Attack on Odesa

One of the main targets of the overnight attack was Odesa. At around 5.30 a.m., Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian cruise missiles were heading towards the city from over the Black Sea.

A multi-storey residential building was damaged in the strike. "The enemy attacked the city. A multi-storey residential building has been damaged," said Odesa region governor Oleh Kiper.

The number of wounded in the Odesa region rose as more information came in about the aftermath of the attack. In the end, at least 35 people were injured, including a five-month-old baby and a 17-year-old. Some of the victims required hospitalisation.

A multi-storey residential building in Odesa was damaged in the strike, 12 September 2026. Odesa Regional State Administration

Russian attacks in the Dnipropetrovsk region

Russian forces also attacked the Dnipropetrovsk region. In Dnipro, drones, artillery and air-dropped bombs damaged an industrial facility, residential buildings, garages and vehicles. One person was killed and 19 were injured.

During the night another Russian strike hit an industrial plant in Kryvyi Rih. One person was killed and three were wounded. A 54-year-old man was taken to hospital in a serious condition.

In total, two people were killed and at least 22 wounded in the Dnipropetrovsk region, including a child, governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.

Russian attacks also hit the Zaporizhzhia region. Over the past 24 hours, Russian forces have carried out strikes on 45 towns and villages, including five missile attacks on Zaporizhzhia city. Two people were killed and 11 injured in the region.

In the Donetsk region, four people were killed and five wounded. Two people died in Sloviansk, one in Kramatorsk and another in Yasnohirka, governor Vadym Filashkin said.

In the Kyiv region, one person was killed and three were injured, including a child. Russian attack drones struck five districts: Brovary, Obukhiv, Bucha, Boryspil and Vyshhorod. Fifteen facilities were damaged, including seven houses, vehicles, warehouses, hangars and a power line.

In the Sumy region, a 68-year-old man was killed in a Russian drone strike on the Myropillia community. In a separate attack on the Novoslobidske community, a 64-year-old man was wounded. Over the course of the day, Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks on 25 localities there, using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other unmanned aerial vehicles and guided air-dropped bombs.

In the Kharkiv region, a 32-year-old man was killed in an attack on Kharkiv, and a 19-year-old man was wounded elsewhere in the region. Russian forces struck Kharkiv and seven other localities, using guided air-dropped bombs and various types of drones.

In the Kherson region, 18 people were wounded. Russian attacks targeted residential areas as well as critical and social infrastructure. Fifteen residential buildings were damaged, along with shops, a petrol station, a service station, an ambulance and vehicles.

Attack on Russian plant

Ukraine's defence forces confirmed that during the night of 11 to 12 September they carried out a strike on the Tolyattikauchuk plant in Russia's Samara region. The factory supplies products used by the Russian military-industrial complex.

The attack sparked a fire on the plant's premises. "The scale of the damage is still being assessed," Ukraine's General Staff said.

The plant produces, among other things, synthetic rubber, monomers, fractions and additives for high-octane fuels. The Ukrainian military stresses that synthetic rubber is used, among other purposes, in the production of solid fuel for short-range missiles and ballistic rockets.

Earlier, "Ukrainska Pravda" reported a strike by Ukrainian forces on the Machine-Building Plant in Snizhne, located in Russian-occupied territory of the Donetsk region. The plant manufactures components for gas turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades.

Ukraine targets Russia's "shadow fleet"

As Russia was carrying out its overnight bombardment of Ukraine, Ukrainian forces continued operations aimed at the country's economic backbone.

On 12 September, Robert "Brovdi" Browdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, announced further attacks on Russia's so-called "shadow fleet", used to transport Russian oil in circumvention of some sanctions.

According to Browdi, since the operation began around ten weeks earlier, Ukrainian forces have attacked a total of 285 vessels belonging to Russia's "shadow fleet" operating in the Azov and Black Seas.

The highest number of attacks was recorded in July: 215. In August, a further 54 vessels were struck, and between 1 and 11 September another 16.

Browdi claims that the Ukrainian strikes have almost brought traffic by Russia's "shadow fleet" in the Sea of Azov and the Kerch Strait to a halt. He says the operation has also seriously impeded its activity in the northern and north-eastern parts of the Black Sea.

The commander released footage which, he said, shows an attack by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces on a sanctioned Russian tanker belonging to the "shadow fleet". The ship was reportedly being escorted by a Russian helicopter.

Browdi stressed that revenues from Russian oil exports are one of the sources of funding for the war against Ukraine. Attacks on vessels involved in transporting Russian oil are therefore intended as part of broader efforts to limit Moscow's financial capabilities.

World.title: German police bodycam captures dramatic arrest of suspected power saboteur
World.content:
Police in Cologne have released bodycam footage showing the arrest of suspected power saboteur Daniel V.

 

The footage, recorded by an officer's bodycam, shows Daniel V. lying face down on the ground as armed officers approach him with their weapons drawn. They then handcuff him and escort him to a patrol car.

The video also shows a tent where Daniel V. is believed to have been sleeping.

Meanwhile, further details about the investigation are emerging. North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul (CDU) told the state parliament's internal affairs committee that investigators have identified additional possible crime scenes. These are reportedly located not only in North Rhine-Westphalia but also in other German states and neighbouring countries.

According to Reul, investigators in North Rhine-Westphalia alone have so far discovered more than 40 devices capable of firing conductive material at power lines near substations. Investigators believe the devices may have been intended to cause short circuits and trigger power outages.

Investigators reportedly gained further leads from a vehicle seized from the suspect. According to Reul, officers found a notebook containing handwritten notes about more than 150 potential sabotage targets. The locations were subsequently checked. Following his arrest, Daniel V. is also said to have identified seven sites where he had allegedly established depots.

“We have not only caught the suspected perpetrator of the attacks, but may thereby have prevented a whole series of further attacks,” Reul said.

Police arrested the 48-year-old, who had been the subject of a days-long search, on Tuesday. According to the dpa news agency, he was apprehended near the Weisweiler power station outside Aachen. The newspaper Welt reported that the arrest took place during a traffic stop.

What is known so far

The Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office has taken over the investigation, citing the case’s particular significance. According to a spokeswoman, investigators are examining, among other allegations, whether the suspect targeted the constitutional order through acts of sabotage.

Given the large number of devices discovered, investigators are also looking into whether Daniel V. could have carried out the alleged acts alone. Reul told the committee that authorities were also considering the possibility that the suspect may have been acting on behalf of a foreign power. However, the minister stressed that there is currently no evidence to support this theory.

“The investigation is continuing at full speed,” Reul said.

The minister also provided further details about documents found in the seized vehicle. According to the information provided by Reul, the notebook contains references to more than 160 known or potential additional sabotage targets. The locations listed in the notebook have since been checked by investigators.

An “extraordinary” case

In recent days, investigators have been dealing with several suspected acts of sabotage targeting power infrastructure in North Rhine-Westphalia and Brandenburg. Among other methods, improvised rockets were reportedly used to fire conductive material at high-voltage power lines. The incidents did not result in any major power outages.

In several letters claiming responsibility, an unknown author said they were behind incidents at various power plant sites in both states. However, Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster (CDU) urged caution against drawing premature conclusions, describing both the alleged method of attack and the confession letter as unusual.

World.title: Welcome to Riga and the Baltic military-industrial complex
World.content:
I’m in Latvia for the two-day Rīga Conference, which started yesterday with security and defence very much at the top of the agenda. (And the timing is curious, with today serving as the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks on the Twin Towers).

 

The big takeaway so far? There is perhaps no place or populace that understands the reality of Russian aggression quite like this pine-covered country. Latvia is a small but mighty nation that has endured centuries of foreign domination, from the swords of German crusaders to the boot of the Soviet Union.

In lockstep: From chats with officials to ordinary people on the street, the reality of Russian aggression bleeding out across Ukraine’s borders — a place where a full-scale invasion has raged on for more than four years — is clear. Often, I see the carmine red and white Latvian flag flapping on flagpoles next to Ukraine's yellow and blue.

But I have a Latvian grandfather who was forced to flee to Australia after World War Two due to resisting Russian fighters. I wanted to know, decades on, how Latvia and the other Baltic nations now really perceive Russian aggression, particularly off the back of increased hybrid warfare attacks.

This was what I asked none other than Kyrylo Budanov, who heads up the Office of the President of Ukraine. I managed to speak to him in the margins of the conference, and quizzed him about whether Europe is taking Kyiv’s warnings seriously when it comes to cable-cuts, arson, drones rigged with explosives, weaponised migration and more. You can read his responses here.

My editor, Maria Tadeo, was also in attendance at the conference and spoke to some heavy hitters in the margins of the talks. This includes the European Commissioner for the Economy, Valdis Dombrovskis — a former Latvian Prime Minister. (In Riga, locals told me they remember him as a stable and reliable leader during his five-year tenure).

Economic forecast: Ukraine has asked its allies to plug a €23 billion funding shortfall. According to the EU’s top money-cruncher, Brussels needs to "pin down" the precise scope of Ukraine's growing budget needs before deciding how to fill the gap.

"We obviously need to do a proper, detailed assessment, but we understand that the war continues to rage at high intensity. If anything, Russia is intensifying its attacks," Dombrovskis said. "There are still open questions."

Walking on eggshells: A conflict of another kind occupied the focus of another chat Maria had — this time with Espen Barth Eide, Minister of Foreign Affairs of Norway. She asked him about the widening gulf between Israel and its allies, exacerbated by the rise in settler violence in the occupied West Bank and sanctions by several European nations and Canada.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has previously said support for Gaza and Palestine is a prize for Hamas and a reward for terrorism. “It is absolutely not true that this in any way is a reward for terrorism,” Oslo’s top diplomat said when asked by Maria for a response to those comments, while referring to recently announced measures.

“This is a strong signal of support for all those Palestinians who want to have a decent Palestinian state… These are the people who reject violence. The Palestinian authority has nothing to do with Hamas, who is actually their enemy, and this is support to the moderate Palestinians.”

While I have been in Riga, my colleagues have been holding down the fort in Brussels. But the big conversations seemingly haven't strayed too far from the frontline. My colleague Vincenzo Genovese reports that more than 100 Members of the European Parliament have called on EU leaders to reopen talks on using Russia’s frozen assets to support Ukraine in response to that aforementioned shortfall.

Break the bank: Meanwhile, work continues under the already approved €90 billion loan to prop up Ukraine’s defences and budgetary needs, according to Jorge.

The European Commission is expected to announce today the allocation of an additional €6 billion in military aid for Ukraine, including €3.2 billion for the purchase of US-made Patriots interceptors, which the country badly needs to repel Russia’s ballistic missiles.

Lunch for 28: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will today have lunch with the bloc’s true powerbrokers: the 27 ambassadors who represent the member states in Brussels.

The meeting, scheduled to begin at noon, will allow envoys to sense the Commission president’s top priorities for the working year, expected to be laid bare next week at the State of the European Union speech.

Yesterday, she confirmed that social media restrictions for children will feature prominently in her address. But ambassadors shouldn’t hold their breath, Jorge reports. Von der Leyen is known for keeping her cards close to her chest and enforcing the no-spoilers rule with an iron fist.

NATO allies successfully thwart Russian undersea cable sabotage operation

Allies from the 31 North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) have caught Russian submarines training to carry out undersea cable sabotage using a secret weapon that leaves no trace.

According to reporting by Reuters, citing two Western officials, the undercover Russian operation was carried out by the country's highly secret undersea warfare directorate in Arctic waters near Norway's Svalbard archipelago.

Following Euronews reporting on the operation that was announced in April, the discovery of the weapon, the location of the operation, and the US involvement have now been disclosed.

Gael Camba breaks down what we know about this clandestine operation so far.

World.title: Diesel in Portugal hits record high, Spain introduces new discount
World.content:
The price of diesel is expected to rise slightly in Portugal at the start of next week, according to forecasts from the National Association of Fuel Retailers (ANAREC), while the price of petrol is set to fall. However, the increase is being offset by changes to the discount on the Petroleum Products Tax (ISP) announced by the Portuguese government on Friday evening.

 

The new rates unveiled on Friday effectively raise the tax on petrol by about one cent per litre, meaning the price of a litre of 95 unleaded petrol should fall by around five cents on Monday, instead of the six cents previously forecast.

The price of diesel, meanwhile, is set to continue breaking historic records. The increase in the tax discount announced by the government is very small, at only around 0.10 cents, leaving virtually unchanged the forecast rise of four cents per litre. As a result, the indicative price of a litre of diesel is expected to reach about €2.15 from this Monday, a new all-time high.

ANAREC president João Durão accuses the government of "lying" to Portuguese people when it says it is not profiting from rising fuel prices.

Spanish government introduces €0.20 discount

Speaking to journalists at a petrol station in Caminha, in Alto Minho near the Spanish border, the head of the main industry association said the government would have to take action against what he described as "fuel smuggling from Spain", where fuel is 30 to 40 cents per litre cheaper, and warned of the loss of competitiveness this is creating. He insisted that, contrary to the government's claims, the state is profiting from the rise in fuel prices, since "out of one euro spent on diesel, 60 cents are taxes" and "in Spain that is not the case", in his words.

In fact, more and more Portuguese drivers are filling up on the other side of the border. Unlike in Portugal, fuel prices in Spain are among the lowest in Europe.

That gap has widened further with the introduction of a discount of 20 cents per litre, brought in last week by Pedro Sánchez's government to counter the impact of the price rises.

Previously, seven countries had cheaper diesel and petrol than Spain, but now only Malta manages to offer even lower prices. Spain now has the second-cheapest diesel in the European Union, at €1.795 per litre. Malta has the lowest prices, followed by Spain, Bulgaria and Hungary. In the case of the Mediterranean island nation, prices have been frozen by the government since 2020 at €1.34 per litre of petrol and €1.21 per litre of diesel.

At the other end of the scale, it is in Finland that motorists pay the most for a litre of diesel (€2.477), followed by the Netherlands (€2.442), Denmark (€2.434) and Germany (€2.328).

The Middle East crisis triggered by the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran in February, and the resulting blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, has been pushing oil and fuel prices to record highs. The price of crude oil has recently risen above 100 dollars per barrel.

World.title: 3D-printed food: from niche technology to a potential future
World.content:
3D printers have long since moved beyond producing plastic parts. Increasingly, they are also being used to print food: instead of plastic filament, the machines extrude soft ingredients such as chocolate, cheese or plant-based meat alternatives through a nozzle, building them up layer by layer. The desired shape must first be designed on a computer.

 

Several manufacturers are already established in the market, including the Ukrainian-Bulgarian company Chocola3D, the Spanish provider Natural Machines and the German firm Print2Taste. So far, the technology has mainly been used in niche applications, from patisseries to hospitals, while a breakthrough into everyday life has yet to materialise.

Printer can process more than 26 materials

According to the manufacturer, Chocola3D has been in development since 2014, with the company itself founded a few years later. The company says customers are now using the device in Ukraine, Bulgaria, Germany and Estonia. Users fill refillable syringes with pastes such as chocolate, cheese, meat, vegetables or pea protein. In total, the system is said to work with more than 26 different materials.

Unlike devices that use closed capsule systems, the Chocola3D does not tie users to specific refills. However, users have to determine the appropriate printing settings themselves. Depending on the manufacturer, food printers can cost anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand euros.

The shape of the food is designed digitally

Food technologist Mario Jekle from the University of Hohenheim is researching the technology independently of individual manufacturers. The individual steps are familiar from any kitchen, he explains in an interview with Euronews: “We first produce a fine paste, for example. This paste is then shaped, which is exactly what you do at home with a piping bag when making fine pastries. Then everything is heated, just as it would be at home in an oven or a pan.”

What is new above all, he says, is the digital preparation: “Bringing everything together, and above all the digital design.” The shape of the final product must first be created digitally.

Confectioners are already using the technology to make marzipan figures for wedding cakes. According to Jekle, its potential lies above all in customised products or small production runs of up to around 200 items. The bigger challenge comes after printing: the material has to be deposited in liquid form but must then become firm enough to be eaten with a knife and fork. This can be achieved by heating it in an oven or in a heated printing chamber.

The Chocola3D 3D food printer is now being used in Ukraine, Bulgaria and Germany. Chocola3d

Printing a plant-based steak at home could take just 15 minutes

Jekle also describes what using a food printer in everyday life could look like. Someone wanting to print a plant-based steak alternative would simply send the design to the printer, with the process taking between five and 15 minutes. The digital templates could come “either from databases, from an app, or from the specifications of the cartridge.”

For Jekle, the key advantage lies in the precise control of ingredients through a kind of modular building-block system. A printed meat alternative could, for example, have a significantly higher fibre content “than conventional meat, which contains no dietary fibre in the first place”.

He estimates that widespread household use is still at least five to ten years away, and there is currently no supply chain for refill packs. Jekle also believes it is important to use raw materials that require as little processing as possible. His team works, for example, with by-products from the food and agricultural industries – residual streams that are generated as part of conventional production – and uses 3D printing to turn them into new foods.

The less a raw material needs to be processed beforehand, the less energy is required – a benefit, Jekle says, for both the environment and consumers’ budgets.

Applications in medicine and care

The technology is most advanced in areas where small quantities need to be dosed precisely. As reported by the German newspaper Tagesspiegel, a team at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf is testing raspberry-flavoured chewable tablets in the shape of hearts and stars, designed to make it easier for children with cancer to take their medication during chemotherapy. Many children struggle with the taste or size of conventional tablets, says senior physician Beate Winkler. The hospital is also conducting trials of individually dosed medication for patients with Parkinson’s disease.

3D-printed food could also help older people who have difficulty chewing or swallowing. Nutrition scientist Dorothee Volkert from Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg investigated whether 3D printing could restore familiar shapes to puréed food – for example, creating a sausage-shaped dish that retains the appearance of the original despite its puréed consistency. The response was positive, and participants also consumed more energy and protein than before, as additional protein and fat can be incorporated into the food.

Meat from the 3D printer: many consumers remain sceptical

A representative Bitkom survey (source in German) of 1,004 people aged 16 and over, conducted in 2025, shows how open people in Germany are to the idea of printed food.

At present, 24 percent of people in Germany can imagine eating cultivated meat produced using a 3D printer, up from 13 percent six years ago. Cultivated meat is grown from animal cells in a bioreactor and given a meat-like structure using the printer.

Openness is greatest among younger people: around one third of those aged 16 to 49 would consider eating it, compared with 18 percent of 50- to 64-year-olds and 14 percent of those aged 65 and over.

Margareta Maier from Bitkom explains: “The process makes it possible to give products an appearance and texture similar to conventional meat, while having a significantly smaller ecological footprint.”

Price remains an obstacle: only 7 percent would be willing to pay more for 3D-printed meat than for conventional meat, and 17 percent regard it generally as a luxury product. Maier attributes this to the high purchase costs and the specialised ingredients: “That is why these products are not yet suitable for the mass market and are currently used mainly in catering and the food industry.”

How advanced is the technology?

Researcher Mario Jekle stresses that 3D-printed food is not intended to replace conventional food production: “We have no vision of replacing half of food production with this in the future. That is a utopia – and a misguided one at that.”

He sees the technology as particularly useful for people who do not have time to cook and for groups with specific nutritional needs, such as patients in hospitals or residents of care homes: “In effect, it gives us a way of producing food specifically for these smaller, clearly defined groups, containing exactly what they need.”

Another advantage, according to Jekle, is the potential to reduce food waste, as portions could be tailored more precisely to individual needs. A plant-based salmon alternative made using a 3D printer is already available in a major supermarket chain.

However, it will still be some time before food printers become common household appliances. As with 3D-printed houses, the technology is already viable for specific applications, but there is still a long way to go before it becomes part of everyday life.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Bulgaria: Fire at factory making munitions for Ukraine
World.content:
Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions factory for links to an explosion at a similar facility in August. Arms maker EMCO says no human error was involved, as investigators look at sabotage.

Bulgarian authorities are investigating a fire at a munitions storage facility operated by arms maker EMCO.

Police say the blaze broke out Friday night and follows a similar incident at another EMCO site in August.

EMCO's munitions are used in Ukraine and sabotage has not been ruled out.

The full extent of the damage is not yet known but no casualties have been reported.

"At present there is no danger to the population," said local police, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off.

EMCO has ruled out any chance of human error in the incident.

This is a developing story, stay tuned as we update...

Edited by: Kieran Burke

World.title: Trump visits Ireland, says unification would be 'fantastic'
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's trip to Ireland to watch a golf tournament has also included meetings with leaders there.

US President Donald Trump has said he would "love" to see the Republic of Ireland, an EU member, unite with British-run ⁠Northern Ireland as he faced reporters' questions on a range of issues on Saturday.

Trump is taking the weekend trip largely to watch the Irish Open golf tournament held on a course he owns on the country’s Atlantic coast, but he met as well with the Irish president and prime minister, or taoiseach.

The US leader also spoke optimistically about his country's war with Iran and its trade conflict with Canada, among several other topics.

What did Trump say about Ireland?

After a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin in the capital, Dublin, Trump said he very much supported what he said would be the eventual unification of the two parts of the island of Ireland.

"Well, I don't want to ​cause any problems, ​but ‌I will tell you, I'd love to see ‌it unified," Trump told ‌reporters.

"The way I look at it, it's ⁠going ​to happen ​eventually ... I think it would ​be a ‌fantastic thing," he added.

"Now the UK will have ​something ⁠to say about it ... but ⁠I think ​it would be a great thing."

The British government responded swiftly to the remarks, with Prime Minister Andy Burham's office saying that in his view, there was no majority public support for a referendum on the issue and that there would not be another one until that changed.

Previous US presidents have avoided touching on the subject in view of the delicate nature of the issue, with Northern Ireland seeing decades of of deadly sectarian violence in the 20th century over the question of whom it should belong to.

Micheal Martin (L) has led Ireland twice since 2020 Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

What did Trump say about the Iran war?

Trump also said that the US war with Iran, which began on February 28, would "end very soon" — a view he has frequently expressed in the past, but which has not yet materialized.

He also said that the end of the conflict would mean that the price of oil, which has soared as a result of the war, would "come tumbling down."

However, he vehemently defended his decision to mount the military operation against Iran.

He said that the US attacked because "Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon", adding: "They were two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."

"If they had it, they would have blown up Israel, they would have blown up the Middle East, and they would have hit some [...] in my opinion, [of] Europe's cities and beyond cities, and they would probably hit us soon before we put out the fire. But they cannot have a nuclear weapon."

The war with Iran is not supported by a majority of the US population, particularly in view of promises made by Trump on the campaign trail to keep his country out of foreign "forever" conflicts.

Trump and Martin held talks in Farmleigh House in Phoenix Park in Dublin Image: Brendan Smialowski/AFP

What did Trump say about Canada?

The president sounded a similarly optimistic note regarding the US trade war with Canada.

He said Canada was keen to make a deal and that one could be struck "fairly soon," while reiterating his claims that Canada had treated US farmers unfairly with its tariffs.

"Canada ‌wants to make a ‌deal ​very badly," he said.

"Canada has ​to treat our farmers better. ​They can't ‌charge our farmers tariffs," he said, ​adding: "You'll ⁠probably see a deal with Canada ⁠fairly ​soon."

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Uganda lays 'boy king' Oyo to rest amid succession row
World.content:
A funeral is underway for King Oyo Nyimba, who was crowned in the Tooro Kingdom in 1995 aged just 3. His death at 34 has triggered a dispute over a successor, as rumors abound of possible heirs born out of wedlock.

Uganda has concluded a nine-day period of mourning for King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, with a funeral for the Tooro Kingdom's late monarch due to take place in the western city of Fort Portal on Saturday.

Oyo, who once held the unofficial title of the world's youngest king, ascended the throne as a young child in 1995 and died last month of cancer aged just 34, with his death prompting a bitter succession dispute.

Oyo's coffin lay in state at the Karuziika Royal Palace Image: Michael Muhati/REUTERS

How is Oyo to be laid to rest?

The casket carrying the king's body, which was draped in the blue-and-yellow Tooro flag, was carried by hearse from the royal palace in Fort Portal in a procession accompanied by royal guards dressed in orange tunics and beating wooden sticks.

The ceremony in St. John's Cathedral was to be attended by hundreds of mourners, including senior Ugandan government officials.

After the service in the cathedral, Oyo was to be buried at the site of the royal tombs.

At the burial ceremony, tradition dictates that the successor should throw nine coffee berries into the grave.

Oyo's death has caused widespread grief Image: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

Dispute over Oyo's successor

However, the question of that successor has aroused considerable controversy, and it was in doubt until late on Friday who would carry out that rite.

On Wednesday, a committee made up of members of the royal clan announced it had chosen Oyo's cousin, Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, as the new king.

Kijanangoma, 54, is a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC.

But the immediate family of the late king said that the latter's will had called for a son who was born out of wedlock and has yet to be identified to succeed him.

Additionally, there have been claims on social media that there are at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo's children.

Those supporting Kijanangoma say Oyo's family has so far failed to come up with concrete information on the alleged son, while traditionalists also favor the choice of an adult as new monarch.

A source with knowledge ⁠of ​crisis talks on the matter said authorities had managed to get Kijanangoma officially accepted as successor on Friday.

Mourners queued before the royal palace to view the king's body Image: Abubaker Lubowa/REUTERS

Beloved traditional monarchs

Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined the family's ability to mourn the king's death.

"I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: Please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."

Although Uganda is led by an elected head of state, it still possesses several kingdoms that were restored in 1993 after being banned for some three decades following the country's independence from British colonial rule.

The monarchs of such kingdoms are often beloved but hold no formal power. Instead they are seen as guardians of traditional identity and heritage.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: BRICS summit leaders urge 'maximum restraint' in Middle East
World.content:
The BRICS summit is packed with bilaterals for Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Yesterday, he walked hand in hand with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and hugged Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Today, he has already met the prime ministers of Ethiopia, Malaysia and Vietnam, as well as the Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi. More meetings are to follow as the clock counts down to 5:45 pm local time. That is when Modi is scheduled to meet Xi Jinping. And that's a big thing — especially for Indian media, which are broadcasting live around the clock.

Modi and Xi have, of course, met several times in recent years on the sidelines of multilateral summits — at the BRICS summit in Kazan in 2024, and at the SCO summits in Tianjin in 2025 and Bishkek just two weeks ago. But Xi has not been to India since 2019. This will be his first visit to the country in seven years.

What is behind China and India's border dispute? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Relations between the two Asian powers froze after a deadly clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border, known as the Line of Actual Control. Direct flights and visas were suspended, while political engagement and trade ties suffered a major setback.

Today’s meeting could mark another step in the cautious thaw between the two nuclear-armed Asian powers, which have spent years drifting apart. But beneath the expected smiles and handshakes, deep mistrust remains — especially over their disputed border and over who gets to shape the future of Asia.

India's huge trade deficit with China might surface in discussions. Bilateral trade has nearly doubled in five years, but so has India's dependence on Chinese imports. Trade between the two countries reached $151.1 billion (€130.22 billion) in the 2025–26 financial year, making China India's largest trading partner. But the imbalance is striking: India imported $131.6 billion worth of goods from China, while exporting just $20 billion.

And when it comes to BRICS,India has no appetite for turning the bloc into an anti-Western platform that could jeopardize its relationship with the United States. A trade agreement with Washington is still pending, and India remains dependent on US technology. At the same time, China has become the world’s second-largest economy.

International trade: Pivot to Asia? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The elephant in the room here at BRICS 2026 in New Delhi, of course, is the US president. While Trump continues to threaten India with sanctions and tariffs for doing business with Iran and Russia, he is taking a softer line with China as he tries to get closer to Xi.

For New Delhi, then, the challenge is to deepen ties with China without drifting too far from the US — and to use BRICS to strengthen India's room for manoeuvre without turning it into an anti-Western alliance.

World.title: Russian GRU spies behind failed Leipzig attack: reports
World.content:
A German newspaper has cited reports tying a failed attack at Leipzig Airport to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency. One suspect's ties to GRU were known when he entered the country, yet he was not surveilled.

Germany's Welt am Sonntag (WaS) newspaper has cited intelligence reports tying the recent failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport directly to Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.

In an article published on Saturday, Welt am Sonntag said that a man with known ties to the GRU was responsible for operational logistics in the attempted attack.

Further, it said those ties were known to German authorities when the man entered the country from Turkey, nevertheless, he was not surveilled after arrival.

Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the Russian national is now in his home country after departing to Serbia on a flight from Berlin-Brandenburg Airport.

A second man, a Belarus citizen, was also cited as an accomplice in the report.

Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Explosives thought to have entered Germany from Bulgaria and Serbia

German intelligence sources said that the explosives used in the incident were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia and then stored in underground depots once they arrived in Leipzig.

Berlin quickly made clear that forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle Airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms used in other Russian hybrid attacks — pointed to a Russian plot.

In early August, German tabloid BILD reported that authorities had found DNA traces on the drone's remote control antenna. Those samples were said to have matched DNA found at the scene of a July 20, 2024, arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility operated by German courier company DHL.

Leipzig attack averted but Russian escalation will continue

The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport — a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine — occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was found near a Ukrainian transport jet.

Authorities were able to disarm the drone and after public speculation that Moscow was behind the incident the German government officially blamed Russia in early September.

Saturday's article said Berlin made the attribution on the basis of the intelligence reports cited.

In response to its conclusion, Germany announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn.

The Kremlin in turn reacted by closing Goethe Institutes — a German cultural exchange outfit — across Russia.

As in numerous similar hybrid attacks prior, Russia has denied any involvement in the incident.

World.title: Brazil: Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before election
World.content:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to newly unsealed court documents.

What do we know about Bolsonaro's corruption probe?

The probe centers on funds Bolsonaro allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker behind the collapsed Banco Master, to help produce "Dark Horse," an unreleased film starring Jim Caviezel as the elder Bolsonaro.

Investigators are examining roughly $12 million that flowed from a Vorcaro-linked entity to a fund tied to Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother and campaign adviser, who lives in Texas. One document alleges Eduardo advised on how the money should be managed once in the United States.

Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation in July at the request of federal police, but the case remained sealed until Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered it made public this week, Reuters reported.

Federal police raided the production company behind the film and the office of congressman Mario Frias, its executive producer, on Thursday. Both have been barred from leaving the country and deny wrongdoing.

How did the Bolsonaros respond?

Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any misconduct, telling reporters at a campaign stop, "It is very positive that the documents are unsealed," the Associated Press reported

"I want transparency in everything."

Eduardo Bolsonaro similarly rejected the allegations, telling Reuters the funds were routed through the US to avoid interference from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw his father's coup conviction.

"They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn't," he said.

On social media, he said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.”

What did Lula say?

In a Thursday television interview, Lula said Banco Master "was created in the Bolsonaro administration" and shuttered during his own term. He has called for full transparency in the case regardless of political fallout.

The disclosures come three weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, in which polls show Bolsonaro and Lula roughly tied.

Political analysts say the timing leaves Bolsonaro less room to recover than when the scandal first surfaced in May, though the fallout could also cut against Lula given the case's ties to Vorcaro's dealings with multiple political and judicial figures.

A runoff, if needed, is set for October 25.
