World.title: Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019013/Frog Gone: China’s Beloved Traveling Game Is Going Offline
World.content:
A mobile game beloved by millions of Chinese users about a traveling frog is set to shut down after the game operator and the IP holder failed to reach a licensing agreement.

Announced Tuesday by its official account on microblogging platform Weibo, the game, Travel Frog: China Journey, will discontinue on Dec. 8.

“This time, the little frog is going on a long journey, with no set date of return,” the announcement read. “But that quiet companionship will always remain in our hearts.”

A video game insider told domestic media that the IP holder, Japanese gaming studio Hit-Point, sought harsher terms from domestic operator Lingxi Games, including stripping it of its right to collaborate with other companies and sell game-related merchandise. After multiple rounds of negotiations, the companies could not reach an agreement, though the insider disclosed that they are in a final round of talks.

Travel Frog, released in 2017, is an idle game, meaning gameplay progresses with little player input. Chinese users began downloading the Japanese version before tech giant Alibaba secured authorization to publish it exclusively in the Chinese mainland under its gaming division, Lingxi Games, a year later. By then, the original version was already popular, with iOS downloads in China alone exceeding 30 million.

At its peak, the game was more popular than the domestic, Tencent-produced game Honour of Kings, topping the domestic App Store free chart. Lingxi Games was acquired by the private equity firm Trustar Capital in August this year.

In Travel Frog: China Journey, the protagonist, a frog who lives alone in a cave, passes its days reading, writing in its diary, eating, and whittling wood. It also travels around China, such as to the Great Wall in Beijing and West Lake in the eastern city of Hangzhou. While on the road, it meets fellow animal travelers, brings back local specialties, and sends home postcards, which devoted users post on WeChat.

After learning that the game would be discontinued, a graduate student in Shanghai surnamed Fang spent a day trying to redownload it. She had played since her first year of university but hadn’t reinstalled the game after changing phones, not thinking it would shut down permanently.

“(I will have to) think of it as a child growing up and setting off on a new journey — a solo trip where the parents don’t need to worry anymore,” Fang said. “I really loved my frog … It felt like a real little baby.”

Another player, surnamed Wang, in the southern city of Guangzhou, first tried the game’s Japanese version in 2018. The frog’s ability to travel, rest, and meet friends whenever it wanted — moved her, as she said that adult life is all about KPIs, responsibilities, and pressure.

When she learned the game would be taken offline, Wang told Sixth Tone that she was devastated. “This isn’t just a game,” she said. “It’s a second life.”

Online, some called the move the “tears of an era,” a Chinese internet slang term referring to something that evokes a strong sense of nostalgia. Others lamented that their “youth is over,” or said they could not bear to delete the game, hoping it might one day be restored.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot from Travel Frog: China Journey. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.title: She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018994/She Preserved the Memory of the Mogao Grottoes. Now It’s All She Remembers.
World.content:
Chang Shana, one of China’s most treasured artists, is sitting on her living room sofa in Beijing, her eyes fixed on a TV documentary about Dunhuang, the northwestern oasis city where she spent much of her childhood. When a familiar face appears on screen, the 95-year-old breaks into a broad smile.

“That’s my father,” she says, pointing out Chang Shuhong, an accomplished painter best known for his research on the ancient Buddhist murals at the Mogao Grottoes.

Alzheimer’s disease, the most common cause of dementia, has robbed Chang Shana of most memories, yet her face still lights up the moment anyone mentions Dunhuang.

“Apart from Dunhuang, her family, and the caregivers who attend to her day and night, my mother has largely forgotten the people and things outside her immediate world,” says her son, Cui Donghui.

Gone are her memories of studying under world-renowned masters, of her mother walking out on the family, of helping design state gifts and landmark buildings like Beijing’s Great Hall of the People and the Cultural Palace of Nationalities, of losing her beloved husband, and of her tenure as the longest-serving president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, now Tsinghua University’s Academy of Arts and Design.

On a desk in her bedroom is “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” which compiles 328 color illustrations of cave murals and sculptures from various periods. “I drew this book. It’s all decorative motifs,” says Chang, standing up. After catching her breath, she points out another book: “This one, ‘Dunhuang! My Father’s Call,’ was written by my father, but I contributed many of the illustrations and written materials.”

Would she like to return to Dunhuang one day? “Yes,” she replies in a soft voice, without hesitation. Then, she slowly wanders back to the sofa to continue watching her documentary.

Life on the move

Chang Shana was born in Lyon, France, in 1931. Her father was among China’s first generation of French-trained artists, and both her parents went on to attend the prestigious Beaux-Arts de Paris school.

After being moved by a photobook about the Mogao Grottoes that he discovered in a secondhand book stall beside the Seine, Chang’s father returned to China alone in 1936 to head the fine arts department at the National Art School in Beiping, predecessor of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts.

However, as invading Japanese troops advanced toward Beijing, he was forced to flee, eventually moving with the academy to Nanjing in the eastern Jiangsu province — where he was joined by his wife, Chen Zhixiu, and daughter — and then to the southwestern city of Chongqing, which served as the nation’s wartime capital during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression. In 1943, the family relocated again to Dunhuang in the northwestern Gansu province, where Chang Shuhong was appointed director of the National Dunhuang Art Research Institute.

Chang Shana found it difficult adjusting to their austere life among the arid dunes. In her 2013 memoir, “Yellow Sands and Blue Sky,” the artist recalls that first winter night, eating cold noodles with only salt and vinegar, and her father promising, “Things will get better.”

Yet despite the lack of material comforts, she instantly found an abundance of inspiration at the Mogao Grottoes. On days without school, she would walk the dirt roads, past the shimmering poplars, and climb into the grottoes to copy the murals. “I loved going into the caves to draw. I was always eager to do it. My parents never had to tell me to go,” she wrote. She would also chat with the many visiting artists and scholars, laying a strong foundation for her artistic development.

Previously, students had typically copied the murals with tracing paper, which they secured to the walls with thumbtacks, leaving tiny holes. Chang Shuhong prohibited this practice to prevent further damage to the relics, meaning his daughter had to recreate the originals stroke by stroke through observation alone. Although laborious, it helped her develop extraordinary levels of precision.

But the desert took as much as it gave. Under the strain of his responsibilities, Chang Shuhong was often irritable, and his relationship with his wife became fractious. She eventually left him and moved back east in 1945.

Chang Shana was 14. She dropped out of school and stayed home to help with the housework and to knit sweaters for her 4-year-old brother.

That same year, the Nationalist government ordered the Dunhuang Art Research Institute to close. As funding dwindled and workers left, Chang Shuhong traveled extensively to enlist fresh support, eventually recruiting a group of teachers and students from art academies in Chongqing and Chengdu, capital of the neighboring Sichuan province.

With the institute’s future secured, he instructed his daughter to make copies of representative murals covering various Chinese dynasties. In her memoir, Chang recalls her work to recreate the figures of warriors from the Western Wei dynasty (535–556): “The lines followed my feelings; my brushwork was especially free and expressive.”

Finding faith

When Chang turned 17, a Canadian friend of the family sponsored her to study in the United States at what is today Tufts University’s School of the Museum of Fine Arts. There, she took classes in drawing, anatomy, art history, perspective, color, painting, and design.

Although confident in French, she initially struggled with some of the highly specialized English terminology. What baffled her most, though, was the painting course. With abstract expressionism on the rise, her professors required students to create work without recognizable forms or subjects. In a letter to her father, she wrote, “Perhaps I just don’t understand.”

According to her son, Chang’s diary entries from the early 1940s are filled with confusion and unease. She occupied her time with sketching and knitting, often questioning the meaning behind such pursuits. Yet her letters home in 1950 reveal “a completely different person,” he says.

In one, she wrote about “finally finding faith,” and expounded on her belief that art should be accessible and serve the people. In other letters, she displayed a weariness with life overseas. “Staying here, depending on others for everything, life feels so empty,” she wrote. “I have a perpetual sense that something is missing, like I owe a debt.”

Chang returned to China in December 1950 without completing her degree. She immediately began helping her father organize an exhibition of Dunhuang cultural relics in Beijing, featuring copies of murals she and several art researchers had made.

The following year, she was introduced to the influential architects Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin, who agreed to recommend her for a teaching assistant position at Tsinghua University’s School of Architecture. Under Lin’s guidance, she and two other students applied traditional cloisonné enamelwork techniques and motifs to everyday items such as table lamps, cigarette cases, and plates.

With a growing portfolio, Chang was commissioned to design themed gifts for the 1952 Asia and Pacific Rim Peace Conference, held in Beijing. She created a silk headscarf and large cloisonné plate with peace dove motifs, inspired by Dunhuang cave paintings from the Sui dynasty (581–618).

When China began reforming its university system in the early 1950s, she transferred to the Department of Applied Arts at the Central Academy of Fine Arts before ultimately joining the Central Academy of Arts and Design in 1956.

Gone too soon

Chang met her first husband while studying in the U.S. The couple married in China in 1953 but divorced after just a few years. The artist barely mentions this time in her memoir, not even naming him.

Her second husband, Cui Taishan, was a Japanese-language interpreter. They met while part of a Chinese cultural delegation to Japan in 1961 and were married two years later, spending 26 years together until Cui’s death in 1989.

The artist’s friend, Huang Xuanzi, recalls that Chang often talked to her late husband’s photo before she developed dementia. “She’d grumble at him for leaving her too soon, then turn to me and say, ‘Look at him, always smiling at me like that,’” she says, adding that Chang still sometimes recognizes him in photographs. “One day, she suddenly smiled and said to me, ‘Cui Taishan was very handsome.’”

Huang recalls a thick stack of flower studies Chang had painted when she was pregnant, each accompanied by a short poem handwritten by her husband. “They were never published, so almost no one outside the family knows about them,” she explains. “You can clearly feel the depth of their affection in those paintings and poems.”

In 1983, Chang was appointed president of the Central Academy of Arts and Design, leaving her less time for family. Around the same time, Cui was diagnosed with diabetes and then liver cancer. Even during his final days, she was unable to stay with him full time, yet he would always reassure her, “You go ahead with your work. I’m fine.” He was just 62 when he died.

The artist struggled to cope with the combination of grief and work stress. “There were photos of her husband everywhere in the house,” says her sister-in-law, Wang Fulan. “She would always say, ‘He left us too soon. He was so young.’ She felt that she had devoted herself entirely to her work and left household matters to her husband, and that was what had worn him down.”

In later years, Chang told a friend: “I have done right by everyone and everything in my life. My father Chang Shuhong wanted me to carry on the cultural legacy of Dunhuang, and I spent my life doing so. Lin Huiyin mentored me to become a designer, and I devoted myself to that career. The only person I failed was my husband, Cui Taishan.”

Forever home

Shortly after losing her husband, Chang’s father was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. His condition remained largely stable until he took a serious fall at age 92. After that, his memory began deteriorating rapidly, and he passed away two years later in 1994.

Huang says Chang Shana was also healthy and mentally sharp until her early 90s. She might forget small things, but a little prompting was enough to bring her back.

During the pandemic, her son Cui Donghui couldn’t visit in person; he could see her only through the security camera installed at her home. When he checked late at night, he often saw her lying alone on the sofa watching television. When he was finally able to return, she opened the door, looked at him, and said, “Who are you?”

Leafing through his mother’s book, “Clothing Patterns of China Dunhuang Mural,” he proudly remarks, “This is her life’s work. She systematically cataloged the motifs from different periods and defined their evolutionary progression. This foundational body of work is still essential today, whether for research or for the development of cultural products.”

All the detailed illustrations inside were completed during a special trip Chang took to the Mogao Grottoes in 1959 with two colleagues. For the artist, it was a joyous return to the place she once called home.

“We were young then,” she wrote in her memoir. “We rode horses and camels, climbed the Singing Sand Dunes barefoot, and had an absolutely wonderful time.”

At 95, the journey to Dunhuang is impossible. Yet smiling at that flickering TV screen, she is already back among the caves. The memories are gone, but the patterns remain.

This article, reported by Li Mei, edited by Peng Wei, originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Contributions: He Kai; translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019014/Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.title: Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019014/Pizza Bao, Spaghetti Stir-Fry: Chinese Students Hack Home Cooking Abroad
World.content:
Liu Zhenchao stands at a kitchen counter in Germany, filming himself making baozi, or Chinese steamed buns.

The 27-year-old student from Hefei, capital of China’s eastern Anhui province, chops onions and minces beef for the filling, then seasons it and mixes it by hand in a bowl.

But when it comes time to make the dough, he suddenly reaches for a cardboard box from a local supermarket.

Inside is a sheet of premade pizza dough.

“Both pizza dough and traditional baozi dough rely on yeast to ferment,” Liu told Sixth Tone, slicing the dough into neat rounds. “It allows the dough to expand, whether you steam it or bake it.”

Liu’s pizza dough baozi hack soon struck a chord with Chinese students abroad. Viewers called him a “genius,” marveling at a shortcut that eliminated the need to make dough from scratch and cut preparation time in half.

Like Liu, a growing number of Chinese students studying abroad are turning cooking videos into viral hits across Chinese social media. On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, the hashtag “international students hunong cooking” — using the term “to do something halfheartedly” — has amassed 2.1 billion views.

The trend dates back to March this year, when a Chinese student in Italy posted a video on how to make gong jin bao dan, or crispy-fried eggs coated with a sweet-and-sour sauce. His recipe tutorial video went viral, garnering more than 2 million likes and triggering a wave of netizens to attempt the dish and share their results online.

Chinese students are the largest overseas student population in the world, with over 570,600 Chinese going abroad in 2025 alone, according to China’s Ministry of Education.

For these students, improvised dishes from back home made with whatever ingredients they can find have become a category of their own, jokingly dubbed the country’s “ninth cuisine” after its eight official regional cuisines.

Comfort food

Liu traces his love of cooking to his childhood, when he spent hours watching cooking programs on TV.

When he arrived in Germany in October 2020 to pursue a master’s in engineering economics, it was only natural that he began cooking his own meals to cut costs; a meal at the school cafeteria cost 6 euros on average, but cooking at home kept his expenses below 5 euros, he said.

The choice was not only about saving money. Liu grew up with dishes known for their rich sauces, bold flavors, and vibrant colors.

The novelty of Western foods quickly wore off after he arrived. “The longer I stayed abroad, the more I found myself craving the familiar tastes of home,” Liu said. “Common Chinese dishes like stir-fried shredded potatoes with green peppers just suit my taste better than cheese and steak.”

Recreating those same flavors, however, was not easy. With many key ingredients unavailable in German supermarkets, he learned to improvise, replacing familiar ingredients from home with local ones. In one recipe, he uses Italian spaghetti in place of Chinese noodles, stir-frying it with green peppers and pork.

For Liu, cooking also had to fit around the intense pressure of studying. During exam periods, he would study from around 9 a.m. until midnight, so cooking had to be quick and simple, while also tasty and authentic.

“Good food is important to me,” Liu said. “During exam periods, when the pressure is already so high, if the food doesn’t turn out well, I feel like I have nothing to look forward to that day.”

When he launched his Douyin account in 2024, he initially wanted just to capture his everyday life abroad. But as he shared more of his life overseas, cooking gradually took center stage.

“I found that cooking is what resonates most with viewers online,” Liu said. He has since attracted more than 780,000 followers.

“Such content also has a particularly powerful sensory appeal,” Hu Zhiwen, a critical food studies scholar with a Ph.D. from the University of Georgia, told Sixth Tone. Images of cooking can trigger memories of smell, taste, and texture, which resonate strongly with audiences, he said.

Food has also become a way for Liu to connect with his contemporaries abroad. He often invites local friends over to try his cooking, including the baozi he made with store-bought pizza dough.

“They found it magical because store-bought pizza dough is something they’ve seen all their lives, yet no one had thought to use it this way,” Liu said. “Some even tried making them at home.”

The food sometimes gives his friends ideas for innovating foods from their own cultures, too. His Italian friends, for example, compared Chinese dumplings to their own filled pastas.

Cooking can offer overseas students a path to independence, emotional comfort, and cross-cultural connection, Hu, the food scholar, noted. “When you are in a new environment, there is a natural desire to seek out things that make life feel more familiar.”

In China, where food is deeply woven into everyday life and regional cuisines offer enormous variety, cooking can be more than a practical necessity, Hu added.

“Chinese students will be particularly drawn to cooking when they move to places where the food culture is markedly different from what they grew up with,” he said.

For Chen Wan’er, cooking abroad was a different kind of challenge. She had barely cooked before leaving China, but after a month in the UK, she was making almost all of her meals herself — and not only for the economic benefits.

In a new country, seven hours away from her family and friends and with no close connections, cooking gave her days meaning and shape. Even when a dish didn’t turn out perfectly, she enjoyed the satisfaction of making something from scratch.

Chen began filming her cooking and posting it on China’s lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, but unlike Liu, she maintains a small audience of roughly 1,000 followers. Initially, she saw the account as a way to give her parents a window into her new life abroad, letting them glimpse her daily routine and easing their worries about how she was doing.

Her parents were surprised when they saw a video she posted of herself making mian geda tang, a northern Chinese homestyle dish of small pieces of dough cooked in soup. Chen grew up in the eastern Chinese city of Wenzhou, where noodles were not part of her family’s cooking tradition and flour was rarely bought. Now, living alone in Britain, she taught herself to make a dish she had never cooked before.

Away from home, Chen has discovered that she actually enjoys cooking without worrying about getting everything right. At home, she was often hesitant to cook with her mother nearby, reminding her not to make a mess.

“Here, I can just let myself go with no one watching over me. The fact that I can feed myself is already good enough,” Chen said. “I don’t have to worry about whether the kitchen is messy.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Screenshots from Liu's cooking videos on Xiaohongshu.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019007/Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.title: Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019007/Top-Ranked Chinese Netflix Series Divides Viewers at Home
World.content:
Chinese romantic drama “The Early Spring,” an adaptation of a 2021 web novel, has become the highest-ranked Chinese series on streaming giant Netflix’s weekly non-English TV chart. However, the show has divided domestic viewers over whether it romanticizes an unhealthy power imbalance between its protagonists: a male boss and his female subordinate.

The TV series, which premiered Aug. 26 on both Netflix and Chinese streaming platform Youku, follows the workplace romance between demanding advertising agency corporate executive Luan “Luke” Nian, played by Jing Boran, and 22-year-old newcomer Shang “Flora” Zhitao, played by Sun Qian.

After a drunken encounter, the two begin a secret relationship. Over time, Shang advances in her career, while Luan’s harsh and arrogant demeanor softens.

“The Early Spring” ranked No. 2 on Netflix’s global weekly chart for non-English TV series from Aug. 24 to 30, garnering 2.4 million views. The series also made Netflix’s weekly Top 10 in 22 markets, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Brazil, and ranked No. 1 in Thailand and Vietnam.

In China, the series recorded 547 million views and topped domestic entertainment data platform Maoyan’s weekly popularity ranking on Sept. 7.

Many domestic social media users praised the chemistry and sexual tension between the two leads — developed with the help of an intimacy coordinator, a role still relatively uncommon in Chinese television, according to the show’s producers.

Liu, a viewer in her 30s who works in the arts in Shanghai, said that the show’s appeal lies in its escapism via a “straightforward” romance.

“It’s simply: I like you, so I like you,” Liu told Sixth Tone, in reference to the show’s driving sentiment. “Physical attraction is unavoidable.” Unlike many Chinese romance dramas that typically withhold physical intimacy between their leads, she added, “The Early Spring” brings Luan and Shang together almost immediately.

Liu also praised the 24-episode TV adaptation for bringing more warmth to its relationships. She said that compared with the original work, published under the pen name Guniang Bieku on the literature platform Jinjiang, the TV series more clearly establishes Luan and Shang as two people in love rather than primarily a sexual relationship. It also fleshes out Shang’s friendships, giving her a stronger support network.

Critics, however, have questioned whether Luan exploits his workplace authority to pursue Shang, pointing to scenes where he belittles her professional abilities. For example, when he suspects she is considering another job, he describes her as “cheap” and “obedient.”

Xu Xin, a 29-year-old media professional based in Beijing, said she agreed with much of the criticism, particularly over the couple’s first sexual encounter. “Imagine this happening in real life: a young woman fresh out of college gets drunk, and her sober male supervisor takes her home and has sex with her. That’s problematic,” she told Sixth Tone. “Even if they are attracted to each other, did it have to happen that night, when she was drunk?”

“It feels like a female fantasy,” she added. “In male-oriented fantasies, the protagonist turns his life around by becoming rich or powerful. Here, the fantasy is that a woman starts invisible, works her way up and becomes ‘better’ — and then the man comes back for her.”

For her, the series also reflects how messy real relationships can be. “People aren’t always rational, nor can they always live up to their own feminist ideals.”

The power-dynamic debate has extended to the web novel the series is based on. In it, after Shang quits her job and starts her own business, she initially decides to hire only men. The TV adaptation omits this plotline, which some had previously criticized as “discriminatory.”

Two prominent female influencers — Zhan Qingyun and Pang Ying, who are known for discussing gender equality issues in China — have also faced criticism after promoting the show.

In a Sept. 6 video posted on domestic lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, the two discussed the show, arguing that a good relationship “does not require two people to be perfect from the beginning” but can involve “two imperfect people growing together.” The video was later taken down.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “The Early Spring.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019008/One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.title: One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019008/One Last Night With Shanghai’s ‘Sleep No More’ Superfans
World.content:
SHANGHAI — On Aug. 30, Dong Minghai returned to Shanghai’s McKinnon Hotel one last time. It was his 518th visit to “Sleep No More.”

The 44-year-old machine vision quality engineer had been going roughly once a week since the production opened in 2016, enough to see nearly one in five of its 2,670 performances. “I’ve spent enough on it to buy an EV,” Dong said. “The number always shocks people.”

Over nearly a decade, the immersive production — co-produced by Shanghai Media Group and British theater company Punchdrunk — transformed a former power station into a six-story theatrical world set in 1930s Shanghai, drawing more than 750,000 visitors before its run ended. A new production of “Sleep No More” is planned for China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen in 2027.

Audience members locked away their phones, put on white masks, and roamed freely through 90 rooms as 25 characters performed simultaneous storylines inspired by Shakespeare’s “Macbeth,” the novel “Rebecca,” and the Chinese folk tale “The Legend of the White Snake.” Because scenes unfolded at the same time across the building, no one could see everything in a single visit.

Macbeth scrubbed blood from his hands in a bathtub, splashing water onto nearby spectators. At the White Snake’s wedding, paper flowers rained down over the newlyweds and audience. Elsewhere, visitors could wander through a bamboo forest smelling of damp earth, a psychiatric hospital sharp with disinfectant, or a speakeasy bar scented with whiskey.

Tang, a 38-year-old supply chain manager who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons, had attended more than 160 times since 2018. She compared repeat visits to “collecting pieces of a puzzle,” returning to see how different storylines intersected and to discover scenes she had missed.

Over time, some repeat visitors became increasingly invested in the show’s private “one-on-one” encounters. A performer could single out an audience member, lead them away from the crowd, and perform for them alone — removing their mask, sometimes clasping their hand or pulling them into an embrace. The encounters could not be reserved, and the choice was entirely the performer’s.

For fans who returned again and again, that uncertainty became part of the attraction. Being chosen could bring the thrill of feeling seen; being passed over could sting. Over hundreds of visits, those moments could begin to feel personal.

“I know how the trick works,” Tang said. “And it still works on me. But perhaps that doesn’t make the happiness any less real.”

Choose me

On Tang’s first visit, she watched an actor playing Malcolm, a prince in “Macbeth,” choose her friend for a private one-on-one scene. The actor led her through a door and closed it behind them, leaving Tang outside with no idea what was happening.

It took Tang another 20 visits to be chosen for the same encounter.

Inside, Malcolm crushed a dust-covered bird’s egg in her palm, part of a scene tied to the murder of his father, King Duncan.

“That is the final piece of the ‘Malcolm’ puzzle,” Tang said. “Only the two of you know what happened in that room at that moment. You share the same secret.”

To choose someone, a performer might turn toward a room full of masked spectators and study the crowd, ignoring people directly in front of them before reaching past others for someone farther back.

When Dong entered the same one-on-one with the same performer for a second time in 2017, the actor greeted him: “It’s you again. I’m glad you are here.”

Only later did Dong realize it was a standard line. “The line is deliberately written to create the suggestion that he recognized me,” he said.

But after enough visits, recognition could also be real. Fans said performers learned to identify regulars even behind identical white masks, picking up on their build, gait, or other physical cues.

“It’s a very clever business model,” Tang said. “It gives you the illusion that the actor favors you.”

She compared the encounters with romance-themed jubensha, live-action role-playing games where customers pay for personalized attention. “Here, everyone pays for a ticket, but the actor can still refuse you,” she said.

Fans also developed favorite performers. Different actors could give the same character markedly different personalities, Dong said.

“I’ve seen the same role played as sad and desperate, playful, or even as someone who picks on the weak,” he said. “That keeps the show feeling fresh no matter how many times I see it.”

Because casting was not announced in advance, regulars called buying tickets “gambling on the cast,” trying to work out performers’ schedules before spending around 700 yuan ($98) in hopes that a favorite would appear.

Some fans began studying performers’ apparent preferences and adjusting their own behavior accordingly. They compared who favored regulars or newcomers and who seemed drawn to particular genders, body types, or styles of dress. Some stood in particular places, wore conspicuous clothing or wigs, and kept spreadsheets tracking performers’ selections. Rival groups traded gossip about one another’s visits.

When Tang first began following a performer she liked, she would position himself at the front of the crowd and wait to be chosen. After being passed over repeatedly, she learned to “manage expectations” and step back.

One performer she liked once told her: “I didn’t pick you because I thought you’d seen the show so many times that you must have already had this interaction.”

After the final performance on Aug. 30, Tang heard a young woman crying in the bathroom after apparently being passed over during an interaction. “Why did they let go of my hand?” the woman asked her friend.

“That’s why being chosen in front of so many people feels far more intense than happiness you can simply buy,” Tang said.

For Liu, a 20-year-old university student who had seen the show 254 times since 2021, the imbalance became harder to ignore when a performer she repeatedly followed through the show stopped choosing her for interactions. On one milestone visit that she had told him was important to her, he chose a stranger instead.

“I began to realize that this model gives actors too much power,” Liu said, asking to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons. “The relationship isn’t equal. We are the ones asking for the interaction, and the performer is the only person who can decide whether we get it. So they can hurt you very easily.”

Last dance

Liu often wondered whether she had fallen for a performer’s characters or for the performer himself. “At first, I was stubborn with myself. I told myself it was only this place that had given him that magic,” she said.

But she eventually realized she still enjoyed watching him even in roles she thought did not suit him particularly well. Over time, rejection bothered her less; she found herself paying more attention to his dancing, improvisations, and the small ways he departed from the script.

“That psychological shift was a little painful for me,” Liu said. “Was it a romantic attraction? I didn’t really dare admit it.”

She eventually stopped trying to define the feeling. “Love doesn’t have such clear divisions,” she said. “It’s difficult to say, this is romantic love, and this is admiration. You can’t really separate them.”

Outside the theater, Liu found herself “unusually shy” around him and struggled to start conversations at the stage door. “But eventually I stopped trying to guess what he thought of me,” she said. “I really appreciate what he does onstage, and I’m still happy watching him. That’s enough.”

The experience also made Liu think differently about what she wanted from relationships.

“I hope that in other relationships in the future, I’ll be a braver person,” Liu said. “If I date someone next, I hope I find someone who loves me a little more. Recently, I’ve become used to being the one who gives, and even giving without expecting anything in return.”

For Tang, meanwhile, attending “Sleep No More” on important dates became “a habit, and a kind of ritual.”

“At first, it was the unpredictability of the show that attracted me. Later, it was the opposite: its certainty,” she said. “So many uncertain things happen in the real world, and I can’t control all of them. But inside this building, I know what will happen at every point in time, with every piece of music. That’s what kept bringing me back.”

All three formed friendships through the show that lasted for years. Tang became a part-time performer in another immersive production and met the man who is now her boyfriend. Dong, meanwhile, was already planning to see “Sleep No More” in Seoul and said he would return when a new production opens in Shenzhen.

On the final night, familiar scenes began to change.

In one encounter, a witch who normally trapped a mortal in an endless cycle instead left him a letter: “You are free.” Elsewhere, performers kissed and embraced, exchanged small handmade bouquets, and arranged black sand from the set into the shape of a mask.

In the finale, when Macbeth was hanged, the audience erupted in applause. On ordinary nights, the moment was met with gasps and stunned silence.

Performers, including some who had not appeared that night, emerged around the audience. Together, they sang “A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square,” the song normally played as spectators left the building. Some went off-key as they cried. Audience members sobbed too.

Then the lights went out.

Tang was the last audience member to leave. As staff closed the door behind her, she thought of an adapted line from “Rebecca” that appears in one of the show’s one-on-one encounters:

“We can never go back to Manderley again, that much is certain. But sometimes, in my dreams, I do return.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header Image: Lady Macbeth washes away blood in a bathtub. From @SleepNoMore上海 on Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019002/Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.title: Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019002/Chinese Auto Supplier Faces Backlash for Firing 107 Recent Grads
World.content:
A Chinese auto parts maker has apologized for firing 107 recent university graduates just weeks after they began working, stating that four managers had been disciplined following public backlash.

In an apology published on its website on Sept. 7, the company, Changzhou Xingyu Automotive Lighting Systems, based in the eastern Jiangsu province, said the decision to reduce staff and reorganize positions was “incorrect.” It admitted it had caused “immense physical and psychological harm to the students” and “a serious negative impact on their families and society.”

The company also announced disciplinary measures against four managers, including withheld salaries and reassignments. It said it had dismissed its human resources director, while the head of the human resources department had been demoted and transferred. However, domestic media later reported that the company had no such human resources director at the time of the incident.

Xingyu is one of China’s major automotive lighting equipment manufacturers, producing 80 million headlights per year. It also supplies international automakers such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, and BMW.

During a university campus recruitment drive earlier this year, the company signed employment agreements with 440 students set to graduate in 2026, and later hired 372.

According to its apology, however, company management decided in July to reorganize staff and reduce its workforce based on order outlook and staffing needs.

The company said that in early August, its human resources department approached 140 of the 372 new employees and informed 33 that they would be allowed to remain in their original positions. The remaining 107 signed termination agreements.

Of the 107 terminated employees, 75 held bachelor’s degrees and 32 had master’s degrees. Sixty worked in manufacturing, 39 in research and development, and eight held other roles such as quality control and project engineering.

A recent graduate who was among those terminated by the company told domestic media outlet Beijing News that they were given only two options: to “voluntarily” sign a resignation agreement for “personal reasons” or be forcibly transferred to a manufacturing line position. The graduate said they also were not offered additional compensation for the sudden termination.

The move sparked widespread backlash online, with users noting that in China, “recent graduate” status applies only in the first two years following graduation and is voided upon employment. To improve employment prospects for recent graduates, many junior positions are available only to those with “recent graduate” status, meaning such positions are no longer available to them once terminated.

On Aug. 25, local authorities said they deemed Xingyu to have used “simple and harsh” methods and failed to communicate sufficiently and effectively with employees.

In its apology, Xingyu said each of the 107 terminated workers would receive 15,000 yuan ($2,200) to ease their living costs while seeking new employment. The company added that it would offer free accommodation in its dormitories and help connect them with other employers. Those who remain unemployed by the end of November will also receive compensation equivalent to six months of their previous salary.

As of Sept. 7, 71 of the recently terminated employees had found new jobs, the company said. Local employment authorities have also organized special recruitment events and recommended positions to those affected by the cuts.

Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, and BMW separately confirmed to domestic media that they had received details on the matter and launched their own investigations into Xingyu.

“Respecting the legitimate rights and interests of workers is a core principle that the Volkswagen Group adheres to in all its business activities,” a Volkswagen spokesperson told domestic media. “This principle also applies to the management of our supply chain system, and we require that all fundamental values and rights be fully guaranteed.”

Circulating screenshots also showed that Mercedes-Benz responded to an anonymous report regarding the incident via email, stating that Xingyu’s behavior was “inconsistent with Mercedes-Benz’s corporate principles” and that it intends to forward the report to the relevant department for further review.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018995/How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.title: How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018995/How a Rotten Apple Brought China’s Internet Into a Mushroom Lab
World.content:
What are the odds that two compatible spores from a wood-rotting fungus would land on the same apple, enter through its stem, germinate, meet, and eventually produce a mushroom inside the fruit?

“About the same as winning the lottery,” said Mu Liheng, a researcher at the Yunnan Wild Mushroom Protection and Development Association, in Kunming, capital of southwestern China’s Yunnan province.

In July 2024, Mu’s colleague Xu Rongju came across a photograph on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, that appeared to show exactly that: a white, fan-shaped mushroom was growing from the stem of an apple beside a woman’s kitchen sink.



Suspecting the mushroom might be worth studying, he contacted the user, a woman surnamed Deng living in the eastern Zhejiang province, and asked her to send it to him. Two days later, the rotten fruit arrived at the team’s laboratory in Kunming.

Xu’s posts about the team’s subsequent experiments helped turn the discovery into an online sensation, prompting people across China to send in mushrooms found growing on grapes, mangoes, garlic, and even used coffee capsules.

Over the next two years, the researchers drew on some of those specimens, along with strains from an existing breeding program, to develop what they called eight numbered “generations” of split-gill mushrooms.

Two varieties have emerged as particularly promising, and one could eventually reach the shelves of a major supermarket chain.

Rotten luck

The day after the apple arrived, Xu commented beneath Deng’s photograph. “This strain is very strong and has research value,” he wrote, promising to report back when the team made progress.

In one Xiaohongshu update, Xu placed photographs taken a day apart side by side. A dense white network of fungal threads, known as mycelium, had spread farther across the rotten apple. Other images showed the fungus growing rapidly in a Petri dish and thick individual threads under a microscope.

DNA sequencing identified the strain as Schizophyllum commune, commonly known as the split-gill mushroom. The team planned to isolate and purify the culture before moving on to cultivation trials.

Split-gill mushrooms normally grow on dead wood, making the inside of an apple an unusual place to find one. On Deng’s apple, no mycelium appeared in sections that remained intact. It grew most densely in tissue that had already decayed, suggesting the fungus was feeding mainly on the rotten portions.

The apple culture joined more than 1,000 split-gill strains at the team’s laboratory. The team selected about 400 for further crossbreeding.

Edible split-gill mushrooms, known in China as bai shen, can have a dry texture and mildly bitter taste. Mu, who joined the work in 2023, was looking for strains with better flavor and texture, as well as lower spore production, which could reduce respiratory risks for growers.

Some strains in the collection had previously been sent into space through a collaboration with China’s human spaceflight program, including aboard the Shenzhou-12 spacecraft in 2021. After returning to Earth, they were screened for potentially useful mutations, and promising strains were used in further breeding. The apple strain itself was not sent into space.

As Xu’s updates spread online, users gave the apple mushroom a name: “Guo Jun Wang,” or the “King of Fruit Mushrooms.” In Chinese, the name sounds like “Prince Guo,” a character in the hit Qing dynasty (1644–1911) palace drama “Empresses in the Palace.” The pun helped propel the mushroom to the top of the trending rankings on microblogging site Weibo.

Xu used the nickname in a Xiaohongshu update: “You Give Me a Rotten Apple, I’ll Give You Back the King of Fruit Mushrooms.”

“Thank you, Xiaohongshu. I really didn’t expect to find research material here,” he wrote. “Once the experiment is complete, I’ll include everyone in the acknowledgments.”

People asked what the mushroom tasted like, whether it might have an apple flavor, whether it could be grown commercially, and when they might be able to eat it.

A month after mailing the rotten apple to Kunming, Deng received mushrooms cultivated from its strain. She chopped them up, mixed them with eggs, steamed the dish, and documented the entire process online.

By then, more than a dozen people a day were tagging Xu in photographs of mushrooms they wanted him to identify. Over the following year, the researchers received specimens found growing on more than 40 different fruits, foods, and everyday objects, including persimmons, pomelos, cantaloupes, garlic, and used coffee capsules.

One of the earliest contributors was Huang Cheng, a 37-year-old medical equipment business owner in central China’s Hubei province. Days after seeing the apple mushroom online, he removed a used capsule from his coffee machine and noticed several small, white, fan-shaped mushrooms growing from it.

“Normally, I might have just taken a picture and thrown it away,” Huang said.

Instead, he remembered that Deng’s apple had been sent to a laboratory. He photographed the capsule, posted it online, tagged Xu, and asked whether it might also be useful for research.

The post drew thousands of likes. Other users began directing Xu to Huang’s photographs, and within two days, the capsules had arrived at the lab. The team later received similar coffee-capsule specimens from Shanghai and Kunming.

“We were able to see different mushrooms from all over the country, growing on different fruits and all kinds of unusual things,” Xu said. “This really went from a small laboratory to a much bigger laboratory.”

Fruit loop

In the lab, the team isolated a strain from Huang’s coffee-capsule mushroom and crossed it with one of the space-bred strains in the collection.

Their offspring was crisp, heat-resistant, and faintly apple-scented. The team classified it as the fourth generation of the “Guo Jun Wang” series and named it “Xiang Fei,” or “Fragrant Concubine,” after a legendary Qing dynasty consort said to have carried a natural fragrance.

Many of the “Guo Jun Wang” generations, including the Xiang Fei, were not descended from Deng’s apple strain. As the project expanded, researchers used the name for promising varieties they developed, drawing on samples sent in by people online as well as strains already held by the association.

Producing those varieties meant repeatedly crossing and testing hundreds of strains. Mu often worked until midnight, preparing thousands of Petri dishes and checking newly cultivated samples.

“It was too much,” he said. “We didn’t really keep count at the time. There was no set amount of time we spent on it.”

For Xu, the experiments came on top of his doctoral research. “I just thought that if we could grow it and give the internet users an answer, that would actually be something meaningful,” he said.

The first generation of Guo Jun Wang mushrooms “tasted bad and bitter,” Xu recalled. By the second half of 2025, the team had selected more than 10 promising varieties and invited dozens of mushroom enthusiasts to cook and taste them.

“Some have an average texture but look beautiful. Some grow particularly fast. Some have high levels of polysaccharides,” Xu said, referring to the complex carbohydrates that can give mushrooms immune-boosting benefits. “The one that grew on grapes has a very good, crispy texture.”

After more than a year of breeding and selection, another variety stood out in February 2026. Provisionally designated the eighth-generation Guo Jun Wang, it had an unusual growth form and produced very few spores.

The two traits were unrelated, Mu said. The low spore production resulted from a gene segment involved in spore formation failing to be expressed, while a different gene controlled the mushroom’s unusual shape.

In July, Deng received both the eighth-generation and Xiang Fei mushrooms from the laboratory, two years after sending her rotten apple to Kunming.

Small batches of the mushrooms have also been sold through Xu’s Xiaohongshu account for 19.9 yuan ($2.80) per 100 grams. Mu said split-gill varieties identified in China are edible, and that large-scale production would require routine safety checks, including tests for heavy metals and pesticide residues.

However, the number of buyers remains limited because public awareness of split-gill mushrooms in China is still relatively low, Xu said. “If someone has eaten bai shen before, they might have tried them once and thought they don’t taste very good, so won’t eat them again.”

The team has been in contact with e-commerce giant Alibaba’s supermarket chain Freshippo about potentially selling Xiang Fei, which the researchers say tastes better and stores more easily than conventional varieties.

But commercial production remains beyond their current capacity. The team lacks the funding and manpower to grow the mushrooms at scale, while questions remain over who would cultivate them, how they would be transported, and how consistent quality could be maintained. For now, the researchers grow small batches by hand; outsourcing production, they say, could make quality harder to control.

They are also studying why crossbreeding produces such pronounced differences in the split-gill mushroom’s shape, work they hope could eventually help guide the breeding of other fungi.

“We’re happy that after all the attention in 2024, the story didn’t simply disappear,” Mu said. “There have been new developments over the past two years, and at least we’ve gotten two results that we wanted.”

In the hunt for a suitable name for the eighth-generation mushroom, the researchers have turned to the internet again.

One Xiaohongshu user suggested “Popcorn,” because its unusual shape resembles popped kernels. Another proposed “Ba Xian Wang,” or “Eighth Prince” — another Qing dynasty prince and a brother of Prince Guo.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Split-gill mushrooms growing from the apple after it arrived at the laboratory, July 2024. Courtesy of Xu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018997/End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.title: End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018997/End of the Vine: China’s ‘Calabash Grandpa’ Cuts Down His Famous Gourds
World.content:
A 75-year-old man who became a sensation in China for the calabashes hanging outside his home — reminiscent of the opening scene of a classic domestic TV series — has triggered widespread debate after removing the gourds, citing exhaustion from the subsequent flood of tourists.

The man, Chen Jin’ao, went viral on Aug. 29 after a local media outlet in the eastern city of Shaoxing posted a video of the gourds on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. The video quickly climbed the platform’s trending list, and tourists soon followed.

Chen, nicknamed “Calabash Grandpa” by tourists in reference to the character from “Calabash Brothers” — a 1986 animated series about seven brothers born from calabashes who use their superpowers to rescue their grandfather from demons — initially greeted the tourists outside his home, telling them that the gourds would bring them good luck.

In China, the calabash, or hulu, is a symbol of good fortune as its name sounds similar to the word for blessing — fulu — and represents prosperity and fertility due to its round shape and plentiful seeds.

But on Saturday, Chen cut the gourds down after his wife suffered a dizzy spell, reportedly from exhaustion caused by the volume of tourists.

The local tourism bureau told domestic media on Friday that Chen “is not an internet celebrity but an amiable and lovable Shaoxing elder … These days, we have been reflecting on the balance between viral ‘check-in’ tourism and private life. To properly guide visitors, we also ask that tourists be more considerate …”

On Sunday, a local tourism official told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that removal of the calabashes was Chen’s own decision. The official said Chen and his wife were exhausted by the constant visitors — some of whom even tried to enter their home — and the riverside location posed crowd safety risks.

Before Chen decided to remove the gourds, the local community tried to intervene in the surging crowds, putting up a sign on Sept. 2 that read, “Please do not shout. Grandpa is resting,” to no avail.

Despite the overwhelming fame and surging crowds, Chen and his wife, Shen Hualing, told domestic media that the virality has also had a positive emotional impact on them. “We rarely used to open the door and were basically closed off,” Shen told domestic media on Sept. 3. “People online have opened our hearts.” The elderly couple’s only daughter died 25 years ago, and they have no grandchildren.

The story has sparked 160 million views and 27,000 discussions on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday, with most supporting Chen’s decision to remove the gourds and lamenting that excessive online attention had spoiled a heartwarming tale.

Now, the seven cut calabashes are neatly arranged on the second floor of Chen’s home. “I won’t grow calabashes again — this experience was enough for me,” Chen said. “Thank you all for your kindness.” He added that he would take good care of the gourds.

“The calabashes are my children.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Chen Jin’ao poses for a photo alongside the seven gourds he grew in Shaoxing, Zhejiang province, Sept. 5, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Bolick redeems self, Ahanmisi catches fire as Gilas Pilipinas rips Kazakhstan in Asian Games
World.content:
Robert Bolick and Jerrick Ahanmisi spearhead Gilas Pilipinas' scoring spree from three-point range as the defending champions earn their first win in the Asian Games and boost their chances of advancing to the quarterfinals

MANILA, Philippines – Robert Bolick rebounded from a scoreless outing, while Jerrick Ahanmisi shot the lights out as Gilas Pilipinas claimed its first win in the Asian Games, dealing Kazakhstan a 109-78 beating at the Aichi International Arena in Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday, September 12.

Held scoreless in a narrow 89-85 loss to Bahrain the day prior, Bolick fired 20 points in just a little over 15 minutes to help the defending champion Philippines improve to an even 1-1 record in Group C and boost its chances of advancing to the quarterfinals.

Ahanmisi, meanwhile, erupted for a game-high 22 points on a 7-of-11 clip from beyond the arc, torching the Kazakhs in a fourth-quarter scoring spree that allowed the Filipinos to break the game wide open.

Gilas Pilipinas held a slim 18-15 lead at the end of the opening period before Bolick took charge and scattered 13 points in the second frame as it mounted a 50-37 halftime advantage.

Ahanmisi then picked up where Bolick left off, knocking down five three-pointers in the fourth quarter and singlehandedly outscoring the entire Kazakhstan team, which managed just 12 points in the final period of the 31-point blowout.

Calvin Oftana, who erupted for 31 points in the loss to the Bahrainis, still made his presence felt with 12 points, while Sedrick Barefield contributed 11 points, 5 assists, and 4 rebounds as he redeemed himself after going scoreless last game.

Zavier Lucero also delivered a near double-double outing of 10 points and 9 rebounds in the win, which saw the Filipinos sink 16 of their 29 attempts from long range for a healthy 55% shooting.

Bolick and Barefield, who both went 0-of-5 from three-point land against Bahrain, made 4 and 3 triples, respectively, this time around.

One of the few bright spots last game before he tweaked his right ankle late in the fourth quarter, Adrian Nocum played just a little under 16 minutes against the Kazakhs, contributing 4 points and 3 assists.

Anton Bykov produced 15 points and 10 rebounds to show the way for Kazakhstan, which fell to 0-2 after also absorbing a 38-point drubbing from China.

Given a one-day break, the Philippines turns its attention to unbeaten China in its last game of the group stage on Monday, September 14, with a win sending the Filipinos to the quarterfinals.

Only the top two teams from each of the three groups and the two best third-place teams will reach the knockout rounds.

The Scores

Philippines 109 – Ahanmisi 22, Bolick 20, Oftana 12, Barefield 11, Lucero 10, Baltazar 6, Arana 6, Abarrientos 6, Trollano 5, Nocum 4, Ganuelas-Rosser 4, Bates 3.

Kazakhstan 78 – Bykov 15, Marat 12, Maydekin 12, Neff 11, Rabchenyuk 9, Murzagaliyev 8, Fedchenko 7, Ivanov 2, Sakhipov 2, Severgin 0, Marchuk 0, Kuanov 0.

Quarters: 18-15, 50-37, 82-66, 109-78.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Multi-sport athlete Chino Sy finds Olympic calling in judo
World.content:
DREAMS. Filipino judoka Chino Sy hopes to make it to the grandest stage in sports: the Olympics.

Also a standout athlete in sambo and wrestling, Chino Sy has shifted his focus to judo as he pursues an Olympic berth that would fulfill not only his dream, but also that of his family

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino judoka Chino Sy learned at an early age to make the most of every opportunity.

Hailing from Davao City, Sy developed a sense of responsibility to perform whenever he and his family traveled to Manila for combat sports competitions, knowing that they invested not only time and effort, but also money, just to be there.

As he embarks on his biggest challenge yet to make the Olympics, Sy is taking that same approach.

“I feel like those experiences shaped how I compete today and my mentality towards sports. Even when we were young, we were told that we couldn’t come home with a loss. For one, we already spent money on plane tickets. We also paid entry fees and covered all other expenses,” said Sy in a mix of Filipino and English.

Sy, 25, grew up immersed in combat disciplines.

His father, Paolo Tancontian, represented the Philippines in judo, winning medals in international competitions including the Southeast Asian Games and the Arafura Games, and now serves as the president of the Pilipinas Sambo Federation.

Sy’s older sister, Sydney, is currently the fifth-ranked sambo athlete in the world in the women’s +80kg division and has won medals in the last three Asia and Oceania Sambo Championships, including gold in 2025.

With martial arts deeply rooted in his family, it comes as little surprise that Sy found success in the field that he captured medals in three different sports in the SEA Games.

At 18 years old, Sy delivered a sambo gold when the country hosted the biennial showpiece in 2019. Four years later, he earned a wrestling silver in the 2023 edition in Cambodia.

But Sy has shifted his focus on judo, the sport in which he dominated the UAAP by winning gold medals in four seasons at UST and earning two MVP awards, as he sets his sights on qualifying for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

And he showed promise in that pursuit by striking a judo gold in the men’s -100kg division in the 2025 SEA Games in Thailand.

“Every athlete’s dream is the highest stage, the Olympics,” said Sy. “I feel like I’m at the peak of my career as an athlete. I’ll grab this opportunity and I’ll do everything I can to make it to the Olympics.”

Sy is not pursuing the Olympic dream for himself alone, but also for his family, revealing that his father once dreamed of competing in the 2000 Sydney Olympics — hence his sister’s name.

“This is not just my dream, it’s also my family’s dream. Papa may not have made it to the Olympics, but he’s doing everything he can to help me achieve our dream,” said Sy.

“If all goes well, this will truly be a milestone for our family.”

And with an Olympic dream in sight, Sy knows his belief in himself has to match his ambition as he eyes a rare judo medal in the upcoming Asian Games, which will be hosted in Nagoya, Japan, from September 19 to October 4.

The Philippines has won only one judo medal in Asian Games history courtesy of Kiyomi Watanabe, who bagged the women’s 63kg silver in the 2018 edition in Indonesia.

“My target is to win. I know it will be difficult, but I’m doing everything I can in training and preparation,” said Sy.

Sy also looks to Watanabe, who represented the Philippines in the 2020 Tokyo and 2024 Paris Games, for inspiration, hoping to learn from someone with Olympic experience as they team up in the Asian Games.

“[Kiyomi] has been competing for a long time and I’m looking forward to seeing how an Olympian thinks, how she prepares, and how she approaches every match,” Sy said.

And just as he did in his early years, Sy is determined to live up to the trust placed in him — this time, not only by his family but the entire country.

“I never want to let our country down, myself, or everyone who has put their trust in me,” said Sy. – Rappler.com
