World.title: Azerbaijan's green energy policy opens up new options linking Caspian, Central Asia, and Europe – analyst
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 12. Azerbaijan's green energy policy opens up new options linking Caspian, Central Asia, and Europe, political analyst Azer Garayev told Trend.

According to Garayev, the 4th Climate Week, held in Baku from September 7 through 11, served as further evidence of Azerbaijan's growing role in the global climate agenda in recent years.

He said that one of the event's key messages was the need to accelerate the transition from climate commitments to concrete action. In this context, Climate Week wasn't merely an international discussion platform for Baku; it also provided an opportunity to showcase initiatives taking shape ahead of COP29 in 2024 and to highlight the next phase of Azerbaijan's green energy policy.

"Namely COP29 was one of pivotal starting points for strengthening Azerbaijan's position on the climate agenda. At the conference held in Baku in November 2024, an agreement was reached to increase climate finance for developing countries to $300 billion annually by 2035. Simultaneously, a call was made to scale up public and private financing from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year. Another significant outcome of COP29 was the agreement on key mechanisms for carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

However, in its post-COP29 activities, Azerbaijan is focusing not only on international climate diplomacy but also on transforming its own energy system. For many years, Azerbaijan has been known as an oil and gas exporter. Now, it is striving to develop 'green energy' alongside traditional energy by rapidly increasing the share of renewable sources in its energy strategy," he noted.

According to him, the figures illustrate the scale of this transformation.

"Azerbaijan's onshore technical potential for renewable energy sources is estimated at 135 GW. Meanwhile, the technical potential for offshore wind energy in the Azerbaijani sector of the Caspian Sea stands at 157 GW. Currently, renewable energy plants with a total capacity of 2,070 MW are in operation across the country. Of this total, 1,443.5 MW comes from hydroelectric plants, 306.5 MW from wind, 278.2 MW from solar, 37 MW from bioenergy, and 7.3 MW from hybrid plants.

The targets for the coming years are even more ambitious. Based on signed projects, plans are in place to establish 6 GW of solar and wind energy capacity by 2030 and 8 GW by 2032. A target of 8 GW of renewable energy capacity has also been set for 2035, with the intention of utilizing this potential to meet both domestic demand and export needs," the analyst mentioned.

Garayev pointed out that a key aspect of this policy is transforming Karabakh and East Zangezur into a green energy zone.

"The restoration of the liberated territories is not limited merely to rebuilding infrastructure; alongside new settlements and industrial and agricultural facilities, a more resilient energy system is being established there. Hydropower, in particular, is a key area of ​​focus for Karabakh and East Zangezur. Over the past five years, nearly 40 small hydroelectric power plants have been constructed in the region using state funds, with a combined capacity exceeding 300 MW. New projects in this sector are currently underway. In July 2026, the Aghbulag-1, Aghbulag-2, and Sheylanli hydropower plants—with a total capacity of 32.95 MW—were commissioned on the Hochaz river in Lachin. Plans are in place to further expand small-scale hydropower in the region and to harness a significant portion of this potential for electricity generation through future projects," he explained.

The analyst emphasized that one of the major advantages of Azerbaijan's green energy strategy is the creation of opportunities not only to generate electricity but also to export it to foreign markets. To this end, several regional energy corridors are being developed in parallel.

"One of the most significant of these is the Caspian Sea–Black Sea–Europe Green Energy Corridor. Also known as Black Sea Energy, this project envisages transporting Azerbaijan's renewable energy potential to Europe via Georgia and across the Black Sea. A key element of the project is an underwater electricity cable planned to be laid beneath the Black Sea. A strategic partnership agreement regarding this initiative was signed between Azerbaijan, Georgia, Romania, and Hungary in 2022.

The first and second phases of the project have been included in the 2026 development plan portfolio of the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E). The project has now entered the development phase. Establishing this infrastructure is considered a key avenue for bringing Azerbaijani green energy to the European electricity market," he noted.

According to him, another important initiative is the Central Asia–Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor. In 2024, within the framework of COP29, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan signed an agreement on a strategic partnership for the development and transmission of green energy. Subsequently, the operators of the three countries' energy systems has established a joint venture, and work on the project's feasibility study has commenced.

"The scope of this initiative extends across a broader geography. Central Asia's solar and wind energy potential could be transported to Azerbaijan via the Caspian Sea and subsequently to European markets through the South Caucasus and Türkiye. Thus, Azerbaijan is positioning itself not merely as an energy producer but as a key link in the transit of 'green energy' between Central Asia and Europe. The project's potential to create additional opportunities for developing energy connections along the Middle Corridor further enhances its strategic significance.

Furthermore, the electricity interconnection being established along the Azerbaijan–Georgia– Türkiye–Bulgaria route could expand the geographical reach of future energy exports. Rather than remaining isolated initiatives, these projects are gradually evolving into components of a unified regional energy network. This marks a fundamental shift in Azerbaijan's energy strategy: the country is no longer solely establishing export routes for oil and gas but is also building infrastructure for the future export of electricity—specifically green energy," the analyst said.

Garayev noted that the potential of the Caspian Sea warrants special attention within this process.

"The existence of a technical wind energy potential of 157 GW in Azerbaijan's sector of the Caspian Sea offers the country significant opportunities in the long term. Naturally, fully realizing this figure requires substantial investment in technology, infrastructure for the grid and exports, and other areas. However, it's precisely this potential that places Azerbaijan among the countries capable of becoming a major regional producer of green energy in the future.

On the other hand, simply building new power plants is not enough to integrate growing renewable energy capacities into the system; modernizing energy grids and establishing energy storage systems are also essential. Azerbaijan has already begun developing battery-based energy storage systems. This represents a crucial step toward managing the variability inherent in solar and wind energy generation," he noted.

The analyst stressed that, against the backdrop of Baku Climate Week, the path ahead for Azerbaijan is quite clear. While COP29 has secured the country a more prominent role in the global climate agenda, the next phase involves translating this political and diplomatic capital into concrete energy projectsş

"The creation of green energy zones in Karabakh and East Zangezur, the harnessing of the Caspian's wind potential, the rapid expansion of solar and wind power plants, the establishment of energy connections with Central Asia, and the development of routes to Europe via the Black Sea are ushering in a new phase in Azerbaijan's energy policy.

The defining characteristic of this phase is that Azerbaijan is shaping its energy map not merely around the resources it extracts, but also around the destinations and infrastructure used to deliver the electricity it generates. Thus, a new map is emerging within the country's energy strategy: 'green energy' links stretching from the Caspian to Karabakh, and from Central Asia to the Black Sea and on to Europe, are becoming the key projects that define Azerbaijan's future role in the energy sector," added Garayev.

World.title: At least 30 missing after inter-island ferry sinks off Vanuatu coast
World.content:
Vanuatu authorities have been searching for survivors after an inter-island ferry carrying 34 passengers and 11 crew members sank in critical weather conditions on Friday.

The ferry sank while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo. (Supplied: Tui's Shipping/Facebook)

Seven people have been rescued, with an estimated 38 people still unaccounted-for, as boats and a flying doctor plane search for more survivors 24 hours after the vessel sank in the north of the country.

Police told national broadcaster VBCTC that MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday while sailing between the islands of Ambae and Santo.

Police said one survivor made it to shore on the island of Santo, where a diver took him to the local community for help.

A video showing the man, named Jefferson, covered in a blanket and being offered a cup of hot tea has been shared widely on social media.

"We floated to Ambae but the tide was too strong … I swam … until I ended up here (Santo)," he said.

There were also calls for communities on the coast of the Ambae Islands to keep an eye out and help possible survivors as the search continues.

Former foreign minister Matai Seremaiah, who was aboard the vessel LC Mahalia, rescued a number of survivors.

He posted on Facebook that two additional survivors had been spotted by a plane, though darkness made retrieval difficult.

Flying Doctor Mark Turnbull used his plane to drop life jackets and helped locate survivors for rescue vessels.

Terry Ngwele, harbour master of Luganville on the island of Santo — who was on another rescue vessel — said the search would continue tomorrow.

"We rescued two people today," he told ABC News.

ABC has sought comment from the Vanuatu government, police and Vanuatu's Maritime Safety Authority.

World.title: Zelenskyy willing to meet Putin at Miami G20 Summit
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he is willing to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at the G20 Summit in Miami in December.

Mr Zelenskyy was asked by German broadcaster Deutsche Welle if he would meet his Russian counterpart.

"We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions," he said.

" It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter. Matters only result. Result matters. That's it. "

The United States this year holds the presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.

The 21st meeting of the Group of Twenty (G20) will be held on December 14 and 15 at the Trump National Doral Miami. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is also expected to attend.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov (right) says Moscow is yet to decide whether it will attend. (Reuters: Sputnik/Grigory Sysoev/Pool)

Moscow is still yet to decide whether Mr Putin will travel to the G20, Interfax reported, citing Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

"We don't know yet whether we'll be going to Miami," Mr Peskov said.

In response to Mr Zelenskyy's remarks on potentially meeting his Russian counterpart in Miami, Mr Peskov reiterated Moscow's long-standing position that if the Ukrainian leader wants to meet Mr Putin, he should come to Moscow.

Separately, G20 leaders are also expected to meet in Houston next week to discuss energy concerns.

Russia will send officials to the Houston meeting, diplomat Marat Berdyev announced on Telegram on Saturday, but no similar announcement has come from Ukraine.

Putin rejects suggestion of peacekeepers

As the war nears its fifth year, the two countries continue to trade strikes, fuelling talks of a potential peacekeeping force into the region.

Talking to journalists at the BRICS summit in India on Friday, local time, Vladimir Putin said that sending European troops into Ukraine would amount to direct conflict with Russia.

"Now they're talking about how they're considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia," he said.

"We do not threaten, nor do we intend to threaten, European countries."

Explosion at Bulgaria munitions facility servicing Ukraine

An explosion and fires have hit an ammunition storage site in central Bulgaria, police said Saturday, weeks after a blaze at another munitions facility in the country.

The latest incident happened late Friday at the warehouse operated by Bulgarian arms maker EMCO, whose munitions are used in Ukraine, near the central village of Gorni Varpishta.

No casualties were reported, and the extent of damage was not immediately clear.

"At present there is no danger to the population," local police said in a statement, adding that employees had been evacuated and the area cordoned off.

The incident came about a month after a fire at an ammunition depot at another nearby EMCO plant in Bulgaria, a NATO member and supporter of Ukraine.

Firefighters work at the site of a non-residential building hit by a Russian drone strike, on September 11, 2026. (Valentyn Ogirenko via Reuters)

EMCO ruled out human error in that case, and prosecutors are investigating.

Separately, six Russians have also been charged with terrorism over four explosions at arms facilities in the country between 2011 and 2020.

Prosecutors said the four blasts were remotely triggered and suspected the incidents were linked to efforts to disrupt arms supplies to Georgia and Ukraine.

Russia, Ukraine trade strikes on industrial sites

Industrial facilities in Russia's Samara region were attacked by Ukrainian drones on Saturday morning, Interfax reported, citing regional governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev.

Mr Fedorishchev did not specify which facilities were targeted or whether they had been damaged.

A resident stands near an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Odesa, Ukraine, September 12, 2026 (Nina Liashonok via Reuters)

Ilya Sukhikh, mayor of the city of Togliatti in Samara region, said several residential buildings were damaged and one person was injured.

Ukraine later confirmed one of Russia's largest synthetic rubber producers in Togliatti sustained damage in a strike, causing a fire.

(Nina Liashonok via Reuters)

It said in a statement that the Togliattikauchuk plant specialised in the production of synthetic rubbers and fuel additives that are used in fuel for Russian missiles.

In a separate attack, four commercial properties were set ablaze in the city of Taganrog in the Rostov region, local mayor Svetlana Kambulova said, according to TASS.

Rescuers work at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike, September 12, 2026. (Nina Liashonok via Reuters)

Russia's Defence Ministry said its forces had downed 230 Ukrainian drones overnight over more than a dozen Russian regions, as well as over Crimea and the Azov and Black seas.

It also said its forces struck two cargo vessels overnight in the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Interfax reported.

Three civilians were killed and dozens wounded in Ukraine, local officials said Saturday.

Two people were killed in the city of Zaporizhzhia in south-eastern Ukraine and one in Mr Zelenskyy's native city of Kryvyi Rih, the president said on Telegram.

In the port of Odesa and the surrounding area, 28 people were wounded in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a "massive attack." Among the buildings hit was a residential high-rise, with the upper floors completely destroyed.

The ministry added Russian forces hit Ukrainian steelmaker Zaporizhstal in the city of Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro and several plants in Kryvyi Rih, including the Northern Iron Ore Beneficiation Works complex.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Four-year-old dies in house fire east of Cowra
World.content:
A four-year-old child has died in a house fire in central western New South Wales.

Fire crews were called to the home in Woodstock, about 20 kilometres north-east of Cowra just before 3pm today.

They arrived to find the property well alight.

A woman and two other children were able to escape the blaze, but the four-year-old remained unaccounted-for.

Firefighters later found the body of the child inside the home after they managed to extinguish the fire.

The woman was taken to Cowra hospital in a stable condition with smoke inhalation.

Police have set up a crime scene, with inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the blaze ongoing.

World.title: Sharks hand Dragons NRLW wooden spoon and Eels down Cowboys
World.content:
Parramatta has scored a thrilling 33-28 come-from-behind victory over the Cowboys, and the Sharks have handed the Dragons the wooden spoon with a 16-8 win in the final round of NRLW action.

None of Saturday's teams were in finals contention, but pride was still on the line, and both games were genuine contests.

The matches were played under the experimental rule that allows the side conceding a try to choose whether to kick off or receive, and both games saw teams use the latter option and score shortly after.

In the day's first game, the Eels scored five second-half tries and overcame a 16-point deficit to win a thriller at Western Sydney Stadium.

After losing their opening six matches of the season, the Eels ended 2026 with four wins from their last five starts.

The Cowboys' Charlize Lloyd-Phillips got the scoring under way after just four minutes, but suffered a suspected ACL injury in the process.

Parramatta took less than three minutes to reply, strike centre Rory Owen crossing for her sixth try in four games, before former Wallaroos star Ash Marsters posted the only other try of the half to see the Cowboys up 10-6 at the break.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Cowboys hooker Alisha Foord snuck over two minutes into the second half, and another four-pointer followed quickly to Makenzie Weale to give North Queensland a 22-6 lead.

However, with veteran Kennedy Cherrington sin-binned, the 12-player Eels scored tries to Zali Fay and Jasmin Morrissey to get within six points.

Keilee Joseph then made it three tries in eight minutes to tie things up.

Cowboys interchange hooker Nadia Windleborn put her side back on top, before Joseph again tied the scores.

Experienced half Rachael Pearson stepped up to nail a one-pointer for Parramatta with four minutes remaining, before Owen sealed victory with a stunning 90m effort moments later.

In Saturday's second game, the Sharks came out firing in the second half to defeat the Dragons at Sydney Football Stadium, handing their local rivals the wooden spoon.

It marked Cronulla's first back-to-back wins in 2026 following their upset of the Warriors in Auckland last week.

It took 20 minutes for the first points to be registered, Dragons front-rower Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis powering over from 12 metres out for the only score of an opening half littered with 15 errors.

It didn't take as long for points in the second period, with Sharks half Chantay Kiria-Ratu delivering a beautiful short ball two minutes in for China Polata to run 50m to score.

Four minutes later Georgia Hannaway dived over from dummy half for Cronulla's second.

Ellie Johnston made it three tries within 13 minutes for the Sharks, and when Dragons centre Tyra Ekepati was sin-binned for a high shot it looked like Cronulla may run away with it, but the Dragons held strong in those 10 minutes.

Shenae Ciesiolka scored a consolation try for the Dragons in her 50th NRLW appearance, but it was too little, too late.

AAP

World.title: Wild pursuit and carjacking across Sydney's west leaves two children injured
World.content:
There have been scenes of mayhem across Sydney's west, with a carjacking, collision and stabbing after a motorist drove into oncoming traffic on a busy motorway with two children on board.

Police were called to carry out a welfare check on a 36-year-old driver in Belmore, but began a pursuit after he refused to pull over.

"When the driver allegedly failed to stop as directed, a police pursuit was initiated," NSW Police said in a statement.

"The pursuit continued into Auburn before it was terminated due to the manner of the man's driving."

Police said the man then drove on the wrong side of the M4 Motorway before hitting an oncoming vehicle.

Police say the pursuit was stopped at Auburn due to the "manner of the man's driving". (ABC News)

He then got out of the car with the two children and allegedly tried to steal a car.

A 25-year-old man intervened and during a scuffle suffered a stab wound to his hand.

The offender, police allege, then stole the vehicle of a woman who had stopped to help before bundling the two children into her car and speeding off westbound along the M4 Motorway.

He stopped on the Cumberland Highway at Wentworthville and was arrested by an off-duty police officer with help from bystanders.

He was taken to hospital under police guard.

The children suffered minor injuries and were taken to Westmead Children's Hospital as a precaution.

Police are still waiting to interview the man as they piece together what has happened.

World.title: Lions keep three-peat dream alive with 53-point mauling of Adelaide
World.content:
The Brisbane Lions are through to the AFL's final four, keeping their three-peat dream alive with a 53-point mauling of Adelaide at the Gabba.

Charlie Cameron kicked five goals as the Lions used an outrageous early onslaught to cruise to a 21.18 (144) to 13.13 (91) triumph and will face Hawthorn in a preliminary final next weekend.

Challenged after defeat to Sydney last week, a number of Brisbane's best players stepped up with Zac Bailey, Cam Rayner and Will Ashcroft all terrific in a comprehensive win.

Adelaide champion Taylor Walker kicked two goals in the last quarter of his career before bidding a tearful goodbye after full-time.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Hawks' AFLW win soured by skipper's sickening leg injury
World.content:
Aine McDonagh has fired Hawthorn to an 11-point win over the Western Bulldogs that was soured by captain Emily Bates's serious leg injury.

Bates was taken off the field on a stretcher at the Kennedy Community Centre today after her right leg twisted underneath her in a tackle late in the third quarter.

The decorated 30-year-old, who played her 100th AFLW match a week earlier, was expected to be taken to hospital for further assessment.

The Hawks also lost Laura Stone (concussion) after an early head clash with an opponent and were 11 points down at half-time.

But Daniel Webster's side piled on five unanswered goals in the third quarter — four of those before Bates's injury — to set up their 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30) victory.

The result lifted Hawthorn (3-2 win-loss record) into the top eight, leapfrogging the Bulldogs (3-2) on percentage.

Irish key forward McDonagh kicked a career-best four majors, extending her lead at the top of this season's goal-kicking list.

Eliza West (24 disposals), Tamara Smith (20) and Jasmine Fleming (19) also shone for the Hawks, as did ruck Lucy Wales.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Isabelle Pritchard had match-high tallies of 31 disposals and eight clearances for the Bulldogs, with Elisabeth Georgostathis (19 disposals) also busy.

The Bulldogs kicked three of the first four goals but were held scoreless in the third quarter as the Hawks took control of the contest.

Meanwhile, Sunny Lappin kicked three goals and sparked the second-half surge that led to Gold Coast's 30-point win over Collingwood.

The Suns (3-2) kicked four goals to one in the third term — two of those to Lappin — to set up their 9.8 (62) to 4.8 (32) victory in Carrara.

Maddy Brancatisano kicked two goals, Charlie Rowbottom had 29 disposals and Dekota Baron provided the highlight of the day with a towering mark-of-the-year contender.

Mikayla Nurse suffered a nasty cut on the face after a head clash with Suns teammate Lucy Single late in the match.

Tarni White had 29 disposals for Collingwood (0-5), which remains winless this season.

Cats and Eagles score historic victories

Georgie Prespakis of the Cats and Ebony Marinoff of the Crows. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

Later on Saturday, Geelong's Georgie Prespakis and West Coast's Ella Roberts starred as their teams each recorded a first win over their opponents.

The Cats (4-1) retained a top-four spot, scoring a fourth-straight victory and their first in seven attempts against the Crows (2-3), with an 8.9 (57) to 6.10 (46) win at Adelaide's Unley Oval.

Gun midfielder Prespakis was dynamic for Geelong, racking up match highs of 32 disposals, 19 contested possessions and nine clearances.

In Perth, West Coast (1-4) posted their first win of the season in a 6.10 (46) to 6.5 (41) victory over Brisbane (2-3).

It was their first AFLW win over the Lions in four attempts after three heavy defeats.

Young Eagles superstar Roberts put in a mammoth performance, leading the game in possessions (33), contested possessions (19), clearances (11), tackles (eight) and metres gained (700).

AAP

World.title: Eels star Addo-Carr allegedly returns positive test for cocaine
World.content:
Star NRL player Josh Addo-Carr is being investigated by police after allegedly returning a positive test for cocaine.

Police confirmed in a statement that Addo-Carr was driving in Sydney's inner-west along Enmore Road last night when he was stopped for a random test.

He was subjected to a roadside breath test for alcohol, which returned a negative result.

However, he returned a preliminary drug wipe, which allegedly returned a positive indication for cocaine.

Josh Addo-Carr sacked from the Canterbury Bulldogs Josh Addo-Carr has been sacked by NRL club Canterbury with immediate effect after returning two positive readings to roadside drugs tests last month.

An oral fluid sample was obtained from Addo-Carr and sent for further analysis.

The investigation is ongoing, as police await the results of the forensic analysis.

His current club, the Parramatta Eels, released a statement noting it was aware of an alleged incident involving Addo-Carr.

"The club has notified the NRL Integrity unit and is cooperating with the appropriate processes, as well as providing welfare support to Josh and his family," the statement read.

The Parramatta Eels said it would not be commenting further until the matter was finalised.

In 2024, Addo-Carr was sacked from his previous club, the Canterbury Bulldogs, after he failed a roadside drug test.

Addo-Carr was recalled to the Australian national side, the Kangaroos, and has played for New South Wales.

Across his decade-long career, the winger has scored more than 150 tries and won two premierships with the Melbourne Storm.

The alleged positive test could affect Addo-Carr's chances of being selected for Australia for next month's World Cup.

Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters said Addo-Carr could face consequences if the allegation was verified.

"I had a lot to do with Josh last year on the Kangaroo tour," Walters told Fox League.

"He's a great team player, had a good series, but this may have some ramifications around that as well."

World.title: AFL LIVE: Walker makes tearful exit as Lions respond to ‘nasty’ Fagan’s tough love; preliminary final times confirmed
World.content:
Crows coach Matthew Nicks has painted a positive picture about the potential of his side and his suitability to lead them after their semifinals exit.

Nicks said the Crows were building “something special” but needed more time and improvement.

Crows coach Matthew Nicks. AFL Photos via Getty Images

“There are no guarantees in footy but I’m confident in where we are at and the conversations that are ongoing with the leaders of our football club and my colleagues,” Nicks said.

“We will continue to work together. We have great forward momentum as a football club. We are building something special but we are not there yet.

World.title: Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans

Scott Spits and Steve Barrett Updated September 12, 2026 — 11:38pm , first published 11:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Brisbane Lions lost their first final last year. What happened next? A barnstorming run through their semi-final and preliminary final, back to the big dance, and another premiership to top it all off. They’re on track for a repeat dose this year after obliterating the Crows at the Gabba in what became Adelaide favourite son Taylor Walker’s farewell game. Scott Spits (Brisbane Lions) and Steve Barrett (Adelaide) run their eye over every player in from the semi-final. What a return to form for Charlie Cameron and the Lions. AFL Photos Brisbane Lions



(1) Kai Lohmann: He was creative for most of the match, kicking the opening goal after only 30 seconds. Just as importantly, he put a block on and allowed Zac Bailey to kick his opener after four minutes. 8/10 (2) Sam Draper: Tried and tried but was not among Brisbane’s best as the club’s second ruck. Had close to 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: A good game by the 22-year-old, who is fast approaching 100 matches. He got plenty of early touches (seven in the first quarter) as Brisbane set up their impressive victory. 6/10 View post on X (4) Oscar Allen: There could be a “watch” on the former Eagle after tonight. He had just five touches by the final break and two behinds. The Lions will want a bit more out of him in their flag push. 4/10



(5) Josh Dunkley: One of the Lions’ best and typically strong at the coalface. He did the one-percenters regularly (no surprise there), and spent time on Izak Rankine and nullified his influence. He got plenty of the ball himself, too. 8/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: Yet again, he didn’t get a lot of the ball for a player of his class. It was notable that Chris Fagan came to his defence during the week. McCluggage has had his injury woes this year, but importantly he was up and going early when the Lions stoned the Crows with five goals in eight minutes. 7/10 (7) Jarrod Berry: He finished with 19 touches and was a solid contributor. Unfortunately, Berry was off-line with an early shot at goal when the Lions were heaving. By that stage, Brisbane had 10 forward entries to Adelaide’s zero. 6/10 Will Ashcroft fires off a handball. AFL Photos (8) Will Ashcroft: Despite their qualifying final loss, the Lions have again set themselves up perfectly for another flag push, and Ashcroft’s form reflects that. He got better and better as the match wore on, as the Lions found their groove ahead of next week’s preliminary final against the Hawks. The two-time Norm Smith medallist finished with 30 touches. 8.5/10



(9) Lachie Neale: The veteran star was not among Brisbane’s match-winners, but he still picked up 21 possessions as others lifted around him. That’s probably a good sign for the Lions as they eye off a hat-trick of flags, and needing a multitude of contributors 6.5/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: Quiet by his standards, he spent time on star Crows skipper Jordan Dawson and was probably shaded by him. 5.5/10 (13) Logan Morris: He slotted a brilliant snap goal after eight minutes in the third quarter when he finally got on the board. It gave the Lions a 50-point lead – basically snuffing out any Adelaide hopes. He left the game in the final quarter with injury. 5.5/10 (15) Dayne Zorko: It was a strong game from the super-veteran. Zorko was the other Lion (aside from Zac Bailey) to re-sign during the week, and he showed why they still want him in the side. The 37-year-old kicked a ripping goal in the third quarter and led the Lions for metres gained. 7/10 (16) Cam Rayner: He was oozing with confidence throughout and was involved in plenty of key moments. By midway through the second quarter Rayner already had five score involvements. Go back and witness his goal – Brisbane’s fifth – when he took Alex Neal-Bullen on and kicked beautifully. It gave the Lions a 31-point lead and the tone was set. 9/10



(22) Ty Gallop: He came into the side to replace the injured Noah Answerth. He did his bit with at least 10 touches. 5/10 (23) Charlie Cameron: A non-factor in the Lions’ qualifying final loss to the Swans, in this sudden-death clash he proved his worth and much more. He had his first goal after 90 seconds (Brisbane’s second) and his second after 23 minutes. Cameron is clearly an “energy” player, and with a return of 5.3 against his former side, the Lions and coach Fagan will be rapt. 8/10 (26) Conor McKenna: He had a real crack but was in and out of the game. He finished with 13 touches and 1.2. Look back to his early “toe-poke” pass to Lohmann for a goal. 5.5/10 (27) Darcy Gardiner: The big man was largely quiet but typically handy for Brisbane’s team defence. 5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: I quite liked his game. He regularly gave the Lions something to kick to and played an important role with Morris and Allen both a bit hot and cold. He kicked a goal in the last quarter and finished with 2.1. 7/10



(31) Harris Andrews: He played an intriguing game. The star defender didn’t hit his usual heights, but with so many teammates in hot form against the Crows, that mattered less. He manned Riley Thilthorpe for much of the game and won. Strangely, Andrews picked up a shot at goal in the first quarter after a double 50-metre penalty. His rare chance to score was offline. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fort: Solid and dependable as Brisbane’s first ruck. He split the points with Adelaide’s Lachlan McAndrew. 5.5/10 View post on X (33) Zac Bailey: What a game by the newly re-signed gun. Ever classy by foot, he was nothing short of brilliant – ironically against the club that desperately wanted him. He had a stack of score involvements and was one of the five Lions to get on the board in the first eight minutes. He finished with 23 touches and kicked 3.3. 8.5/10 (35) Ryan Lester: A quality contributor, Lester was heavily involved in the win from the start. Witness a strong defensive effort on the wing (a punch from behind) that helped set the mood. Quirkily, like Andrews, Lester had a rare shot at goal in the first term, but missed. 8/10



(44) Darcy Wilmot: He did his bit. He got enough of the ball and was more than solid in defence and playing as a link player. Thumbs up for an important player in Fagan’s all-conquering side. 6.5/10 Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Two consolation goals in the first half almost masked a forgettable night for the defensive forward. Normally such a spark plug in attack, Keays was unsighted when the whips were cracking and was soundly trumped by Zorko. 4/10 (3) Sam Berry: The hardworking onballer was one Adelaide player who could hold his head high. Berry did his best to stem Brisbane’s early onslaught, chalking up five first-quarter clearances by himself. He finished with a game-high 31 disposals. 7.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: Other than a sprayed shot out on the full early, Ah Chee struggled to get involved early doors at his old stomping ground. He had just three touches in the first half before spending time on the wing in the third term and getting more involved. 5/10



(6) Daniel Curtin: A big second half saw him finish with 22 disposals and seven clearances. Curtin booted the Crows’ first goal and played predominantly on the ball, but he – like many of his mates – wasn’t able to stop Brisbane’s game-breaking mids. 7/10 Daniel Curtin celebrates a goal with Taylor Walker. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: Had his hands full with Andrews in the first half before playing much better footy after the main break, booting two goals and using his body well against the Lions’ skipper. Thilthorpe’s contest was strong, but his ball use wasn’t quite up to scratch. 5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: Enjoyed a second-quarter purple patch when he slotted a major and then handed another one off to Darcy Fogarty. But otherwise, Rachele – fresh off a three-goal haul against the Bulldogs – had a poor evening. He conceded an early 50-metre penalty and was thrashed in the air by Lester. 2/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: He gave it everything he had with 30 touches and 512m gained, but his normally pristine ball use was missing, going at 50 per cent disposal efficiency. Dawson’s six first-quarter tackles said as much about the Lions’ dominance as it did about his own never-say-die approach. 7.5/10



(13) Taylor Walker: Ended his AFL journey with two fourth-quarter goals – to finish with 715 for his career – after being frustrated throughout the first three terms. Not an ending he wanted in his 319th and last top-flight game, but what a star he has been. 4/10 Walker leaves an AFL playing field for the final time with his children. AFL Photos (14) Jake Soligo: Adelaide needed more from him – for much of the home-and-away campaign and in both finals. Soligo was part of the midfield rotation, but struggled to get his hands on the footy. 3.5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The crafty wingman’s usually clean ball use was a touch ragged and, aside from one neat goal assist early, he struggled to influence the match. 4/10 (16) Max Michalanney: There’s no lonelier place on an AFL field than one-out against Cameron in the mood he was in. Michalanney, normally a reliable stopper, was absolutely torched by the Lions’ brilliant goalsneak in the first half, before being mercifully moved to the wing. 1/10



(19) Zac Taylor: After missing the elimination final with a hamstring injury, Taylor ratified his recall instant by providing pressure and contest, while splitting minutes between half-forward and the centre-square. All up, 10 of his 17 possessions were contested. 6.5/10 (23) Izak Rankine: The highest-rated player in the AFL since round 17 was due a downer – and a downer he had, thanks chiefly to the disciplined, iron-fisted glove of Dunkley. Rankine was kickless at quarter-time and still had just two at the half. He was given more room to roam after half-time, but it just wasn’t his night. 5/10 Izak Rankine had his hands full all night against the Lions. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: After enjoying the game of his life against the Bulldogs, when he racked up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions, Worrell wasn’t allowed anywhere near the same the influence to make plays. Although he still finished with 18 touches, he had just four of them by half-time. 5/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: He played major minutes on the wing before taking on the Cameron job late. Nankervis snared a magnificent mark over Levi Ashcroft and goaled to give the Crows a glimmer late in the first period, but otherwise was quiet. 4.5/10



(28) Alex Neal-Bullen: Splitting time between wing and half-forward, the experienced ex-Demon didn’t have a huge impact, particularly in the first half. 5.5/10 (29) Rory Laird: The experienced half-back flanker never waved the white flag, but didn’t give the Lions too many major headaches either. 6/10 (30) Wayne Milera: The dashing All-Australian half-back wasn’t afforded the same time and space that he enjoyed a week earlier against the Bulldogs. Normally so calm and creative, his disposal was hurried thanks to the Lions’ pressure. Kicked a neat late goal. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fogarty: Conceded a horror 100m penalty in a forgettable opening term before springing to life in the second quarter, spearheading Adelaide’s revival by booting two goals and assisting another one to Rachele. But he was unsighted too often. 4.5/10 Darcy Fogarty had a frustrating night for the Crows. AFL Photos



(35) James Borlase: Quiet for four quarters, he rarely intercepted and struggled to have much involvement, despite how much time the Sherrin spent in Brisbane’s attacking area. 3/10 (40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The unsung half-back has barely put a foot wrong since being picked up in the mid-season draft. He wasted very few of his 27 disposals, racked up plenty of metres of rebound and contested well in the air and on the ground. A real find. 7.5/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: After shading Tim English last week, the towering ruckman had his hands full with Draper and Fort. McAndrew matched them both in the air, but it was harder for him on the deck. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: He struggled all night with an aggressive Hipwood, finishing with four kicks and virtually no impact. 2/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: NRL Highlights: Sharks v Cowboys - Finals Week 1
World.content:
NRL Highlights: Sharks v Cowboys - Finals Week 1

See all of the scoring plays, big hits and highlight moments from the Sharks vs Cowboys Elimination Final at Allianz Stadium! Find out who survived and made it to Week 2!

World.title: Fans stay home but Sharks turn up to end Cowboys’ season
World.content:
If you build it, they won’t come.

It may be the one of the best stadiums in the southern hemisphere, a mere 25.2 kilometres from the Sharks’ spiritual home in the Shire. But many Cronulla fans refuse to leave Cronulla.

Not even the siren song of their Mermaids cheerleaders, free public transport for ticket holders, or the chance to witness their team in a finals fixture was enough to bring them to Allianz Stadium.

Loading

An official crowd of 17,429 was posted. That’s only about 2,500 more than the capacity of Shark Park, otherwise known as Ocean Protect Stadium. Understandably, only a handful of hearty Cowboys souls made the long commute from Townsville.

The decision to shift the game here was a controversial one. Head office will hope the extra corporate cash it pockets from playing at Allianz offsets the broadcast images of a stadium less than half full.

The reasons for non-attendance remain unclear. Is it because rugby league is such a good television product? The fatigue of watching the seventh North Queensland-Cronulla post-season clash since 2013? Or just a preference for “Portaloo Park”?

Nicho Hynes celebrates a try. Getty Images

Whatever the case, the Sharks got the job done without the vocal support they would normally get at their regular home.

“It’s not our decision,” Cronulla coach Craig Fitzgibbon said. “I felt like this last year - obviously the amount of sulking that went on about playing at Shark Park, I thought we weren’t any chance of getting it this year. They should have just told us earlier.

“But also, for us, we’re happy to play here. We’re in semi-finals; we want to play in a big stadium. But our members and fans pay their money all year to be able to watch their team make semi-finals and play at home, and we earned that. We didn’t get it … but that’s not up to me. I would imagine it’s a financial decision or viewing optics for the game. I’m not sure.”

A 26-16 win against their old sparring partners was achieved despite their returning maestro playing with the use of only one shoulder. Braydon Trindall took his place after three weeks on the sidelines. Despite being clearly hampered, he passed, tackled and kicked his side to a scrappy victory.

At one point in the second half, “Tricky” gave his shoulder an unnecessary test when he tried to retrieve the football from his own short kick-off. The pivot couldn’t be accused of playing in a dinner suit. When he produced a season-high 31st try assist with a pass to fullback Will Kennedy – not even Nathan Cleary comes near that figure – it was due reward for playing through the pain.

Loading

The Cowboys have been the most curious side in the NRL. They qualified for the top eight despite conceding more points than any other finalist in history. Their devil-may-care attitude is best exemplified by Scott Drinkwater. The Dragons-bound fullback is the ultimate gunslinger. One errant cut-out pass resulted in an intercept that gifted Sione Katoa his 100th NRL try. Undeterred, he threw another one that hit Zac Laybutt on the chest from 25 metres away to give his side hope.

However, it was always going to come down to the Cowboys’ application without the football. They defended stoutly when starved off possession for much of the opening half, particularly when their tryline was peppered. However, those exertions eventually took their toll. When Nico Hynes shaped to kick, but instead stepped off his left foot, their fate was sealed.

There is every chance that the Sharks could be required to return to Allianz next week. Asked whether he hoped more of their fans will follow them there, captain Cameron McInnes deadpanned: “I don’t know. If you can afford it, come. If you can’t, watch it on TV. I couldn’t care less, really.”

World.title: Liberal chivalry lost at Griffin door
World.content:
James Griffin’s reflections on his time in the NSW legislature as a Liberal member present a neat encapsulation of the dilemma now facing the Liberals at the local, state and national levels (“Retiring MP slams Liberal hacks as moderates wane”, September 6). For some reason, they seem unable to accept the world (electorate) as it is, instead focusing on niche issues that frequently appeal to a particular audience, rather than the general one of the electorate. Which, in turn, continues to make them broadly unelectable in the macro sense. Issues around renewables, climate, women, gender, internal politics/governance or global impacts on our economy. They seem to think that much of our current situation is linked to what is happening now, without considering previous policies of theirs. Examples include removing carbon tax, negative gearing (a government subsidy to reduce tax on high incomes at the expense of those on low incomes buying a home), privatisation/outsourcing, robo-debt, aged care reforms and various others. None of these are “nation building” policies, but rather divisive ones that set us against each other. What One Nation is doing is effectively doubling down on this approach, effectively cannibalising them. Until Liberals realise that they are pushing policies that aren’t dealing with the world as it is, rather than some halcyon time of the past, they will continue to flail about and continue to lose ground. Bernard Stever, Richmond

Manly MP James Griffin has decided that he has had enough. Sitthixay Ditthavong

Retiring Manly MP James Griffin stands out as one of the rare figures in politics who appear genuinely decent – not a retail politician who dodges accountability or hides behind the usual excuses when things go wrong. He took his responsibilities so seriously that it affected him when he couldn’t assist one of his constituents. He is young, capable, and possibly a future NSW premier. But he clearly sees what many moderates in the Liberal Party have been feeling for years: the endless culture war battles offer nothing to the voters they are meant to serve. It has become increasingly difficult for politicians with principles, empathy and a moral compass to survive in that environment – let alone thrive. Griffin’s departure is a loss for Manly, for the Liberal Party, and for moderates generally. It is challenging for values-driven MPs to stay the course in a party increasingly defined by internal conflict rather than public purpose. Voters are forgotten. Mukul Desai, Hunters Hill

I recently met James Griffin, and I was left with the strong impression that if the Liberal Party could nurture people of his calibre, there was still some hope left, not only for his party, but for politics in general. His intelligence, capacity to listen and desire to make a positive contribution were clear. It leaves me with immense sadness to hear of his retirement. This is everyone’s loss. Elizabeth Darton, Lane Cove West

Patients deserve better

World.title: Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans

Scott Spits and Steve Barrett Updated September 12, 2026 — 11:38pm , first published 11:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Brisbane Lions lost their first final last year. What happened next? A barnstorming run through their semi-final and preliminary final, back to the big dance, and another premiership to top it all off. They’re on track for a repeat dose this year after obliterating the Crows at the Gabba in what became Adelaide favourite son Taylor Walker’s farewell game. Scott Spits (Brisbane Lions) and Steve Barrett (Adelaide) run their eye over every player in from the semi-final. What a return to form for Charlie Cameron and the Lions. AFL Photos Brisbane Lions



(1) Kai Lohmann: He was creative for most of the match, kicking the opening goal after only 30 seconds. Just as importantly, he put a block on and allowed Zac Bailey to kick his opener after four minutes. 8/10 (2) Sam Draper: Tried and tried but was not among Brisbane’s best as the club’s second ruck. Had close to 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: A good game by the 22-year-old, who is fast approaching 100 matches. He got plenty of early touches (seven in the first quarter) as Brisbane set up their impressive victory. 6/10 View post on X (4) Oscar Allen: There could be a “watch” on the former Eagle after tonight. He had just five touches by the final break and two behinds. The Lions will want a bit more out of him in their flag push. 4/10



(5) Josh Dunkley: One of the Lions’ best and typically strong at the coalface. He did the one-percenters regularly (no surprise there), and spent time on Izak Rankine and nullified his influence. He got plenty of the ball himself, too. 8/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: Yet again, he didn’t get a lot of the ball for a player of his class. It was notable that Chris Fagan came to his defence during the week. McCluggage has had his injury woes this year, but importantly he was up and going early when the Lions stoned the Crows with five goals in eight minutes. 7/10 (7) Jarrod Berry: He finished with 19 touches and was a solid contributor. Unfortunately, Berry was off-line with an early shot at goal when the Lions were heaving. By that stage, Brisbane had 10 forward entries to Adelaide’s zero. 6/10 Will Ashcroft fires off a handball. AFL Photos (8) Will Ashcroft: Despite their qualifying final loss, the Lions have again set themselves up perfectly for another flag push, and Ashcroft’s form reflects that. He got better and better as the match wore on, as the Lions found their groove ahead of next week’s preliminary final against the Hawks. The two-time Norm Smith medallist finished with 30 touches. 8.5/10



(9) Lachie Neale: The veteran star was not among Brisbane’s match-winners, but he still picked up 21 possessions as others lifted around him. That’s probably a good sign for the Lions as they eye off a hat-trick of flags, and needing a multitude of contributors 6.5/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: Quiet by his standards, he spent time on star Crows skipper Jordan Dawson and was probably shaded by him. 5.5/10 (13) Logan Morris: He slotted a brilliant snap goal after eight minutes in the third quarter when he finally got on the board. It gave the Lions a 50-point lead – basically snuffing out any Adelaide hopes. He left the game in the final quarter with injury. 5.5/10 (15) Dayne Zorko: It was a strong game from the super-veteran. Zorko was the other Lion (aside from Zac Bailey) to re-sign during the week, and he showed why they still want him in the side. The 37-year-old kicked a ripping goal in the third quarter and led the Lions for metres gained. 7/10 (16) Cam Rayner: He was oozing with confidence throughout and was involved in plenty of key moments. By midway through the second quarter Rayner already had five score involvements. Go back and witness his goal – Brisbane’s fifth – when he took Alex Neal-Bullen on and kicked beautifully. It gave the Lions a 31-point lead and the tone was set. 9/10



(22) Ty Gallop: He came into the side to replace the injured Noah Answerth. He did his bit with at least 10 touches. 5/10 (23) Charlie Cameron: A non-factor in the Lions’ qualifying final loss to the Swans, in this sudden-death clash he proved his worth and much more. He had his first goal after 90 seconds (Brisbane’s second) and his second after 23 minutes. Cameron is clearly an “energy” player, and with a return of 5.3 against his former side, the Lions and coach Fagan will be rapt. 8/10 (26) Conor McKenna: He had a real crack but was in and out of the game. He finished with 13 touches and 1.2. Look back to his early “toe-poke” pass to Lohmann for a goal. 5.5/10 (27) Darcy Gardiner: The big man was largely quiet but typically handy for Brisbane’s team defence. 5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: I quite liked his game. He regularly gave the Lions something to kick to and played an important role with Morris and Allen both a bit hot and cold. He kicked a goal in the last quarter and finished with 2.1. 7/10



(31) Harris Andrews: He played an intriguing game. The star defender didn’t hit his usual heights, but with so many teammates in hot form against the Crows, that mattered less. He manned Riley Thilthorpe for much of the game and won. Strangely, Andrews picked up a shot at goal in the first quarter after a double 50-metre penalty. His rare chance to score was offline. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fort: Solid and dependable as Brisbane’s first ruck. He split the points with Adelaide’s Lachlan McAndrew. 5.5/10 View post on X (33) Zac Bailey: What a game by the newly re-signed gun. Ever classy by foot, he was nothing short of brilliant – ironically against the club that desperately wanted him. He had a stack of score involvements and was one of the five Lions to get on the board in the first eight minutes. He finished with 23 touches and kicked 3.3. 8.5/10 (35) Ryan Lester: A quality contributor, Lester was heavily involved in the win from the start. Witness a strong defensive effort on the wing (a punch from behind) that helped set the mood. Quirkily, like Andrews, Lester had a rare shot at goal in the first term, but missed. 8/10



(44) Darcy Wilmot: He did his bit. He got enough of the ball and was more than solid in defence and playing as a link player. Thumbs up for an important player in Fagan’s all-conquering side. 6.5/10 Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Two consolation goals in the first half almost masked a forgettable night for the defensive forward. Normally such a spark plug in attack, Keays was unsighted when the whips were cracking and was soundly trumped by Zorko. 4/10 (3) Sam Berry: The hardworking onballer was one Adelaide player who could hold his head high. Berry did his best to stem Brisbane’s early onslaught, chalking up five first-quarter clearances by himself. He finished with a game-high 31 disposals. 7.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: Other than a sprayed shot out on the full early, Ah Chee struggled to get involved early doors at his old stomping ground. He had just three touches in the first half before spending time on the wing in the third term and getting more involved. 5/10



(6) Daniel Curtin: A big second half saw him finish with 22 disposals and seven clearances. Curtin booted the Crows’ first goal and played predominantly on the ball, but he – like many of his mates – wasn’t able to stop Brisbane’s game-breaking mids. 7/10 Daniel Curtin celebrates a goal with Taylor Walker. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: Had his hands full with Andrews in the first half before playing much better footy after the main break, booting two goals and using his body well against the Lions’ skipper. Thilthorpe’s contest was strong, but his ball use wasn’t quite up to scratch. 5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: Enjoyed a second-quarter purple patch when he slotted a major and then handed another one off to Darcy Fogarty. But otherwise, Rachele – fresh off a three-goal haul against the Bulldogs – had a poor evening. He conceded an early 50-metre penalty and was thrashed in the air by Lester. 2/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: He gave it everything he had with 30 touches and 512m gained, but his normally pristine ball use was missing, going at 50 per cent disposal efficiency. Dawson’s six first-quarter tackles said as much about the Lions’ dominance as it did about his own never-say-die approach. 7.5/10



(13) Taylor Walker: Ended his AFL journey with two fourth-quarter goals – to finish with 715 for his career – after being frustrated throughout the first three terms. Not an ending he wanted in his 319th and last top-flight game, but what a star he has been. 4/10 Walker leaves an AFL playing field for the final time with his children. AFL Photos (14) Jake Soligo: Adelaide needed more from him – for much of the home-and-away campaign and in both finals. Soligo was part of the midfield rotation, but struggled to get his hands on the footy. 3.5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The crafty wingman’s usually clean ball use was a touch ragged and, aside from one neat goal assist early, he struggled to influence the match. 4/10 (16) Max Michalanney: There’s no lonelier place on an AFL field than one-out against Cameron in the mood he was in. Michalanney, normally a reliable stopper, was absolutely torched by the Lions’ brilliant goalsneak in the first half, before being mercifully moved to the wing. 1/10



(19) Zac Taylor: After missing the elimination final with a hamstring injury, Taylor ratified his recall instant by providing pressure and contest, while splitting minutes between half-forward and the centre-square. All up, 10 of his 17 possessions were contested. 6.5/10 (23) Izak Rankine: The highest-rated player in the AFL since round 17 was due a downer – and a downer he had, thanks chiefly to the disciplined, iron-fisted glove of Dunkley. Rankine was kickless at quarter-time and still had just two at the half. He was given more room to roam after half-time, but it just wasn’t his night. 5/10 Izak Rankine had his hands full all night against the Lions. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: After enjoying the game of his life against the Bulldogs, when he racked up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions, Worrell wasn’t allowed anywhere near the same the influence to make plays. Although he still finished with 18 touches, he had just four of them by half-time. 5/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: He played major minutes on the wing before taking on the Cameron job late. Nankervis snared a magnificent mark over Levi Ashcroft and goaled to give the Crows a glimmer late in the first period, but otherwise was quiet. 4.5/10



(28) Alex Neal-Bullen: Splitting time between wing and half-forward, the experienced ex-Demon didn’t have a huge impact, particularly in the first half. 5.5/10 (29) Rory Laird: The experienced half-back flanker never waved the white flag, but didn’t give the Lions too many major headaches either. 6/10 (30) Wayne Milera: The dashing All-Australian half-back wasn’t afforded the same time and space that he enjoyed a week earlier against the Bulldogs. Normally so calm and creative, his disposal was hurried thanks to the Lions’ pressure. Kicked a neat late goal. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fogarty: Conceded a horror 100m penalty in a forgettable opening term before springing to life in the second quarter, spearheading Adelaide’s revival by booting two goals and assisting another one to Rachele. But he was unsighted too often. 4.5/10 Darcy Fogarty had a frustrating night for the Crows. AFL Photos



(35) James Borlase: Quiet for four quarters, he rarely intercepted and struggled to have much involvement, despite how much time the Sherrin spent in Brisbane’s attacking area. 3/10 (40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The unsung half-back has barely put a foot wrong since being picked up in the mid-season draft. He wasted very few of his 27 disposals, racked up plenty of metres of rebound and contested well in the air and on the ground. A real find. 7.5/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: After shading Tim English last week, the towering ruckman had his hands full with Draper and Fort. McAndrew matched them both in the air, but it was harder for him on the deck. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: He struggled all night with an aggressive Hipwood, finishing with four kicks and virtually no impact. 2/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Fans stay home but Sharks turn up to end Cowboys’ season
World.content:
If you build it, they won’t come.

It may be the one of the best stadiums in the southern hemisphere, a mere 25.2 kilometres from the Sharks’ spiritual home in the Shire. But many Cronulla fans refuse to leave Cronulla.

Not even the siren song of their Mermaids cheerleaders, free public transport for ticket holders, or the chance to witness their team in a finals fixture was enough to bring them to Allianz Stadium.

Loading

An official crowd of 17,429 was posted. That’s only about 2,500 more than the capacity of Shark Park, otherwise known as Ocean Protect Stadium. Understandably, only a handful of hearty Cowboys souls made the long commute from Townsville.

The decision to shift the game here was a controversial one. Head office will hope the extra corporate cash it pockets from playing at Allianz offsets the broadcast images of a stadium less than half full.

The reasons for non-attendance remain unclear. Is it because rugby league is such a good television product? The fatigue of watching the seventh North Queensland-Cronulla post-season clash since 2013? Or just a preference for “Portaloo Park”?

Nicho Hynes celebrates a try. Getty Images

Whatever the case, the Sharks got the job done without the vocal support they would normally get at their regular home.

“It’s not our decision,” Cronulla coach Craig Fitzgibbon said. “I felt like this last year - obviously the amount of sulking that went on about playing at Shark Park, I thought we weren’t any chance of getting it this year. They should have just told us earlier.

“But also, for us, we’re happy to play here. We’re in semi-finals; we want to play in a big stadium. But our members and fans pay their money all year to be able to watch their team make semi-finals and play at home, and we earned that. We didn’t get it … but that’s not up to me. I would imagine it’s a financial decision or viewing optics for the game. I’m not sure.”

A 26-16 win against their old sparring partners was achieved despite their returning maestro playing with the use of only one shoulder. Braydon Trindall took his place after three weeks on the sidelines. Despite being clearly hampered, he passed, tackled and kicked his side to a scrappy victory.

At one point in the second half, “Tricky” gave his shoulder an unnecessary test when he tried to retrieve the football from his own short kick-off. The pivot couldn’t be accused of playing in a dinner suit. When he produced a season-high 31st try assist with a pass to fullback Will Kennedy – not even Nathan Cleary comes near that figure – it was due reward for playing through the pain.

Loading

The Cowboys have been the most curious side in the NRL. They qualified for the top eight despite conceding more points than any other finalist in history. Their devil-may-care attitude is best exemplified by Scott Drinkwater. The Dragons-bound fullback is the ultimate gunslinger. One errant cut-out pass resulted in an intercept that gifted Sione Katoa his 100th NRL try. Undeterred, he threw another one that hit Zac Laybutt on the chest from 25 metres away to give his side hope.

However, it was always going to come down to the Cowboys’ application without the football. They defended stoutly when starved off possession for much of the opening half, particularly when their tryline was peppered. However, those exertions eventually took their toll. When Nico Hynes shaped to kick, but instead stepped off his left foot, their fate was sealed.

There is every chance that the Sharks could be required to return to Allianz next week. Asked whether he hoped more of their fans will follow them there, captain Cameron McInnes deadpanned: “I don’t know. If you can afford it, come. If you can’t, watch it on TV. I couldn’t care less, really.”

World.title: Warriors toppled by Dolphins in NRL qualifying final
World.content:
The NZ Warriors have been defeated by the Dolphins in their NRL qualifying final, at Go Media Stadium in Auckland.

The Warriors will now have to take the scenic route to the NRL grand final, after bowing to the Dolphins 26-16 on Saturday night.

After finishing second, to earn homefield advantage for the opening round of the playoffs, the Warriors could not take advantage of their fan support and a penalty advantage that had them 12-8 ahead at halftime.

Their only try of the game came when fullback Taine Tuaupiki spun out of a tackle near the line and scooted clear to score. Tuaupiki scored all the Warriors' points, adding a conversion and five penalties, as his team chose to kick for goal, instead of push for tries in the redzone.

They probably should have led by more at the break, but Tuaupiki stretched the margin beyond a converted try, with two more penalties in the second half, before the Dolphins piled on three unanswered converted tries in the final 20 minutes.

The Warriors' cause was not helped by ill-discipline, as centre Adam Pompey was sin-binned for a no-arms shoulder tackle and then second-rower Kurt Capewell was matched for sparking a melee just before halftime.

Dolphins wing Selwyn Cobbo was also sent to the bin in the same incident, after Jackson Ford was dumped in a tipping tackle and the teams came together.

The Warriors lost centre Leka Halasima to injury during the warm-up, with Pompey promoted to the starting line-up in his place.

The Dolphins were good for their win, scoring four tries to the Warriors' one, all converted by wing Jamayne Isaako, and they will now take a rest next week, as they await their opponents for a preliminary final in two weeks.

Meanwhile, the Warriors will host Newcastle Knights next week.

The result broke a six-game winning streak and marked the first time this season they have lost, after leading at halftime.

World.title: Two-thirds of middle-aged adults delay eye tests despite problems - survey
World.content:
More than two-thirds of middle-aged adults are delaying their eye tests despite having problems.

A survey by YouGov commissioned by Specsavers showed that 70 percent of adults between 40 and 59 put off getting their sight checked by more than a month when having trouble with their vision.

Longer delays weren't uncommon with almost half waiting for more than six months to get help, and one in five stalling for more than two years.

Chair of Ophthalmology NZ Dr Sonya Bennett told RNZ it was "probably human nature" to avoid confronting health problems.

"It's not uncommon for us to hear the story that they've put off getting seen until they've got quite significant issues."

She said people would find ways to cope before seeing an optometrist "because they actually don't want to wear glasses" out of vanity or perceived impracticality.

And YouGov's survey found one in five avoided wearing glasses despite needing them because of social perception.

It found half of respondents simply increased texts and display settings on their devices to cope - with a third simply missing out on certain activities because of their eyesight.

Dr Bennett explained that "presbyopia" was the most common age-related cause of eyesight loss, often setting in around middle age.

"It gradually affects your ability to read at near [distance]. Distance vision is usually in most cases okay, but you just lose the ability to see things up close.

"And that's because what we call 'accommodation' - which is the ability to focus - reduces with ageing due to changes in the lens, inside the eye and changes in the muscle that moves the lens."

The survey found nine in 10 had never heard the medical term for this common condition.

She said the only real danger of delaying getting help was if there were another underlying disease, such as glaucoma, where vision could not be regained once lost.

World.title: Man charged after election hoardings damaged in "vandalism spree", police say
World.content:
Charges have been laid against a Tauranga man after what police called a "vandalism spree", damaging political hoardings in Papamoa.

About 30 hoardings were attacked in a two hour period, from about 6:30am on Thursday, police said.

The first damaged were in Parton Road, then more were damaged throughout the suburb of Papamoa.

Senior Sergeant Shannon Clifford thanked the people who had provided information about the damage, which led to an arrest on the same day.

A 43-year-old man faces charges of wilful damage and is scheduled to appear in court again next month.

Ahead of November's general election, the case was a warning that damaging political hoardings is not okay, Senior Sergeant Clifford said:

"The damage in some cases is significant and unfortunately that's an unnecessary cost for the people who own them.

"We won't tolerate this illegal and destructive behaviour in our community."
