The only remaining round one question left to answer at the September Apple event was whether or not the Apple Watch would add a dedicated AI health coach. Although the new Health app for the Watch has plenty of coaching features, we determined that the final answer was no.

Most of the round two questions, which focused on Apple devices, weren’t settled until Wednesday’s event.

The final question of round two was a freebie (any reasonable answer was marked correct) about what you’d like to see change about the iPhone. Readers’ most popular request — a lower price — hit a blocker on Wednesday as Apple announced it was boosting the price of its latest Pro and Pro Max iPhones by $100.

We will be contacting our grand-prize winner via email this week, so please keep an eye on your mailbox if you entered the contest. While you’re waiting, now’s the time to catch up on everything Apple released on Wednesday, rewatch the event and stay tuned to see if you won the CNET Group’s Big Guessing Game.

Tech.title: The 10 Privacy Tricks I Use Around My Own Smart Home (and Why You Need Them)
Tech.content:
With surveillance cameras in our streets and data-collecting TVs in our homes, privacy is always on my mind these days. If you feel the same way, I’ve got a few changes you should make.

In my years of smart home testing, I’ve narrowed down the most impactful privacy changes, and how they make my home feel much safer and more comfortable. If you’re looking for a major privacy boost, here are the steps you take.



1. Keep the shutters on your security cams and smart displays closed

New smart devices have physical shutters and buttons to confirm privacy. Amazon

When smart displays first started appearing, they came with cameras to enable video chats and similar features. When those cameras started making people nervous, makers began putting physical shutters and off buttons on their smart devices so people could quickly shut them down and confirm the cameras couldn’t be used remotely.

In my experience, these cams rarely get much use and are best left turned off permanently until you’re ready to make a video call to a family member. The same is true of the mics in some smart speakers, which you can shut off when not in use if you’re worried about the speaker listening in. For the record, while you can find a lot of internet rumors about eavesdropping speakers, today’s models require the wake word to start listening in, and accidents are typically confined to picking up similar-sounding words in conversations, music or TVs.

The same is true of security cameras. Look for cams that have shutters or “off” positions (like facing down) if you’re concerned about privacy.

2. Switch off opt-in and data-sharing features

You can disable most Ring AI features in one swoop. Ring/CNET

I spoke with Laurie Selkowitz, partner in Greenberg Glusker’s Cybersecurity and Privacy Group, about increasing home privacy with smart devices to find some good advice.

“The biggest mistake people make is treating smart home devices like appliances instead of connected computers. Once you think of them as computers that happen to live in your home, the privacy decisions become much more obvious,” Selkowitz said.

“A good rule of thumb is to enable only the features you actually use,” she said. “Many devices collect far more data than they need to function, so turning off things like unnecessary cloud storage, voice history or activity logs can significantly reduce your exposure.”

You can often change how companies manage and share your home data, but the methods are typically buried deep in settings, so you need to know where to look. I can help with that.

Here’s my guide on Alexa settings you may want to adjust, including options that control how long Amazon saves your voice recordings and other privacy features to help make voice assistant use better.

I also have a complete guide on Ring security features you may want to turn off, including all AI features if those recognition capabilities worry you, automatic data sharing in your neighborhood for tools like Search Party and disabling Amazon Sidewalk so it won’t share your bandwidth with strangers.

3. Shut down facial recognition

You can quickly visit Familiar Faces to see if it’s on, although it should be opt-in. Screenshot by Tyler Lacoma/CNET

One home AI feature has emerged as highly controversial in 2026, and it’s a video doorbell/security cam capability to scan and recognize faces. As a series of recent lawsuits against companies like Ring and Nest allege, facial recognition can scan and save facial data from people who can’t consent. That includes delivery people, strangers passing by on the street at the right angle, distant family members visiting and even your own children.

If you want to prevent your app (and company) from collecting facial data on people, it’s important to double-check that any “familiar faces” technology in the settings is turned off. You usually have to opt into more advanced AI features like this, and they usually require a subscription fee to enable, so it’s unlikely to start gathering data by accident.

Technically, familiar-face technology can be used to automatically unlock a smart lock when the right person approaches, or only alert you if a security camera recognizes an unfamiliar face. But smart homes offer so many alternatives to these tricks, it’s really not necessary for the average user.

4. Use local storage instead of cloud storage

Eufy’s two-pack is an excellent local storage 4K camera option. Eufy

If you use security cameras, you have two choices for saving video (and you really need to save video; otherwise, the camera isn’t much more than live views).

The first option most cameras offer these days is cloud storage. But many people don’t like the idea of trusting companies to manage their video data, and those cloud databases have been hacked or accidentally shared in the past.

The second option, local storage, is much better for your privacy. Local storage uses either a microSD card or a hub with a built-in drive to store video. You may have to clear out videos occasionally, but it keeps your data in your own hands. Lots of brands offer local storage if you choose the right setup, including Eufy, Lorex, Blink and Wyze.

Just remember, even if videos are stored locally, police can still confiscate them with a warrant.

Best Home Security Cameras Without Subscriptions in 2026 See at CNET

5. Close your shades on a schedule

Smart shades like those from Lutron can boost privacy even when you aren’t home. Tyler Lizenby/CNET

People probably aren’t peering through your windows at night, but that doesn’t mean you should make it easy. Today’s smart shades can automatically close on a schedule or when the sun goes down, even if you aren’t home yet. That helps guarantee extra privacy and may even deter burglars scouting for a target.

6. Check old Zillow and real estate listings

You may want to check what information remains about your home on old listings. Bloomberg / Contributor / Getty

If you recently moved into a new home within the past year or two, I suggest checking the old selling or rental listing pages for your address. In some cases, these get left up for years after the home has already changed hands.

Those old listings could be an unwelcome window into exactly where your address is, what your home looks like on the inside and even access points a burglar might want to know. Also, people may get the wrong idea and assume it’s still available to rent or buy — I’ve had more than a few people peer through my windows for just that reason.

It’s better for your privacy if you run a quick check on platforms like Zillow, Trulia and local real estate sites to see if your home is still there. Then you can request it be removed.

7. Blur your address on Google Maps

If you don’t want someone getting a good look at your home from the street, you can blur it on map apps. David Cameron/Getty Images

There’s another place your home shows up to anyone willing to look — Google Maps, especially when using satellite and street view images.

Well aware of this fact, Google offers an option on its website (not its app) to blur out your address for privacy. We have a complete guide on how to do that here, but it’s free and takes only a couple of minutes. Apple offers a similar service in its Look Around map app function.

8. Switch to open-source or third-party smart home controls

Homey’s devices and platforms are more privacy-focused than big-brand home apps. Homey

If you’re worried about big brand names having easy access to your data, you can still get a full set of smart home features by using alternative platforms. You have several choices, notably the open-source, build-it-yourself Home Assistant and the third-party, privacy-first Homey hub and platform.

The catch is that these platforms will take much more work to set up and customize, and they tend to be buggier and require more problem-solving than you’ll find on any brand app. But if you don’t mind tinkering, these are great ways to mandate privacy while getting the high-tech smart features you want.

9. Adopt a home VPN

The Aircove is ExpressVPN’s answer to Wi-Fi 6 routers and smart home privacy. ExpressVPN

We talk a lot about using virtual private networks on our browsers, phones and laptops for greater privacy and reduced risk of third-party data collection, but many of the benefits apply at home, too. It’s even easier to use a VPN at home because many home Wi-Fi routers come with VPNs you can use, or you can add a VPN to them for whole-house protection, which in our tests only takes about 10 minutes.

With a VPN, every device connected to your router, including your smart home devices, typically has its data encrypted when it sends data online, making it harder for companies to glean information about your activity and home habits.

10. Disconnect your smart TV from Wi-Fi and other devices

LG’s TVs may have an eavesdropping problem, but that’s just the start of the issue. Sarah Tew/CNET

A recent report showed that LG smart TVs seem to be listening in on users via their mics and connected devices without consent, although LG has denied these claims. Well, I have unsurprising news: All smart TVs (and nearly every TV is smart these days) are trying to collect as much data about you as possible, including what commands they hear and what’s happening on the screen from moment to moment.

If that’s a privacy problem for you, do what I did and never connect your TV to Wi-Fi at all. If you leave this part of the setup incomplete, the TV can never share data, no matter how much it tries to collect, and you still get access to all the other settings. Then you can use an online device that’s a bit safer (for now), like a set-top box, Chromecast-like plugin, game console and so on.

If your smart TV is already connected to the internet, you can disable the feature in its settings and change your Wi-Fi password so it doesn’t try to automatically reconnect. It’s also worth checking which other smart devices (like speakers or hubs from the same brand) the TV is linked to, possibly without you knowing.

Is it still safe to use foreign-made routers at home?

Earlier this year, the Federal Communications Commission banned foreign-made Wi-Fi routers for national security reasons — sort of. The reasons are complicated, and exemptions were quickly granted to top router brands like Netgear, so I don’t blame you if you’re unsure what to think about router privacy. We spoke to several security experts, and unless you have to buy a new router right away, we don’t think there’s much to worry about. No sudden security threat has made routers any less safe to use than before, but, as always, strong security practices will help keep you safe.

If you’re interested in off-the-grid options, check out my off-the-grid home security guide.

Tech.title: This Is the Biggest 2D Map of the Universe. Here’s How to Use It
Tech.content:
Scientists have pointed telescopes at the sky and mapped the cosmos for centuries. That relentless pursuit is producing maps that are bigger and more detailed than ever. But there’s one map that stands out above the rest, and now it’s the largest 2D map of the night sky ever created.

The best part? Anyone can play with it.

The map, called Data Release 11 or DR11, comes courtesy of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team, a collaborative effort between NSF NOIRLab, the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and other agencies and organizations.

Covering 75% of the sky across 5.6 trillion pixels, DR11 is the team’s most comprehensive map to date, built upon prior versions of the same map. It expands on DR9 by 50% and brings back northern sky coverage missing from DR10. Based on 263,407 ground-based exposures by 160 scientists, the map catalogs 4 billion objects — including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids — in visible and near-infrared light.

Already cited in over 1,800 research papers, researchers and collaborators expect this to remain the premier 2D map of its kind for years. According to co-lead David Schlegel, DR11 also helped identify 60 million targets for the DESI project and to build a full 3D map, which was completed in 2026, with future expansions planned. With billions of targets still unstudied, Schlegel told CNET that “plenty of other discoveries” remain hidden in plain sight for public exploration, and that DR11 is also being used to select additional targets for the 3D map.

Enough talk, let’s play

The map covers 75% of the night sky, with the black swath through the middle obscured by black holes, interstellar dust and other obstacles. Legacy Survey

The map doesn’t look like much at first. But if you pick a spot and start zooming in, you can get a pretty good idea of how vast it really is. What appears to be a cloud of pretty colors is actually billions of objects floating around in space.

You might notice that DR11, which is designed to see out into the universe, doesn’t contain any planets, moons or asteroids within our solar system. That may be a little bit of a bummer for some, but there are plenty of other objects to look for.

Though the user interface is a little overwhelming at first, you really only need four boxes to play around — and all four of them are right next to each other in the bottom-left corner.

Zoom: This indicates how zoomed in you are based on the +/- slider on the top left. It goes from degrees to arc minutes and then finally to arc seconds. I got most of my best results between 20 and 50 arc minutes.

Contrast and brightness: Below zoom, you’ll find the contrast slider, which reduces the background noise of the map. Under that, the brightness slider helps illuminate smaller objects. Adjust these settings as needed to get the best view, but start with the defaults.

Jump to object: This is the most important box, where you can type in the names of celestial bodies to find them on the map. I searched for a couple dozen celestial objects and found them all pretty quickly. Online lists of named black holes, quasars and other cool celestial bodies can be a good starting point in exploring the universe — I have more tips for finding them if you keep reading.

Once you land on something, use the zoom slider in the top-left corner to zoom in and get a closer look. (Don’t use your mouse wheel for this because it zooms in wherever your pointer is, potentially taking you to a completely different part of the map.) You can also drag the cursor around the screen to view everything around the object you’re looking at.

A sky like you’ve never seen it

Arcturus is comparably huge in the night sky, and so it is also comparably huge on the map. Legacy Survey

My first visit on the map was to Arcturus, the fourth-largest star in the sky. Zoomed in, it’s much larger than every other object around it by a rather wide margin, which is why it’s so easy to find in the night sky.

Another search took me to LHS 1140b, the first star ever discovered that sits in another star’s habitable zone with an atmosphere. This one is much smaller than Arcturus and required me to zoom in to 30 arc seconds to see it. It’s quite close to its host star, which makes sense since the habitable zone is pretty close to the star itself. Earth would appear at a similar distance from the sun if viewed from this perspective.

The star that LHS 1140b orbits is also dimmer than many other stars. It’s about 20% the size of the sun, so it almost looks like a big planet rather than a small star.

This binary star system hosts planet HD 80606 b, a planet known to orbit so close to its star that it is scorched. It’s so close, in fact, that the light from the binary star system hides it completely. Legacy Survey

Some stuff is easier to find than others. For example, planet HD 80606 b is so close to its star that it is absolutely scorched, with temperature swings of 1,100 degrees Fahrenheit. Bright glare from its binary stars completely obscures HD 80606 b on the map. It’s still there, though, getting blasted by its star like a blowtorch caramelizing sugar on the top of a crème brûlée.

You’ll notice that the map has a large, sweeping blank spot running through it. These are the parts of the sky that haven’t been mapped yet. Researchers say that this is due to various obstacles, such as space dust, bright stars getting in the way of scans and black holes covering everything behind them.

For example, try searching for Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way. The map shows you where it is — right inside one of those blank bands. The black hole prevents any telescope from seeing the stars and planets behind it, so that part of the map remains blank.

More advanced options

The planet LHS 1140b orbits a star about one-fifth the size of our sun, and is one of the better candidates for a planet hosting life. Legacy Viewer

You’ll also see a box with a ton of options in the top-right corner of the map. For basic viewing, you don’t have to interact with this box at all, but there are some fun things in there if you want to see them.

Images: This dropdown menu lets you select which set of images you want to use. Leave that on Legacy Surveys DR11 because that’s the most recent dataset.

Overlays: This menu is more complicated, as it includes a lot of different datasets you can overlay. Many of them just show which telescopes, instruments and surveys found each separate part of the map. You can leave them all off and still search around the universe for cool stuff.

However, there is one set of overlays that is worth your time: the Bright objects overlay, with options that actually help you navigate the map. For example, the Bright stars option will put blue circles around the brightest stars on the map with names, making them much easier to find. That’s how I learned that the designation for Arcturus is HR 5340.

Bright objects include star clusters, planetary nebulae and some more specific ones — but the most fun is the Constellations overlay, which shows off every constellation in the sky. If you toggle it on, pick a constellation and zoom into each corner and point, you can find the bright stars that humans used to construct these constellations ages ago.

Finding stuff to search for

Constellations such as Ursa Minor can be seen on the 2D map, letting you explore the bright stars that make up their shape. Legacy Survey

The real challenge in using the DR11 app is figuring out what to look up. There are all sorts of celestial bodies, and many of them have some pretty cool stories. However, there really isn’t much of a repository to find these things.

We know AI isn’t great at many things, but Schlegel suggested that a large language model may be pretty good for this application since it can scan the web quickly.

This isn’t without its caveats. Schlegel said that Google Gemini tends to “spit out sexagesimal coordinates” that don’t work in the map’s viewer website because they’re an archaic sky-mapping system. However, Anthropic’s Claude uses decimal-degree coordinates, which work. While the team is looking into supporting both, Schlegel said he prefers the newer decimal system over the archaic system originally invented by Hipparchus and Ptolemy.

The team also gave CNET a list of some pretty neat stuff to look up in the map viewer if you need more ideas. These are some of the most gorgeous pieces of imagery on the entire map:

NGC 5272 – The Globular Cluster

NGC 4826 – The Black Eye Galaxy

NGC 3351 – The Barred Spiral Galaxy

NGC 4486 – Virgo A

NGC 5457 – The Pinwheel Galaxy

NGC 4594 – Sombrero Galaxy

Schlegel also recommended visiting an FAQ web page for more granular guidance on using the search and overlay functions to improve your experience.

Tech.title: Lenovo’s Googlebook 15 Gets a New Specs Leak. Brace Your Wallet for Impact
Tech.content:
Lenovo’s upcoming Googlebook 15 just got its latest and most comprehensive leak, and woof — this is not the affordable Chromebook you’re used to if the specs are accurate. The leak comes from MacObserver, which has the full purported specs sheet, showing that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is very much going to be a premium laptop, though the leak doesn’t reveal a price or exact launch date.

A Google representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Under the hood, we’re apparently looking at an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 processor, 16GB or 32GB of LPDDR5x RAM, 256/512GB storage and a 70-watt-hour battery that can last for up to 11 hours. MacObserver notes that the leaked machine is identified as GB 151PH12, and according to Lenovo’s naming guide, IPH is the platform code for Panther Lake-H, so you can expect an Intel integrated graphics chip.

Google announced the new device in May and said it would go on sale this fall. Google

The laptop sports a 15.3-inch, 2,880-by-1,800-pixel OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate and a 16:10 aspect ratio with super-thin bezels, according to the leaked photos that you can view on MacObserver. Brightness is 500 nits, and it has 100% DCI-P3 color. According to the leaked specs, the entire device will weigh just 2.84 pounds and measure 13.43 by 9.29 by 0.63 inches. It’s also touchscreen.

Another interesting feature on the laptop’s exterior is the Glowbar, a colored Google indicator on the lid that shows battery and charging status. It’s not clear whether this will have additional functionality like the erstwhile Touchbar on older MacBook models did, but we’d guess that you’re able to customize some of the indicator options.

Googlebooks replace the Windows icon with a G on the keyboard. Google

You get a haptic trackpad (150 by 95 millimeters), fingerprint sensor and Google facial authentication, the company’s challenge to Apple’s Face ID and possibly related to the technology at play with Google Pixel’s Project Toscana. According to the leaked specs, for that purpose, there’s a 5MP RGB webcam with dual microphones and a physical privacy shutter, which is a nice touch.

Audio also seems like it’ll be solid, with four Dolby Atmos speakers that are visible on either side of the keyboard in the leaked renders. Speaking of the keyboard, there appears to be a dedicated Google “G” key on the bottom row between the Function and Alt keys. That could be a command key, similar to what we get on MacBooks, perhaps something that activates AI tool Gemini, which the company has said can provide more proactive help. It should sync well with Android phones, letting you access apps and files directly on the Googlebook, a feature available through Microsoft Phone Link on Windows.

It’s currently unclear from the specs leaks whether there will be deeper integration with Android, whether the new proactive help capabilities will be exclusive to Googlebook or whether they will come to other devices in the future. It will be restricted to certain countries and languages, as well as users who are 18 and older.

The main features of a Googlebook. Google

The port loadout looks fairly solid with a Thunderbolt 4 port, USB 3.2 Type-A port and audio jack on the left side. The right features another Thunderbolt 4 port and HDMI 2.0. It comes with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. The keyboard is also backlit.

The specs leak also revealed details about accessories expected to accompany the Googlebook. It looks like there may be a bundle that includes the laptop, along with a Lenovo E310 True Wireless Earbuds and a Lenovo 540 Convertible Tote backpack.

There’s also a Lenovo “AI Mouse,” which has the same colorful LED indicator on it as the Googlebook. Details aren’t available about what makes the mouse AI, but it could be similar to what we’ve seen on Logitech’s productivity mice, like the MX Master series, which offer seamless file sharing and cross-device functionality.

Chromebooks captured the budget and midrange laptop segment for non-Apple users, but the idea of a premium Chromebook never really took off due to Chrome OS and its challenges in handling real productivity. The goal of Googlebook is to give you access to the full range of Android apps on your phone, along with storage for files and improved functionality.

“The basic idea is that using a Googlebook shouldn’t be all too different from using a Chromebook or any other laptop; you’ll just get more Gemini AI-powered tools built in, along with access to the full universe of Android apps,” said Josh Goldman, managing editor for CNET’s computing coverage.

Goldman notes that the biggest advantage of the Googlebook over Chromebooks is that it can bring features originally developed for Android to the device more quickly, citing Circle to Search as an example. “It took roughly a year for the feature to make the jump from Android phones to Chromebook Plus laptops. But now, an AI feature like Create Your Widget — which lets you quickly generate custom widgets and was only recently announced for Android phones — will also be available on Googlebooks.”

The only details we’re really missing at this point are the price and exact release date, though a fall launch is expected, so it may be any day now. For price, if we were to take an educated guess, this is not going to be a cheap laptop. With the specs under the hood here, 9to5 Google points out that you’re looking at a device that will likely be priced similarly to Lenovo’s ThinkPad X9 15 Aura Edition, which starts at $1,519 for the base model and upward of $2,396 for a more heavily specced-out unit.

There’s no doubt that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 is meant for productivity and users of full-fledged MacBooks and Windows laptops, so we’d expect pricing to be in the same range, with the larger memory and storage configurations costing more.

Tech.title: GTA 5 Mod Adds Flock Surveillance Cameras So Players Can Blow Them Up
Tech.content:
Flock automated license plate-reading cameras are rapidly popping up all over the US. In some areas, they’re also going down pretty quick, too.

Widespread opposition to Flock surveillance cameras has highlighted their inaccuracies and potential for abuse by authorities. A movement to “deflock” cities includes everything from canceling municipal contracts to covering cameras with trash bags and various forms of physical vandalism.

Now, if you’re cruising through the fictional town of Los Santos (modeled after Los Angeles) in a new Grand Theft Auto 5 “mod,” you could be tracked by any of the 235 Flock cameras there. But you can also cash in $600 for each one you shoot down.

The mod (a custom addition to the game) is called Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader. Morry Kolman, the mod’s creator, said the in-game Flock cameras are based on “custom-built” 3D models, which subject players to “seemingly inescapable surveillance.”

Almost like living amid Big Brother, these virtual cameras take pictures of you and track your movements. If you commit crimes in the game — like speeding or hitting pedestrians — the cameras will report you to the police. They’ll even occasionally file “false reports” on you, just like the real cameras sometimes do. Players can also save the images captured by the cameras for use in social media posts or as wallpapers.

And, because it’s Grand Theft Auto, you’re also allowed to fight back against the surveillance state, with access to weapons (like rocket launchers) that help you destroy the cameras. Once you’ve carried out an effective deflocking, you can pick up the mutilated remains and grab an in-game reward of $600 (the estimated value of the camera’s internal components based on a teardown conducted by Eyes Off Cedar Rapids). There’s also an integrated timer to keep track of how fast you deflock, allowing you to beat your PB.

A virtual protest

Cameras you destroy give you $600, based on the cost of parts for a real Flock camera. WTTDOTM

GTA 5 is chock-full of social commentary, from the dangers of consumerism to subtle critiques of extreme gamer behavior in characters like Trevor and Jimmy. The new Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader mod builds on the general hatred toward and distrust of the massive Flock surveillance network adorning US roadways.

For some, it’s probably a fun (and less punitive) way to tap into unfulfilled vigilantism. But, according to Kolman, it also makes the game more difficult. “Not only does police surveillance become nearly impossible to evade, but representing Flock’s own history of inaccurate reporting, every time a player passes through a camera’s field of view, the mod creates a 1 in 20 chance that the ALPR will trigger a police chase without any cause,” according to the mod’s download page.

In many ways, the new mod is a reality check for real-world privacy. If having 235 cameras follow you around in GTA feels like an oppressive nightmare in a claustrophobic game world, just remember that the real Los Angeles County has more than 10 times that amount.

Tech.title: A Breakthrough? Or Just Breakable? Apple Unveiled the iPhone Duo, and CNET Writers Have Many Thoughts
Tech.content:
Apple unfolded its new iPhone this week, and we’re still trying to wrap our heads around it. The folding iPhone Duo, revealed at the tech company’s Surprise and Shine event Wednesday, was far from a surprise — and, in a sense, not all that new, since other phone makers have been folding their phones for years.

Still, the rumors were one thing. Seeing the real deal — which is available for preorder Oct. 16 and in stores Oct. 23 — is something entirely different. And once new CEO John Ternus gave us the first look at the $2,000 passport-style gadget, the tech experts at CNET had plenty to say. Here’s a glimpse at what we’re thinking. Like the apps on a folding phone, we aren’t always on the same page.

Will Apple, and its developers, make foldables less boring? What makes a folding phone interesting? It has to be more than a phone that folds. That’s what CNET Editor-at-Large Andrew Lanxon wants to see from Apple — and the people who make apps for this new thing. The duo could remind me that tech is still fun, still exciting and, fundamentally, something I can still care about. We’ll see whether Apple delivers the magic yet again. Andrew Lanxon, CNET editor-at-large 

Apple arrives precisely when it means to Sure, Apple is several years behind other phone-makers in crafting a foldable. But that just means it has waited out the growing pains, says CNET Principal Writer Katie Collins. Apple has a long history of defining product categories that it didn’t invent. Many people still think the iPhone was the first smartphone, which it definitely wasn’t. Katie Collins, CNET principal writer 

The iPhone Duo has two 48-megapixel rear cameras. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET Maybe buy the iPhone Duo, but not this iPhone Duo Having doubts about the crease? Maybe wait to see how the first batches of folding iPhones hold up before spending $2,000 on an experiment, CNET Reporter Katelyn Chedraoui says. When it comes to major redesigns, there’s no harm in waiting until Apple fixes the inevitable pain points with the next-generation device. And if it turns out there aren’t any big issues, you can pay for the device with peace of mind and, hopefully, less money than it would be to buy it brand new. Katelyn Chedraoui, CNET reporter 2 

Is this an iPad Mini killer? Sometimes you want a phone for phone tasks and something a little bigger for slightly-larger-than-phone tasks. CNET Senior Consumer Insights Editor Dashia Milden wonders if the iPhone Duo can do the job of both — and if that spells doom for the company’s smallest tablet. The iPad Mini is bigger than the iPhone Duo, with a screen size of a little over 8 inches. But the iPhone Duo’s functionality and bigger screen size make me wonder if it’s the perfect handheld device if you’re already considering a new iPhone and iPad. Dashia Milden, CNET senior consumer insights editor 

You can get a lot of other Apple devices for the Duo’s $2000… or, at least, two. Patrick Holland/CNET

A familiar touch… ID For some reason, having my phone scan my face creeps me out more than having it scan my fingerprint. The iPhone Duo’s inclusion of Touch ID, which hasn’t been on an iPhone for four years, was one of CNET Senior Editor Lori Grunin’s favorite things about the event. We had some in-chat mockery about the ability to register multiple fingerprints for the Touch ID, but as someone who occasionally has dirty, greasy or otherwise electronics-objectionable hands, being able to use a clean finger sounds nice to me. Lori Grunin, CNET senior editor 

Sure, you can stand it up, but this isn’t a smart display We saw a lot of examples from Apple of people propping the iPhone Duo up like a tent and using it as a home display. But that’s no replacement for an actual smart home display, says CNET Senior Editor Tyler Lacoma. Ginormous pricing aside, the foldable Duo isn’t big enough to take over my favorite roles for a smart display, like serving as a second TV screen while you’re busy, and its speakers certainly can’t compare with the room-filling options most home displays come with these days. Tyler Lacoma, CNET senior editor 

Is the crease still a thing? The dreaded crease. It’s the most annoying thing about folding phones. But did Apple engineer it into nonexistence? CNET Director of Content Patrick Holland could see it… barely. It is nearly nonexistent, and I had to hold it next to a video light to really see it. I can feel it with my finger, but even then, it’s subtle. I’ll be curious to see how well the screen holds up over two, three or four years of use and if the crease gets more pronounced — I imagine that will be the case here, as it has been with all foldable phones. Patrick Holland, CNET director of content 

You can prop the iPhone Duo on its side to quickly glance at the time. Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Finally, an iPhone with a stylus Apple has its own branded stylus, the Apple Pencil, but the company has long resisted letting you use that on the iPhone. The iPhone Duo puts an end to that, writes CNET Senior Editor Matt Elliott. Is the rest of the lineup next? In the case of the Duo, it’s not about the display being too small, but about having a display so large when unfolded that it rivals an iPad’s. Matt Elliott, CNET senior editor

Tech.title: Over 153 Million Driver’s Licenses Were Stolen by Hackers. Here’s What to Know
Tech.content:
If you’ve used your driver’s license to verify your information either in the real world or online, there’s a chance that some of your driver’s license information was stolen by hackers in a security breach against the ID verification giant IDScan that was reportedly active for a year.

“On or around Sept. 1, 2026, IDScan.net received information indicating that certain data may have been accessed without authorization,” IDScan said in a statement on Sept. 4. “Upon this discovery, we took immediate steps to secure our systems and engaged a team of third-party specialists to help determine the full nature and scope of the incident.”

The hack is discussed in more detail by Brian Krebs, a security researcher who runs the website Krebs on Security. He says he was first made aware of the breach after a source alerted him to a post on a Russian cybercrime forum from a hacker offering digital scans of identity documents for more than 170 million people from a service called Nexus.

Krebs was able to access Nexus and verify that it did indeed have the documents it said it had, including a scan of his own driver’s license.

The data includes 153 million driver’s licenses, 10 million ID cards, 3 million travel documents like passports and, according to Krebs, “at least 579,000” medical cards. Most of these records are for US residents, but about 1.1 million Canadian driver’s licenses were also found.

Per IDScan, hackers weren’t able to get every piece of information from those documents, but most likely obtained full names, driver’s license numbers and government-issued ID numbers.

The hackers who ran Nexus boasted that they had obtained the information by “continuously exfiltrating new data for over a year” into a private database from “a major identity verification company.”

The data collected likely came from a range of sources. Krebs says the leak of his information could have resulted from renting a car from Hertz, which uses IDScan to verify driver’s licenses. Other companies named on IDScan’s website as customers included FedEx, GameStop and over 1,000 cannabis dispensaries, car rental agencies and gun shops across 19 states. A screenshot of IDScan’s website also included Target as a customer, and a representative for Target told CNET that while the retailer uses some of IDScan’s hardware, it did not transmit customer data to IDScan and Target customer data was not included in a data breach. IDScan reported that it scanned 150 million IDs in 2024 alone.

The New Orleans field office of the FBI is investigating the matter. The FBI has not responded to a request for comment.

Here’s what you can do

IDScan says it will notify everyone who was affected by the breach and “provide access to free credit monitoring and identity protection services” for those people. If you end up being one of them, IDScan says to contact it at 1-833-516-2980 (Monday-Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET) to enroll in those services.

Those concerned they may have been affected have a few options. The easiest and quickest is a credit freeze, which makes it much more difficult for cybercriminals to open new accounts in your name. CNET has a guide for that if you need help. Freezing your credit is free, but it requires you to set up individual accounts with the three major credit bureaus.

Since cybercrime can strike anywhere and at any time, it’s also good to follow some tips to keep yourself safe, including using strong passwords, familiarizing yourself with the latest AI-powered phishing scams and considering using a VPN to help obfuscate your online presence so you can’t be tracked.

The unfortunate reality is that cybersecurity breaches are getting bigger, and companies are telling consumers less about what’s happening, so it’s worth staying vigilant, even if your driver’s license wasn’t stolen.

Tech.title: Have You Protested AI Recently? Anthropic May Be Watching You for Precrimes
Tech.content:
On Wednesday, investigative reporter Daniel Boguslaw detailed how security officials at Anthropic, the creator of Claude AI, are engaging in monitoring and surveillance, including reporting AI activists to police for potential future crimes.

The report, published in The American Prospect, comes amid the well-known Anthropic-Pentagon standoff, in which the AI company has feuded over how the military deploys mass-surveillance tools and fully autonomous weapons. Anthropic lost several lucrative government contracts in the process. Last week, after US Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick said Anthropic is “back on the right side,” a Pentagon official disputed the claim and said the company remains a “supply chain risk.”

Anthropic told CNET via email that it disagreed with Boguslaw’s piece, saying the headline and framing were inaccurate. “Anthropic is not — and has never said it is — ‘building a predictive surveillance system to monitor activists.’ This is a physical-security function focused on keeping our employees safe, the same as any large company with a global workforce.”

Drawing from postings and interviews with senior security officials at Anthropic, Boguslaw’s report lays out how the AI company is tracking activists who oppose the rapid development of AI near “physical Anthropic assets.” In July, the AI company also told The Wall Street Journal that it made routine reports to police departments about threats against employees, and monitored behavior in an effort to “catch escalation patterns early.”

It all ties together with a recent Anthropic job posting for an “enterprise intelligence specialist,” which describes the role as identifying, tracking and investigating “global threats including geopolitical instability, terrorism, crime, activism, nation-state targeting of the AI sector, and emerging security trends.”

Anthropic did not dispute the wording of the job posting, but said the inclusion of “activism” in the list was just “one of many threat categories a security team monitors for employee-safety purposes.”

Anthropic appears to be casting a wide net to monitor alleged threats. Weiquan Lin/Getty Images

As the backlash over AI ramps up — especially around data centers and automated license plate readers like Flock — the trend of predictive policing also continues to grow. Dubbed “precrime” in sci-fi movies like Minority Report, this kind of crime forecasting has become increasingly integrated into police departments. Algorithmic software and AI tools analyze historical crime data, arrest records and individual “risk scores” to preemptively target criminal activity.

In Anthropic’s case, the company has access to vast amounts of data through its Claude AI chatbot and other intelligence-gathering tools, leading it to report individuals to the police while refusing to share proof of threats or wrongdoing, according to The San Francisco Standard. Also, as Reddit users quickly noticed, Anthropic updated its privacy policy this summer to make it easier to share conversation data with police on its own determination, rather than waiting for a court order.

These reports allege that Anthropic could be bypassing standard legal protocols, not only by reporting “precrimes” without due process but also by withholding evidence from law enforcement.

‘Precogs are never wrong, but occasionally they do disagree’

Precrime’s problem is simple — what happens if someone is innocent? Fox/Getty Images

While today’s AI companies don’t have telepaths in a vat (we don’t think), they do have something similar to rely on — powerful AI agents that can glean personal details in the blink of an eye. Because artificial intelligence models process vast streams of user inputs, it’s virtually impossible for us to know how much of our personal data is harvested. And that’s not the only worrying part. Once that information enters the system, we lose control over where it ends up and who ultimately consumes it.

Anthropic has ways of tracking content in the various versions of Claude AI, sometimes to disastrous results, like broadcasting shared chatbot conversations on Google. Claude was reported to have been secretly monitoring Chinese users this summer, and its agents have also gained unauthorized access to the system data of various private organizations.

The question is over how much access Anthropic’s AI has to social media, forums and similar platforms. Current versions of Claude appear unable to gather data from private accounts, though they can from publicly available social profiles. Likewise, if an email account is directly connected to Claude with opt-in permissions, Anthropic could scrape that data for training and other purposes. Couldn’t that info theoretically be used to track activists and dissidents?

Anthropic’s latest September 2026 threat intelligence report shows how it monitors Claude to detect “malicious activity” like “influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud.” The company says it has an obligation to disclose such risks to make AI models safer.

But the company’s interactions with law enforcement and the findings in Boguslaw’s report raise questions about where Anthropic, a private company, will draw the line between malicious activity and mere anti-AI activism.
